The Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.
Volume Number 17:
The Śrītantrasāra.
Composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, the illustrious Abhinavagupta.
In the Pratividyāprakāśa (Research) Office established by the illustrious Pratāpasiṃha, the great king of Kaśmīra and the sun of the Dharma of Śrī Bhārata.

This was compiled by the Superintendent, Mahāmahopādhyāya Paṇḍita Mukundarāma Śāstrī, with the assistance of other scholars stationed at the designated office, following its collection, critical editing, pagination, numbering, and the addition of explanatory notes and other refinements.
It has been published, printed at the Nirnaya Sagar Press in Mumbai, after being presented in a modern, accessible, and refined style approved by Western scholarly circles.
In the Christian year 1918,
at Śrīnagara in Kashmir,
[he followed] the path of correct reasoning as instructed by the preeminent gurus, beginning with the venerable Śrīkaṇṭhanātha.

Having attained its perfect formulation in this very land from the non-dualism of Śiva, the doctrine of Īśvarādvaita has spread from Kaśmīra with its manifest fragrance, delighting all people in this country like the diffusion of saffron; may it bring joy to the virtuous. (1)
Cross swiftly the ocean of saṃsāra; establish your unwavering footing in the supreme state, which is overflowing with the joy of eternal light.
Contemplate the nectar-like essence of the realization of non-duality as taught by Śiva.
[It is] that which, through its powerfully manifesting and immediate reasoning, causes an internal leaping-up [of realization]. ||2||
Oṃ tat sat! Salutation to Śambhu, whose body is the self-awareness of one's own nature.
Now begins the *Tantrasāra*.
Composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, the venerable Abhinavagupta. The First Chapter.
The Great Mother, the source of ever-new creation, who rests upon the pure creative power (vimalakalā).

May my heart— the family of the nectar of the Absolute (anuttara), consisting of the emission of the state that flashes forth from the union of those two, whose body is full and whose splendor is concealed by five faces— throb intensely; [O Vimalā, may it throb for me, my very self].

May the Heart—the true reality denoted by such terms as "Jagadānanda" (Bliss of the Universe) and so forth—manifest; may it blossom by being devoid of limitation in the three periods of time. To the question of what that [Heart] is like, he says: "From the union of those two.

It is that whose nature is the state of equilibrium between them, and whose being has manifested from the friction [of their union], being independent of anything else and thus arising from itself alone.
That whose nature is an emission (*visarga*) that has surged upward externally, possessing an awakened existence—that is the "Unsurpassed Nectar Family" (*anuttarāmṛtakula*).

This means that its family (*kula*), or body, is unsurpassed (*anuttara*) and supreme (*utkṛṣṭa*), and wherein death (*mṛta*) does not exist; it is the essential nature of the digit (*kalā*) known as *Amā*.

He expresses both of these with the words "the Mother and the Father. That *kalā* (power) whose impurities and limitations have departed—characterized by agency whose sole nature is supreme *vimarśa* (reflexive awareness)—is her support, object, and essential form;
the meaning is that she is of the nature of the power of pure sovereignty (*śuddhasvātantrya*). For this very reason:

She is she whose splendor is characterized by absolute fullness within the primordial, ever-new, and great creation on the path of the Pure Way (*śuddhādhvan*). And what is her progenitor like? He is one whose body is filled (*bharitatanu*), meaning his nature is complete due to the absence of all desire; that is to say, he is autonomous because he does not look toward anything else.

For this very reason, he is one whose *ruci*— the desire directed toward the fivefold cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*)— is protected by the powers (*śakti*) that are his faces, consisting of the energies of consciousness (*cit*) and so forth, and which persist as a continuous stream. Furthermore, [he honors] the mother of the author Abhinavagupta, named Vimalā, and the one called Narasiṃhagupta.
The term "Janaka" (the progenitor) refers to the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of those two as well, because they consist of the immersion (*samāveśa*) of Śiva and Śakti. ||1||
The *Tantrāloka*, with its extensive threads [of exposition], cannot be fathomed—that is, discerned—by everyone;

that is, by those who have not undergone the labor of mastering the sharp sciences of logic (*tarka*). Its language is straightforward, for here "straightforwardness" consists in the absence of sharp logic. It is not at all possible for everyone to penetrate it.
Therefore, listen to this *Tantrasāra*, composed of straightforward words. ||2||

The contraction [of my intellect] has been dispelled by the light falling from the feet of the sun-like Śrī Śambhunātha—[for Śrī Śambhunātha is indeed the author’s guru who instructed him in the Trika scriptures;
he is both the Sun as the Supreme Self and the Sun as the physical luminary]. His feet are knowledge and action, and his rays are the [feet themselves].
By their descent, through the radiance of its flashing light and by the blossoming of its own true nature free from contraction,
the lotus-heart of Abhinavagupta shone forth; for just as a lotus blooms at the falling of the sun's rays, so did his heart blossom through the splendor of the feet of the venerable Śambhunātha.

By implication, this also includes the scripture (śāstra) that has emerged from it. Through this, it is described by way of a figurative turn (*bhaṅgyā*) that the very nature of this Light is its own self-reflection (*svarūpa-vimarśa*). Therefore, discern this:
the worship of the Great Lord is the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) [of Him] as one's own Self; for that purpose, there is this analytical investigation (*vivecana*).

The meaning is that the fruit is the recognition of Maheśvara. For once Maheśvarahood is attained, what need is there for any other fruit? This is the intended sense. [The reading is *prabhāvagatasaṃkocam*].
O you who seek to worship the Great Lord, pluck this lotus-heart of Abhinavagupta! (3)

In this context, knowledge—[knowledge whose nature is the manifestation of the Fullness]—is the cause of liberation, because it is the opposite of ignorance, which is the cause of bondage. [As the opposite of ignorance, knowledge is the cause of liberation;
for in reality, a relationship of cause and effect between these two is not possible.]

The Śaiva Siddhānta maintains that liberation is indeed the full manifestation of one’s own nature in every respect; however, unlike the Naiyāyikas, powers such as knowledge and the rest are not admitted to exist as distinct from it. As it has been said: "Liberation is indeed nothing other than the manifestation of one's own essential nature."

"And the nature of the self is consciousness... [Thus it is said. Furthermore, ignorance is twofold: residing in the intellect (*buddhi*) and belonging to the person (*pauruṣa*). Among these, that which resides in the intellect has the nature of non-determination;
[non-determination is the ignorance of the real nature. It consists of erroneous determination.

[The conceit of self in that which is not-self is a perverted certainty. Furthermore, the human [condition], whose nature is conceptualization and which consists of contracted manifestation, is itself the root cause of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra);
this we shall explain in the *Malanirṇaya*. In that regard, human ignorance is [removed] by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth. [It is given...]
"The latent impression of the bound soul (paśu) perishes through the presence of knowledge"—such is the definition of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Even though [rites] such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) continue to exist as residual traces from the beginning, they may indeed cease; however, initiation itself is not possible as long as there remains ignorance (*ajñāna*), which consists of a state of non-determination within the intellect (*buddhi*).
Because initiation— which consists of the purification of reality and union with Śiva— is preceded by the determination of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, in that context,
knowledge consisting of ascertainment and residing in the intellect (*buddhi*) alone is primary; and that very [knowledge] is...
Even human effort, when practiced, destroys ignorance, because the practice of consciousness consisting of conceptual thought culminates in non-conceptual consciousness;
for the Self, whose nature is Śiva, is of the essence of the light of consciousness that is uncontracted by conceptual thought.
Thus, in every respect, knowledge that is focused on all things and consists of right ascertainment is to be accepted;

and that [knowledge] is preceded by scripture [the remainder being that it is not to be reached through inference]. And scripture is authoritative only when spoken by the Supreme Lord. As for the matters taught in other scriptures, [they are not to be accepted].

[Regarding those things taught by the Buddhists, Vaiṣṇavas, and others in their respective traditions: because they are accepted there with distinctness, and because of the determination of what is established by reasoning beyond the meaning of those [traditions], [those meanings— namely,
those stated in other scriptures such as the Buddhist and Vaiṣṇava scriptures— are distinct and different from them].

The reasoning (*yukti*) consists in the determination of that which is called the *śivatattva*— the nature of the full and uncontracted expansion of consciousness— by means of investigating the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward all external and internal objects, such as blue, pleasure, and so forth.

Therefore, the knowledge taught in other scriptures liberates only from that much bondage, not from everything; however, the scripture of the Supreme Lord, consisting of the five currents (*pañcasrotas*)— namely, consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action— liberates from everything.

The five currents (*srotas*) consisting of the forms of Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Aghora constitute the scripture (*śāstra*) composed of them. There are ten Śiva-bheda divisions that express duality (*bheda*);
eighteen Rudra-bheda divisions that express both duality and non-duality (*bhedābheda*); and eight [Vāsudeva-bheda divisions] that express non-duality (*abheda*), multiplied by the eight Vasus.

There are sixty-four divisions of Bhairava. [This system is] divided into ten, eighteen, and eight [divisions]. Even more than all of those, the essence is the Trika scriptures (*ṣaḍardhaśāstra*). And even more than those, it is the *Mālinīvijaya*.
The meaning contained within that is impossible to describe exhaustively even by summarizing; nor is it...
The state of being liberated or the capacity to liberate belongs only to pure knowledge, because it is of that very nature for one who has not yet ascertained the reality of things.
Since the supreme human goal is rooted in well-practiced knowledge, this [treatise] is commenced for the sake of its accomplishment.
Regarding "ignorance" (*ajñāna*): the particle *kila* indicates the disagreement among all disputants. Ignorance is the falling away from one's own true nature (*svasvarūpapracyuti*).

In the scriptures, such as the *Śivasūtra*, that very ignorance is traditionally known as *mala*. It is divided into the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* types; thus, "all ignorance" refers to this threefold [ignorance] which must be uprooted.

By that same reason—the absence of even *saṃskāra*—it is declared in the scripture to be the cause of bondage; it is known as *mala*. Upon the arising of even a fraction of perfect knowledge, all of that goes to its very roots.

And when there arises the self-consciousness in which all impurities have been destroyed, liberation occurs; therefore, by means of this scripture, I shall reveal the entirety of that reality which is to be known.

The introduction (*upodghāta*): [The prefix *upa* means "near oneself"; *udghāta* refers to that which strikes like a hammer—the recognition of the Lord—whereby one rests; thus it is called *upodghāta*.
In this regard, here [in this philosophical system], intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone is the supreme object to be accepted, and that is...

The point is that for all entities, their very nature is manifestation (*prakāśa*) alone, and not blue or other such qualities. Since it is impossible for that which is non-manifestation to possess the nature of manifestation—[for if something were non-manifest in nature, how could it ever appear; and how could such a thing have manifestation as its own essence?]—and since that manifestation is not manifold, [it is one].

Regarding the impossibility of light entering into a nature other than its own: [the sense is that if light were to enter into a form other than its own, then it would possess duality, just as the form of clay possesses duality through the entry of the form of a jar.]

Because there is no difference in its essential nature (*svabhāva*), neither space nor time can be its differentiators, since they too have the nature of being manifested by it; thus, light (*prakāśa*) is one alone, and that itself is consciousness (*saṃvit*), for consciousness is indeed the manifestation of objects— of this all are without dispute.
And that light is not dependent; for dependence consists precisely in being illuminated, and being illuminated necessarily requires another light.
Since there is no other light whatsoever, light is one and independent. And because of this very independence, being devoid of limitations by space, time, and form, it is all-pervading and eternal.

Its nature consists of both all forms and the absence of form; its sovereignty is the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*); its wonder is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*); its luminous nature is the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*); its essence of self-reflection is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*);
and its union with all forms is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Thus, although it is endowed with these primary powers in reality...

He who is endowed with the powers of will, knowledge, and action, who is the undivided Light, resting in his own bliss, is Śiva himself. By his absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), manifesting himself as contracted, he is called the *aṇu* (the limited soul).
Furthermore, he again manifests his own self through his sovereignty, by which—

It manifests precisely as the nature of Śiva, whose light is uninterrupted. Even there, by virtue of its sovereignty, it manifests itself either without means (*anupāya*) or with means (*sopāya*). Regarding the state of having means, there is a threefold division—namely, will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), or action (*kriyā*)—according to the distinctions of the Śāmbhava, Śākta, and Āṇava [paths].
In this context, these fourfold forms of immersion (*samāveśa*) are taught in succession.
This Śiva, whose very body is light, is the autonomous Self; by the impetuous play of His sovereignty, He [reveals] His own essential nature.
That which, having been completely covered, is again made manifest in its fullness—either through the power of succession and non-succession, or else by way of the threefold division. ||5||
This Self, whose nature is luminosity like a shadow, spontaneously presents its own form;
then, it suddenly reveals the essence of Śiva through the ultimate truth, either instantaneously or by way of gradual stages.
This very hope, O self-reliant one, is independent; it is a drum-beat, a sound, a roar.
Again, O protector, it is a sudden burst, a thundering, a movement of desire.
The nectar of Śiva is for those who seek the ultimate goal.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Divisions of Consciousness," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 1.
Now begins the second chapter.
Now, we shall first explain that which is indeed without means (anupāya)— [here, as in the expression "a girl with no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*), the negative particle *nañ* has the sense of "little"].

When, indeed, pierced by a firm descent of power (*śaktipāta*), he himself discerns in this way, having grasped the Guru’s word all at once, then— being devoid of further means (meaning: devoid of the means to be described hereafter,
for he is "himself")— he is eternally awakened.

[This is] immersion (*samāveśa*). If it is asked, "In this context, how does one discern that reasoning (*tarka*) alone is a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*)?", it is said: Regarding this Supreme Lord, who is one's own self (*svātmā*) and whose nature is self-luminous—what could be accomplished by a means? It is not the attainment of His essential nature (*svarūpa*), because He is eternal.
Cognition, because it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśamānatvāt*),
does not consist in the removal of an obscuration, since no obscuration whatsoever is possible;
nor does it consist in the penetration of such an obscuration, since there is no distinct entity that could penetrate it.
And what is the means here? Since even that [means] is untenable as something distinct,

therefore all this is one single reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātratattva*), unmeasured by time, undivided by space, unfaded by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), unrestricted by forms, and undefined by words.

The reading is *asaṃdaṣṭam*. That independent reality—which is not elaborated by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which exists from time onwards up to the limit of the means of knowledge, and which obtains its own nature solely by its own will—and which is precisely that "I," wherein the entire universe is reflected within me as something firmly established; thus [it is].

For one who discerns [the truth] at all times, the immersion into the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-samāveśa*) is indeed without means (*nirupāyaka*); nor does it have any restriction such as mantras, worship, meditation, or conduct. [Restriction (*niyantraṇā*) is the rule that "this should be done" and "this should not be done. There is no such constraint whatsoever.
"A web of skillful means does not reveal the auspicious; for what can a jar illuminate the thousand-rayed sun?
Thus did he of noble vision discern.
One shall enter, in an instant, the self-luminous Śiva.
"Wherever the vibration of the shadow manifests, that entire Pure Supreme Lord shines within me;
knowing that He alone is the Self in the ultimate sense, there is no further task to be done. Abandon, abandon all vibration!
That entire universe is the Supreme Lord;
it is spoken of as the pure Self. O dancer, He is Śiva, the ultimate reality.
O friend, there is no work whatsoever that remains to be done.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Anupāya," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, the Śāmbhavopāya.
When, within that aforementioned Śiva-principle which is of the nature of light, [the mind enters] into the undivided sphere—

When one is unable to enter [into that state], then by perceiving the very power of autonomy as supreme— [the sense being that the nature of a reality does not actually exceed its own being, even through the mere conceptualization of it as "supreme"]— one experiences the non-conceptual immersion into Bhairava; and this is his instruction.
This entire collection of phenomena is a mere reflection within the sky of awakening, because it possesses the characteristics of a reflection.

For this is the characteristic of a reflection: that which appears as distinct yet lacks the capacity for independent existence, appearing only through its intermingling with others. As it has been said: [citation].
Ah, let the face reflect; let the mirror likewise reflect it.
But that in which the mirror itself reflects must also be known.
Thus it is said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
"In this way, a form appears similarly within the eyes, a mirror, the sky, and water;
for indeed, within a clear medium, it is the form itself that is manifested."

A woman secretly filled with passion does not find satisfaction even while touching with her jar-like breasts a mirror made beautiful by the reflection of her beloved; it is like the form of a lover in a mirror, or like the aesthetic flavor (rasa) in the water of the mouth.
Like fragrance in the sense of smell, like the touch of a couple in the organ of bliss, or like the touch of a spear, a trident, and so forth, in the internal tactile organ,
or like an echo in space— that is not the primary flavor (rasa).

Because its effects, such as the alleviation of disease, are not observed [therein]; nor are smell and touch primary qualities of that substratum, because in the absence of those [qualities], they would be impossible and because they do not initiate a series of effects. Nor is it the case that they do not exist, since we observe the dusting of the body and excretion; and sound also is not primary, for no one says "it speaks."

Because it is heard like an echo as if it were approaching; thus, just as this reflection appears, so too does the universe appear within the light of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-prakāśa). [Note: The reading *bimba-pratibimba* is found in manuscript k; the reading *parameśvara-svarūpaṃ nānā spaṣṭam* is found in manuscript kh.]

Now, one might ask: what could this "original object" (*bimba*) be here—[the characteristic of an original object being such that it appears as something unmixed and independent, like a face]? Let it be nothing at all.
But then, is it without a cause? Ah, in that case, the question of its cause arises: what is it?
By the logic of the reflection, the cause will be none other than the power of the Supreme Lord, which is synonymous with absolute freedom (svātantrya);
and because He bears the reflection of the universe, the Blessed One possesses the nature of being the Self of the universe,
for the universe is indeed composed of consciousness (saṃvit).

Since it is the locus of the manifestation of consciousness, this very universe is here perceived [within Him]; thus, His state of being the bearer of reflections is His nature as the Supreme Lord, whose essence is consciousness,
and that nature remains ungrasped [as distinct from Himself].

Because the non-apprehension of one's own nature is logically untenable. For if there were no apprehension of one's own nature, there would in reality be nothing but insentience (*jaḍatā*). Furthermore, this apprehension is not merely conventional; rather, it is said to be inherent in the supreme primordial sound (*paranāda*), being inseparable from the very essence of consciousness itself. And that...

He contemplates the entire collection of powers of the Supreme Lord, which is as vast as that which establishes the universal order—as expressed in the statement "His powers are the entire universe"—and which constitutes the power of those energies to establish the universal order.
Among these, there are primarily three powers of the Supreme Lord: Anuttara...

"Will" (*icchā*) and "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*): this triad of reflective awarenesses is *a-ha-u*. From this very triad, the entire expansion of powers (*śaktiprapañca*) is articulated. For bliss is indeed repose within the Absolute (*anuttara*), and it resides precisely within Will.
(The definition of the power of Will is as follows:)

In this collision, that reflective awareness which consists of the nature of consciousness and so forth is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). [It is] rest (*viśrānti*), sovereignty (*īśana*), and unfolding (*unmeṣa*). As it has been said:
That self-reflection which previously existed as the solitary hero (ekavīraka) is proclaimed as the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), whose nature is the unfolding of the universe to be known. Indeed,
that very wave of rest, which is the commencement of the power of action (kriyāśakti), is itself this triad of reflective awarenesses.

The final triad of reflective awarenesses, being solar in nature, consists primarily of the bliss of repose and is lunar in nature to this extent, as long as there is no entry of the karmic portion [meaning that the aspect of the power of action is subordinate to the power of knowledge]. However, when—
In both desire and mastery, the object enters into the action— that which is desired and that which is mastered—
as it has been said:
"The power of will is said to be twofold, namely, the agitated and the unagitated."
For that object which is being desired would manifest in a twofold form. It is said:

then it has two divisions—the *la*-sound by way of mere manifestation, and the *ra*-sound by way of resting; for *ra* and *la* have the nature of manifestation and stability (where "stability" means firmness).

And that which is being desired is not manifest like an external object; for if it were of a manifest form, it would be a mere magical creation (*nirmāṇa*) rather than a desire or a sovereign power (*īśana*). Therefore, precisely because it is unmanifest, it is merely heard [and is not directly a phoneme].
There is no stable existence of *r* and *l* as there is for consonants.

This group of four phonemes—*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*—is neuter because it bears the shadow of both [the male and female principles], that is, because it possesses the nature of both the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*). For this very reason, the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* states: "It is like the interval between Narasiṃha and Vajrāsya. This refers to the two [phonemes] following the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*) and Bliss (*ānanda*).

When there is an outward flow toward desire (*icchā*) and the other powers, then there are the two phonemes *e* and *o*. Therein, moreover, from the union with the Absolute (*anuttara*) and Bliss (*ānanda*), there are the two phonemes *ai* and *au*. This is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and those same four phonemes are *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*. Then, once again, at the end of the power of action, everything—
This extends to the state of being the effect, up until one enters the Unsurpassed; and as it is said in the *Mālinī-vārttika*:
"Beginning from the Unsurpassed and ending with the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), such is this [sequence];
however, the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) itself abides in the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) through its lordship."
Grasping even a minute fraction of the state of manifestation, she has attained a state of being counted;
and that which consists of will and the rest [proceeds] from the union with the preceding and subsequent blisses.
Then, through the conjunction of initial coalescence (*ādiśleṣa*), the four diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) arise;
thereafter, from the attainment of the consciousness of one's own essential nature (*svarūpasaṃvitti*), the state beginning with the *bindu* is established.
Then, within that which possesses a form filled with the entire composition,
there is indeed the emission belonging to Śakti, which is known as "projection" (vikṣepa).
The seventeenth digit is the disjunction of emission itself;
in some cases, that same [digit] becomes the eighteenth through the application of further agitation.
This supreme Kaulikī Śakti, who is beyond the family (akula), is the ultimate power of the unsurpassed form that takes the shape of Parabhairava.
This very emission is that [Supreme Lord]; from it this world was born.
Its capacity for agitation is the emergence of the creative process of agitation.
Because it is devoid of the state of agitation and fullness, that sequence of Akula does not descend;
thus, it arises from the oscillation of self-reflection whose nature consists of the sixfold group.
Because its nature is unsurpassed, it is the unfolding of the very First One;
that alone is the Blessed Lord, whose essence eternally vibrates within.
He whose central power is filled with the flood of all internal states,
who is beautiful with the bliss of the universe arising from the nature of the agitation of his own will.
That union of Śiva and Śakti, eternally throbbing and beautiful with the essence of the full visarga, is designated as "affection" (sneha).
In this very state of the full emission (pūrṇavaisarga), in order to attain entry,
they practice the oral tradition beginning with licking, churning, and so forth.
For thus, presiding over the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), the supreme radiance animates the entire body by drawing from elsewhere the intensely agitated nectar.
That which attains the state of emission proceeds toward the wonder of bliss;
however, that [emission] alone is incomplete, whereas that which consists of the Lord is complete.
Therefore, this single power of emission unfolds;
it is emission itself that becomes agitated due to the doubling of effort.
"The letter *ha* is the progenitor of all consonants;
yet, through its union with the bindu, it again resorts to its own very ground, the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*). This state of 'So'ham' is what is intended here. Thus far for the previous [section].

By virtue of having consciousness as its essence, it exists as the mere luminosity, as the *bindu*, in the form of "A. Then, right there, the emission (*visarga*) of the Absolute (*anuttara*) arises as "Aḥ. Thus, the sixteenfold nature of the seeds of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is described. Arising from that... [kh]

The reading is "tad uktam" (it has been said). That which consists of phonemes (*vyañjana*) is the form of the womb (*yonirūpa*). In that regard: "For thus, from *Akula*, the first group [of consonants], consisting of the power of the word (*padaśakti*), has arisen;
and after that, from *Icchā*, whose form is not yet fully manifested."

Following that [the letter *ka*], there are two beginning with *ṭa* and *ta* for those who resort to fire and earth; then those beginning with *ṣa* arise from the unfolding (*unmeṣa*). Thus, the stops (*sparśa*) are proclaimed.
The power of will (icchā-śakti) is twofold, according as it is agitated or unagitated by its own nature;
when it is oriented toward that which consists of a portion of a heterogeneous power, it moves toward that [object].
That very [consciousness], when its objects of knowledge have been more rapidly acquired and it is stained by turbidity,
undergoes the states of *ratva* and *latva* due to its orientation toward heterogeneous [objects].
In the same way, the power of unfolding (unmeṣa-śakti), which possesses two forms, enters the power of Vaijrāti;
it attains the state of the letter *va*, which sets in motion the essence of emanation.

Thus, in the *Mālinī-vārttika* itself: from the Absolute (*anuttara*) comes the *ka*-group; from Faith (*śraddhā*), that is, Will (*icchā*), comes the *ca*-group; from Will accompanied by action come the two groups, *ṭa* and *ta*; from Expansion (*unmeṣa*) comes the *pa*-group; and through union with the fivefold Power (*śakti-pañcaka*), there is the state of being fivefold.

From the threefold Will (icchā) alone arise the letters *ya*, *ra*, and *la*; from the Unfolding (unmeṣa) comes the letter *va*; from the threefold Will alone come *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*; from the Emission (visarga) comes the letter *ha*; and the letter *kṣa* is born from the union of the womb (*yoni*). Thus, this Blessed One is indeed the Absolute (anuttara) himself in the form of the Lord of Kula (kuleśvara). And his is the one Kauliki power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), by which—

From the form of bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*) onwards, up to this much—the external creation—the reflective awarenesses of the classes of consonants (*varga*), beginning with *ka* (or as the reading goes, *kakāra* etc. and *kavarga* etc.), which are the pulsations [of consciousness], have attained the state of being external principles (*tattva*). [The vowels from *a* to the visarga constitute the Śiva-principle.]

The five gross elements (bhūta-pañcaka), beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṅa*, starting from earth (*dharā*) and ending with ether (*nabhaḥ*); the five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka), beginning with *ca* and ending with *ña*, starting from smell (*gandha*) and ending with sound (*śabda*); the five organs of action (karmendriya-pañcaka), beginning with *ṭa* and ending with *ṇa*, starting from the feet (*pāda*) and ending with the organ of excretion (*vāk*); and the five organs of perception (buddhīndriya-pañcaka), beginning with *ta* and ending with *na*, starting from the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) and ending with the sense of hearing (*śrotra*).

The five organs of cognition (buddhi-karaṇa-pañcaka); the group beginning with *ṣa* and ending with *ma*; the pentad known as mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and spirit (*puruṣa*); the principles (*tattva*) known as attachment (*rāga*), knowledge (*vidyā*), limited agency (*kalā*), and illusion (*māyā*), which are denoted by the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *va*; and those internal ones called "retentions" (*dhāraṇā*)—these all sustain [the body].
They are called *dhāraṇās* because one conceives of them as being separate entities. And this very emission (*visarga*) is threefold, beginning with the *āṇava*. As it was stated previously:
"Having first emitted everything that is to be done into the fire of emptiness..."
This state known as the repose of the mind (*cittaviśrānti*) is proclaimed as the *āṇava* [means]. That which consists of the repose of the mind is the *śākta*;

that characterized by the awakening of the mind is the *śāmbhava*; and that which consists of the dissolution of the mind is likewise [the *śāmbhava*]. Thus, emission (*visarga*) itself is the power (*śakti*) of the Lord in the generation of the universe. In this way, within this [extent]... [Note: *kh* reads *iyati* as an alternative reading.]

And: when the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) occurs precisely as undivided, then the one Lord alone is both the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) and the power (*śakti*) through the state of being seed and womb (*bījayonitayā*). When there is a distinct reflective awareness of the eight [phonemes], this occurs in conjunction with the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*), which means in conjunction with the phoneme *kṣa*.

In the group of nine, when each individual reflective awareness (parāmarśa) is predominant, there is a nature consisting of fifty. Even there, when the possible distinctions of parts are reflected upon—[the parts being in the form of half-morae (ardhamātrā)]—there is a nature consisting of eighty-one. In reality, however, there are only six reflective awarenesses.
By way of expansion and reabsorption, there are twelve: when [the Absolute] has expanded in the form of the supreme bliss, desire, and so forth, there are six;
and when it again reabsorbs into desire and the others, there are the six beginning with *e*. Therefore...

"Excluding the neuter vowels, there are twelve. Thus, you sustain the Supreme Lord’s state of being filled with universal power (*viśvaśakti*). Since these very powers consist of the nature of self-reflection (*aparāmarśa*), they are the divine Śrī Kālikās. [They are called *Kālikās* because they "measure" (*kalayanti*) and "proceed" (*kramante*). As it has been said:]

"Because they consist of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), through their connection with emission (*visarga*) and withdrawal (*ākṣepa*), and because of the knowledge that calculates their measure (*iyattā*), they are sometimes called *kālikās*. Thus they have been defined.

And these, being of the nature of power (*śakti*), are pure reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) within the state of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), existing as both supreme (*parā*) and non-supreme (*aparā*).
Due to the contraction caused by the mere unfolding of Māyā, they assume the forms of the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras— or as another reading has it, the forms of the Mantras. Furthermore, within Māyā...
Those [phonemes] which, having manifested as distinct divisions, assume the state of being phonemes of *māyā*,

and having attained the status of being functional within *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*, culminate in the attainment of the nature of external objective reality— they are the phonemes of *māyā*.
Furthermore, because they are like a body— meaning that the phonemes belonging to Māyā are like a body devoid of a soul,
whereas their reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is like a soul, for otherwise they would be ineffective— the sense is that when they are perceived,
and when... [their function occurs].

When a reanimation is effected by these aforementioned pure reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), which stand in the place of life, then they become endowed with vitality; and such being the case, they bestow both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus, [the state] consists solely of resting within all reflective awarenesses.

For one who perceives the Self as containing within it the reflection of all categories (*tattva*), elements (*bhūta*), and worlds (*bhuvana*), there arises liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) through the Śāmbhava immersion (*samāveśa*) characterized by non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*). Here, too, as before, there is no constraint whatsoever such as the use of mantras and so forth.
Just as the entire universe shines within itself here through its manifold arrangement, like a variegated design within a mirror,
so too does consciousness shine forth solely by following the savor of its own self-reflection.
Thus is the reading; there are alternative readings such as *vimarśanasārayuktyā* and *sārayogāt*.
However, a mirror does not reflect the universe in that same way.

[In this mirror of stainless consciousness, this reflection shines forth as the truth— the entire vibrating essence of one’s own nature, its form released through the secret savor of contemplative awareness. *saṃvedaṇa* (consciousness).
In the stainless mirror,
the entire radiance is insubstantial;
it is impetuous with the savor of the act of beholding.
The beautiful form shines forth with its own luster.

[Having heard this, he who unites his own stainless self, which consists of all things, with that [Bhairava], becomes Supreme Bhairava and attains supreme bliss. Having heard this— his own self, which consists of all things.
Whoever meditates on the Self becomes the Supreme Bhairava and attains the supreme state.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Śāmbhava Means" (or, according to the reading in manuscripts *k* and *g*, "The Illumination of the Supreme Means"), in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now follows the means of power (*śāktopāya*).

In this regard, when one gradually refines conceptual thought— refinement being the production of further qualities, which occurs through the varying degrees of excellence in practice— in order to enter the nature just described:

At that time, there is the utility of the stages of cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*), preceded by sound reasoning, authentic scripture, and the instructions of a true guru. For it is precisely through the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that living beings imagine themselves to be bound;
that conceit (*abhimāna*) is the cause of obstruction to *saṃsāra*. [In the manuscript *kh*, "saṃsārapratibandhahetuḥ" appears as "saṃsāraprabandheti," where *prabandha* means continuity.]

The reading "saṃtatiḥ" is provided as a synonym. Therefore, the conceptual construction (vikalpa) that arises in its opposite form shatters the conceptual construction that is the cause of saṃsāra; thus, it is the cause of spiritual prosperity (abhyudaya). And that [conceptual construction] is of such a nature that it transcends all the principles (tattvas), from those of limited nature up to Śiva.
That very [reality], whose nature is undivided pure consciousness alone, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);

it is the locus for the establishment of all things, the vitality (*oja*) of the universe, by which the universe breathes; and that indeed am I. Therefore, I am both transcendent to the universe and the self of the universe. And this is...

It does not arise for those blinded by illusion because of the absence of right reasoning (*sattarka*) and the like; for the Vaiṣṇavas and others are restricted by the principle of attachment (*rāga-tattva*) within the scripture (*āgama*) to that extent alone, and thus they do not turn toward even the higher vision (*ūrdhvadarśana*). Therefore...
They are indeed haters of right reasoning, the authentic scriptures, and the instructions of the true Guru. As it is said in the *Pārameśvara*:
"All those such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others are colored by attachment to their own limited knowledge;
deprived of the wisdom of the Omniscient One, they do not find the supreme reality. [Kh: ...the Omniscient One]
The reading is "sarvaśaktikam."

Thus, therefore, only those who have been pierced by the firm *śaktipāta* of Śambhu purify their conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) through the sequence of the true scriptures and so forth; for as it is said regarding the purification of conceptual thought: "Just as a conceptual thought, once purified, gives rise to another conceptual thought that has been purified by its own nature."
He too [creates] one equal to himself; he too another; and he too yet another of similar nature.
"Unmanifested, becoming manifest; fully manifested, consisting of manifestation," and so forth.
[Thus they] enter the supreme essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, one might object: "In this way, would not the supreme reality (*tattva*) take on the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
Not so; for conceptual construction consists merely in the association with the latent impression (*adhivāsa*) of duality.

Since the supreme reality, having already accomplished its purpose, is self-luminous everywhere in every form, no conceptual construction (vikalpa) therein serves for anyone’s benefit or refutation. In that regard,
for one who has been pierced by an exceedingly firm descent of power (śaktipāta), a correct reasoning (sattarka) arises spontaneously as a matter of natural attainment (sāṃsiddhika).

It is said that one is initiated by the goddesses. We shall explain in detail, in the *Śaktipātaprakāśana*, [the initiation] of another according to the sequence of the scriptures (*āgama*), and so forth; however, the function of the scripture lies in the determination of the arrival of the Guru.

The function [of reasoning] consists in the arising of appropriate conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) which are based on the production of a continuous stream of that same kind, free from doubt. Such a continuous stream of conceptual constructions is called "correct reasoning" (*sattarka*).

And that very [stream] is also termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), because by means of it, even though an object is real, it is cultivated as if it were unreal until it becomes clear; for it brings about clarity through its lack of clarity [in previous stages].
And here, there is no other limb of yoga apart from *sattarka* (correct reasoning), which is of the nature of the light of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
[The limbs of yoga are: breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), meditation (*dhyāna*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*)].
Reasoning and meditative concentration—this is called the six-limbed yoga.

Thus, these are well-known from those scriptures. Directly, austerity (*tapas*) and so forth constitute the category of observances (*niyama*), while non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest constitute the types of restraints (*yama*). [Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—these are the *yamas*.]

Since the category of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), beginning with inhalation (pūraka) and so forth, is restricted solely to the object of knowledge, what kind of operation could it possibly have upon consciousness? Even withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) would merely bring excellence to the level of the instruments [of perception];
and even meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and absorption (samādhi), though accomplished through a successive order of practice, [function in the same manner].

They would cause the meditator to attain identity with the object of meditation. Furthermore, practice (*abhyāsa*) is simply not possible regarding the supreme reality, which is one's own nature as Śiva. For practice consists of fixing the vital breath, intellect, and body—which have already become rooted in consciousness—upon that very consciousness. Indeed, [that which resides in consciousness...]

Practice consists of performing that which is grounded in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. But in the case of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), since there is nothing whatsoever to be acquired or discarded, how can there be practice? If you ask, "Is it not possible even through reasoning?"—it has been stated in this regard:

This is precisely the method for dispelling the latent impression (*adhivāsa*) of duality, and nothing else. Even in worldly practice, the purpose of cultivation (*abhyāsa*) consists in manifesting the desired form of each respective body and so forth by means of their nature as the conscious self (*cidātman*), while simultaneously subduing their other forms. But in the supreme reality (*paratattva*), there is nothing [to be cultivated].
It has been stated that [duality] is to be discarded. Indeed, even that which is called "residence in duality" is not some separate, ontologically real entity;

rather, it is merely the non-apprehension of one's own true nature (*svarūpākhyāti*). Therefore, since it is said that the discarding of duality is performed through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), this ultimate reality is one's own true nature.

The state of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), while being manifest, is itself grasped through its own sovereignty; then, having gradually cast that aside, it becomes oriented toward unfolding, then unfolds, and finally unfolds fully—it manifests according to this sequence.
Likewise, such manifestation is the very nature of the Supreme Lord. Therefore, the limbs of yoga do not apply here.
This is the direct means (*sākṣād-upāya*). However, they may even favor reasoning (*tarka*), as it has been said: "But here, O Goddess of Gods, this is prescribed as a rule:
the mind must be made firm in reality (*tattva*)."...

By the reasoning stated in such passages, [reasoning] serves as an auxiliary to logic (*tarka*). Likewise, even practices such as the *yamas* (restraints) are means for accomplishing those various forms of reasoning. Thus, correct reasoning alone is the direct means therein; that itself is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), and it becomes refined through many modes.

For example, sacrifice, oblation, recitation, vow, and yoga—in these, the abiding of all entities (or, according to the reading, "of all possible entities") is in the Supreme Lord alone; there is nothing else that exists as distinct from Him. Thus, for the sake of establishing the firm conviction (*vikalparūḍhi*) [in this truth], the offering of all entities is made into the Supreme Lord alone.
And that sacrifice, because it is dear to the heart,
is easily accomplished for those who spontaneously resort to entering into pure consciousness;
with this intention, regarding those things which are dear to the heart, it has been said:

"Whatever is pleasing to the mind, regardless of where the senses are directed, when it is joined to the true abode of Brahman, that indeed becomes an instrument of worship. Thus, the external application of flowers, libations, perfumes, and so forth has been described. All things [are thus transformed].

The term "consisting of the splendor of the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvaratejomaya*) is used to establish the conventional conceptualization [of the fire]. The "oblation" (*homa*) is the dissolution of all phenomena, which occurs simultaneously with their reduction to that alone which is its splendor—that is, within the splendor of the fire of the consciousness of the Supreme Lord, which is intent upon the relish of swallowing all existing things. As it has been said:
When the fire known as awakening— dense with the massed tufts of the flames of the seven sense-faculties—
is kindled, the reduction of the category of phenomena to ashes is the propitiation of that fire.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, elsewhere it is stated:
"Wherever there is fuel, even if that forest of duality is death itself, we constantly worship with that extraordinary sacrifice. Likewise:

For the sake of the arising of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that which consists of both [subject and object], and without depending on differentiated entities such as external or internal objects of knowledge, that supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvaṃ*), which is one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), is thus internally reflected upon; this is *japa*. As it has been said:
"Whatever one may do, provided it is rooted in this uncontrived state ascended within the heart—whether breathing or even reflecting—that is all considered his *japa*.
Thus, in every case and at all times, it is for the sake of attaining the identification with the Supreme Lord who is beyond all means (*nirupāya*). [Note: *kh* reads *nirapāya*].

[The reading: The observance (*vrata*) consists in regarding even one’s own body, as well as objects such as a jar, with the same sense of identity as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). As it is stated in the *Śrīnandiśikhā*: "Supreme equality toward all things is the highest observance."

Thus, that innate ultimate reality which shines forth— unconditioned by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)— by means of such diverse conceptualizations that are themselves aspects of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*); for the sake of its ascent into the state of being nothing but that eternal, such manifestation, there is the practice consisting of the contemplation of its own nature.
Yoga is a specific kind of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). In this context, the Supreme Lord has the nature of perfect consciousness;
his fullness itself is his power (*śakti*), his *kula*, his capacity, and his wave. As it is said:
"That which is a slight vibration, yet a manifestation that is non-different [from itself]—this much alone is [the essence]."
"This is a wave of the ocean of awakening; consciousness does not exist without it. Thus, as for the heart, it has been said:
"Because its nature is reflective awareness (parāmarśa), that which is its own inherent resonance (dhvani)..."

"That which is eternally arisen is said to be the supreme and great Heart. Spanda is the essence, and Vibhūti is the *Triśikā*—the sovereign (*īśikā*) of the three powers (will, knowledge, and action).
The teachers also read it as *Triṃśikā*, due to the similarity in the description of its syllables.

She is designated by various names in the terminology of the Āgamas— such as Kālī, Karṣaṇī, Caṇḍī, Vāṇī, Bhoga, Dṛk, Nityā, and so forth— which are applied according to their respective etymological meanings,
so that She may abide in the hearts of those who meditate upon Her in those various forms. And she [is known] through the manifestation of her totality of power (*samagra-śaktitā*).

The consciousness of fullness shines forth, and its powers are innumerable. What need is there for more? Whatever constitutes this universe, those are the powers of this [one whose nature is the consciousness of fullness].
How could they possibly be taught? For the universe is contained within three [powers], by which this [universe] is encompassed.

The Supreme Lord bears, perceives, and illumines everything from Śiva down to the earth as being nothing other than the nature of undifferentiated pure consciousness; she is his venerable Parā-śakti. Furthermore, by means of which [power] he manifests [the universe] through both difference and non-difference—like an elephant reflected in a mirror—she is his venerable Parāparā-śakti. And by means of which [power] [he perceives it] with its constituent parts mutually distinct...

Through differentiation alone, she is his venerable Aparā-śakti. That Blessed One who, by means of her own nature as *anusandhāna* (synthetic contemplation), swallows up these threefold forms within herself through the act of embracing them, is indeed his Śrīparā herself.

These four powers, designated by such alternative names as Śrī, Mātṛsadbhāva, Kāla, and Karṣiṇī, each exist in three ways through their own sovereignty: in emission (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhāra). Thus, they become twelve. For instance: first, consciousness exists within itself...

1) He perceives the state; 2) then he perceives it clearly even externally; 3) having grasped its state of being permeated by passion (*raktimayatā*) right there, he then perceives that very same state with the desire to withdraw it within;
4) and then, the doubt that constitutes an obstacle to that withdrawal—[for doubt arises from the infinity of scriptures...]
Because one perceives the reversal of the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, there arises a state of confusion regarding what should be undertaken;
and she creates and devours—that which was said:
"She who consists of dissolution performs that withdrawal of all entities into herself."
"By means of which she indeed touches [the object], such that it flashes forth: 'I have swallowed this.

And thus, by withdrawing the portion consisting of the apprehension of being swallowed—that is, the portion consisting of the objective state (or, according to another reading, the "weight of the objective state")—she holds it within herself. Therefore, this is my state of being the withdrawer.

Even the notion "this is form" conceives of nothing other than its own inherent nature (svabhāva). Therefore, regarding the conception of the inherent nature of that which synthesizes [experience], it is said:
"Even when the flood of entities has been dissolved, she [the power of consciousness] likewise perceives some entity in that very same way."

"He who remains as the very form of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of doubt should cause [the object] to congeal. Thus, [this refers to] the persistence of some entity in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*),
while for another, it is the state of being reduced to pure consciousness alone.

8. Then, as an inseparable concomitant of the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), it manifests the wheel of instruments (*karaṇacakra*). 9. Then it also manifests the Lord of the Instruments (*karaṇeśvara*). 10. Then it also manifests the constructed form of the subject belonging to Māyā (*māyīya-pramātṛ*).
11. It also manifests the subject who delights in the grasping of expansion that is oriented toward the abandonment of contraction.
12. Then, perceiving even the unfolded form, these twelve divine consciousnesses arise—
whether directed toward a single subject or simultaneously, sequentially, in pairs, in threes,
and so forth— and revolving like a wheel, they manifest externally as well, in the sequence of months, digits (kalās), zodiac signs (rāśis), and so on.

Or finally, even those appearing in the sequence of jars, cloths, and so forth, nourish the sovereignty of the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*) and are denoted by the term "Śrī Kālī. As for *kalana* (the act of reckoning/dividing), it has been said: "In this way, when the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) is experienced, its instruments (*karaṇa*) are also [experienced]."

"Drawing them back, she manifests the twelve [powers] within the Self. Furthermore, these are: movement, projection, cognition, enumeration, enjoyment, sounding, and dissolution into one's own Self. As the venerable teachers, the Bhūtirājas, have said:
"From projection and from knowledge, Kālī [arises] through the power of differentiation...

Thus it is said. And this meaning should be observed in detail here and there in my own composed commentaries, such as the *Prakaraṇastotra* and others. This is not an extreme secret that should be disclosed in one place alone, nor...

"In every respect this must be kept secret," so indeed our teachers have said. Therefore, that which has been described as sacrifice, oblation, and so forth, should be understood as pertaining only to such a Maheśvara [the implication being that it does not apply to anyone else, such as one who holds authority within the womb of Māyā]. For all...

This very form of the ground of what is to be rejected (heyabhūmirūpa)—[with the variant reading "the form of the ground of bondage" (pāśabhūmirūpa)]—is perceived by some as being from Viṣṇu down to Śiva in the state of Supreme Śiva (paramaśivatayā); however, that is a false vision which must necessarily be abandoned by the practitioners of Anuttara Yoga. It is for this very purpose [that the following is taught] regarding the Lord of Knowledge (vidyādhipati).

[Regarding the specific teacher: There is a great zeal in the *Anubhavastotra* toward this fivefold sequence beginning with sacrifice (*yāga*) and ending with yoga (*yoga*); one should practice each of these in its many established modes exactly as they occur, and not merely for the sake of Vedic ritual action alone. By the word "etc. (*ādi*),...

[One grasps what is to be done and what is not to be done. It has been stated in the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures that one should not weary one's own self by means of discriminating between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten, or between purity and impurity—a discrimination that is devoid of the true nature of things (*vastudharma*) and consists essentially of mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*). For purity is not an inherent form of an object like blueness; rather, it exists elsewhere [as a mental state].

If it is argued that, because of an injunction regarding impurity—just as there is an injunction regarding the state of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*)—that [action] is impure for him in that context, we reply: this is the same even with respect to another injunction [proclaimed by Śiva]. An injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that impels one toward an action.
Another injunction is equal [in authority], for that [other view] is sublated by it. [As for one who is outside the Veda...]
If it is argued that "any scripture [to the contrary] is merely a deception," and thus [the opponent's position] is sublated by this, we reply: no.

It is the injunction of Śiva alone that possesses the power of sublation, as established by reasoning and proven by infinite scriptures such as the *Sarvajñānottara*; this we shall explain. Therefore, from the Vedic [perspective]...

It is established that from this point forward, whatever rule, injunction, or prohibition is stated in the scriptures of the Pārameśvara Siddhānta, Tantra, Kula, Ucchuṣma, and others, it is entirely ineffective here. This has been explained at length in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara) and other texts; it should be sought out from the *Tantrāloka*.
That conviction of the ignorant person— "I am inert, I am bound by karma, I am defiled, I am impelled by others"—
is [overcome] by the attainment of success through another firm conviction.
The conscious self immediately becomes the Lord, possessing a universal form.
Just as such a certainty is attained,
so should it always be attended to by the supreme yogi;
not with a vision devoid of the true nature of reality.
One should be wary of groups of teachers who instruct children— meaning those who provide instructions that do not know the ultimate truth, i.e., the instructions of fools.

Just as this shadow here manifests according to the way, the manner, and the time in which a person's mental resolve flashes forth, so too does his corresponding power arise at that very same time. (1)
"I am impure, I am a beast,
or else I am distinct from the entire veil of objective phenomena"—
when one's own heart is thus stained by such firm conviction, [how can there be liberation?]
How indeed can that which possesses the supreme reality even vibrate? ||2||
In the lotus of the heart, fully blossomed by the firm descent of the rays of Paraśiva’s grace,
[resides] one's own nature, manifesting along with the secret teachings.
In the process of awakening to an exceedingly beautiful fragrance: ||3|| Just as, wherever, and for whomever, the noble resolve manifests,
so for that person, in that very place...
Such is the splendor of the Divine. ||1||
Killed is the impure, killed is the beast,
killed is everything else except for the veil of the state of being a woman;
thus, O firm-willed one, take me as your own, as your wife, as your heart’s delight.
Tell me, whose supreme reality is it that is being proclaimed? ||2||
In the lotus of my heart, which has blossomed by the firm descent of the rays of the Supreme Lord Śiva,
the essence of the scripture has burst forth.
This [is] the means for awakening to the fragrance of the beautiful A. ||3||
Having slain Śiva’s son, he proclaims the truth of the world to be entirely full;
thus it resounds,
shimmering like a bee hovering over a blooming lotus.
The splendor of her beauty has surpassed that of Lakṣmī. ||4||
(Illumination) The bee of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) vibrates, uttering the cry: "I am Lord Śiva, completely filled with the reality (*tattva*) of all beings."
It bears its own light as its objective. ||4||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Means of Power" (Śāktopāya-prakāśana), in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 4.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now follows the means of the individual (āṇavopāya).
In that regard, when conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) itself, independently of any other means, brings about a purification within itself;

When he is capable of acting, having fallen away from the operations of the bound soul (*pāśava-vyāpāra*), and having attained the nature of the power of the Supreme Lord through the grace of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), that which is relied upon as the means brings forth Śākta knowledge. And this very thing—
[The knowledge of the Śāktopāya: This has been determined in the immediately preceding chapter.

However, when this [aspirant] requires another means (upāya) for the sake of his own purification, then, by grasping limited forms such as the intellect, the vital breath, the body, and a jar as being the means, he [experiences] the state of being an individual soul (aṇutva).

Having attained the individual (āṇava) knowledge, one manifests it therein; there, the intellect consists of meditation, while the vital breath (prāṇa) is both gross and subtle. The former consists of utterance (uccāraṇa), and "utterance" refers to the five functions beginning with the vital breaths. The subtle [utterance], however, which is denoted by the word "phoneme" (varṇa), will be described as the body.
That which consists of a specific arrangement and is denoted by the term "instrument" refers to external objects such as jars and so forth,
which will be described as means for the worship of the jar, the sacrificial ground, the *liṅga*, and other such supports. In that regard, there is meditation (*dhyāna*).

First, we shall here explain what is appropriate: having meditated upon that very supreme reality— which has been described as self-luminous and inclusive of all principles— within the awakening of one's own heart,
one should contemplate the union therein of the triad of fire, sun, and moon, which consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

One should meditate until that great fire of Bhairava becomes manifest, its form kindled by the wind of meditation— as it has been said: "From the friction of the fire-sticks of that meditation, the consumer of oblations, the Great Bhairava..."
"Blazing in the great sacrificial pit called the Heart, it attains expansion. Thus,

one should contemplate that [consciousness], which is of the nature of a wheel (cakra) surrounded by the twelve flames of its former powers, has emerged through any one of the apertures such as the eyes and has come to rest externally upon the nature of the object of perception.

Once he has rested, he should meditate on how that [external object] is first filled by way of the process of emanation in the form of the Moon; then it is illuminated by way of persistence in the form of the Sun; then it is dissolved by way of the fire of withdrawal; and finally, it is brought to the state of the Absolute (anuttara).

In this way, that wheel becomes completely filled with the non-differentiation of all external objects. Then, by means of that wheel, one should likewise [k: the reading is "itthaṃ tattvāni"] bring about all things without exception.

[The meaning is that it has the nature of the unsurpassed Self. The intended sense is that if the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of any entity whatsoever remains, even that perishes. One should meditate. Thus, for one who meditates without interruption—[there is also a variant reading: *dhyānavātaprabodhite*].
The continuous processes of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal have as their ultimate reality nothing other than one's own self-consciousness.
For the cognizer first creates an object by means of its being manifested; then, for some time, he maintains it while remaining attached to it;
subsequently, reflecting that "this object has been known," he withdraws it; immediately thereafter, enough!
By means of the logic of devouring (*grāsa*), through the attainment of fullness, one brings about the state of being assimilated into the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*).

And for one who ascertains that the ultimate reality of one's own self-awareness consists in the sovereignty over emanation and the other cosmic processes, the state of Bhairava occurs immediately; moreover, through practice, even the accomplishment of all desired goals and so forth follows.
One should meditate upon the self-luminous reality of the entire Self, which abides having internalized the triad beginning with the subject (mātrā), within the abode of the bliss of the heart.
One should meditate upon that all-pervasive Lord, the master of the wheel of rays consisting of the twelve great powers,
who brings about emanation and the other cosmic processes, as he emerges externally through the voids— namely, the cavities of the eyes and other sense organs.
The yogi, resting within himself upon that mandala which has swallowed all external and internal existence, should contemplate; in this way, there shall indeed be the manifestation of his own self.
These are the summary verses. This concludes the section on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Now follows the section on utterance (*uccāra*).
In that regard, one who wishes to utter the vital breath (*prāṇa*) should first, within the emptiness of the heart itself, [make it] non-empty.

When the void has been examined according to the principle stated as "it is empty," consciousness then comes to rest in the external [world], because—according to the definition already stated—"consciousness was previously transformed into breath through the arising of the *prāṇa*. Even beyond that, toward the external, by means of the filling of the moon of the *apāna* (the *apāna* itself is the "moon" because it performs the function of nourishment; by that [filling]...).

Fulfillment is the state of being free from further expectancy; for at that stage, the portions of the objects of knowledge residing within the knower remain embraced [within him]. He perceives his own universal nature (*sarvātmatā*), and consequently becomes free from expectancy toward anything else.
Then, through simultaneous arising, he attains rest in the friction [of the union].

Thereafter, when the fire of *udāna* arises, one experiences the form of the mutual fusion of all objects; the conceptualization of subject, object, and so forth is swallowed up—its nature having been defined by the statement: "The conceptualization of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and other breaths amounts to twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths] during day and night."

Upon the pacification of the fire that devours that [object] and the arising of the *vyāna* breath, one shines forth as devoid of all limitations [due to its pervasiveness, it is characterized by being free from all limitations]. Thus, these very states of rest, beginning from the void (*śūnya*) and ending with the *vyāna*, are respectively *nijānanda* (intrinsic bliss), *nirānanda* (bliss of cessation), and *parānanda* (supreme bliss).
The six levels of bliss (*ānandabhūmi*) have been taught as follows:
innate bliss (*nijānanda*), which resides in the ground of the Mother; joyless bliss (*nirānanda*), which has emerged from the state of the subject (*pramātṛ*);

supreme bliss (*parānanda*), which is produced by the external object of knowledge due to outward orientation; and the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), which is great bliss (*mahānanda*) and the bliss of consciousness (*cidānanda*).
Because it appropriates all objects such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, it is of the nature of Brahman by virtue of being their nourisher; it is Great Bliss (*mahānanda*);

it is Consciousness-Bliss (*cidānanda*) characterized by greatness through the cessation of the agitation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so on; and although it consists of everything, it is of the nature of Consciousness because it transcends that [multiplicity]. Thus, it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
Self-bliss is based solely on resting within the aspect of the subject;
the state consisting of the "blissless" (nirānanda) arises from resting in mere emptiness.

When there is rest in the state of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), supreme bliss (*parānanda*) arises fully; yet, when the object is entirely filled by the convergence of infinite objects of knowledge, [that bliss is realized].
The established position is that it is "Great Bliss" because of its union with the relish [of the object] through the means of valid cognition;
it is the expert in swallowing the perception of every fragment of the entire stream of objects of knowledge.
When one attains a rest that is utterly full and free from limiting conditions,
then indeed there is the bliss of consciousness, which is not augmented by anything insentient.
And there is no fixed state whatsoever that is differentiated or insentient;
wherein there is no limitation of any kind, and which vibrates as the universe itself.

"That which is nourished by the supreme nectar of unextracted consciousness—that alone is the abode of the bliss of the universe; thus our Guru has declared. Thus, there is one who is the synthesizer of these [energies].
Devoid of rising and setting, its ultimate nature is internal rest, the bliss of the universe— [this should be construed with a third-case *karmadhāraya*:
"the universe by means of its own form as bliss," etc.]— having rested in each of these stages of utterance, whether in pairs, by tens, or in their entirety, one moves on to another.

One attains the reality of rest (viśrānti-tattva), which is distinct from that body, vital breath, and so forth. By contemplating that very secret of the utterance of the seeds of emanation and withdrawal, one should purify conceptual thought (vikalpa). And within each of these states of rest, there are five stages according to the gradations of entry.

In that regard, "initial bliss" (prāgānanda) is a specific kind of wonder; and so it is said here: "For one who desires to enter the supreme path by means of the bodily methods through meditative cultivation, initial bliss arises from the touch of fullness."

Thus: "Arising" (udbhava) is due to the influence of the specific lower food; it consists of ascending to the supreme abode. Once rooted in bodilessness (*niḥśarīratā*), because of the firmness of the absence of the sense of "I" regarding the body, there is a "tremor" (*kampa*), which is the abandonment of that firmness—the vigor of the ego-force of one's own power. From the touch of a portion of fullness, there is then an arising for a moment.

From the firm rooting in bodilessness (*niḥśarīratā*), there arises trembling due to the subjugation of one's own power through the loosening of identification with the body; from that, sleep occurs due to the dissolution of outward-directedness [that is, the cessation of external mental activity]. In this way, when the notion of self in what is not-self has dissolved, [one abides in] one's own Self.
Because it consists of everything (*sarvamayatvāt*), the state of non-self (*anātmabhāva*) dissolves within the Self; therefore, this is *ghūrṇi* (the state of whirling).
Thus, *ghūrṇi* is the transcendence of the ten states.
And so, from that, one who has ascended to the plane of reality perceives consciousness as the self-nature of the universe (*viśvātmatvena*).
"By means of consciousness, the whirling [of the mind] stirs, from which the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti) is said to arise.
Thus, due to the emergence of the Great Pervasion, these stages—beginning with waking and ending with that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta)—come into being.
And these stages occur upon entering the wheels of the Triangle, the Kanda, the Heart, the Palate, and the Upper Kuṇḍalinī. In this manner...

We shall explain that the three signs (*liṅga*) are precisely that supreme vibration which occurs at the cessation of utterance— wherein all objects of knowledge have dissolved— and that vibration wherein the object of knowledge is just beginning to emerge, as well as that wherein the object of knowledge has fully emerged.

On its own occasion, moreover, the *liṅga* here is the *Yoginīhṛdaya*. Therein, the primary nature is that of vibration (*spandana*), because, through the emergence of the form of the couple (*yāmala*) consisting of contraction and expansion, one attains rest in the digit of emission (*visargakalā*). Enough said. Here, there is non-manifestation (*aprakāśa*).
Entry:
first resting in one's own consciousness, and thereafter in the object of knowledge, one should fulfill that object of knowledge.
When this [consciousness] is full, it rests;
it then swiftly withdraws the distinction between the knower and the known.
Then, through pervasion, these rest;
together with the void, they are the six stages of means (*upāya*),
beginning with prāṇa and ending with vyāna.
And the phenomenal world, beginning with the waking state, is dissolved [into it].

"But one who is steadfast in practice here shall rest, before long, in the abode of the reflective awareness of emission and withdrawal. These are the internal verses. Thus ends the section on pronunciation.
Now, the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the subtle self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
In this very utterance, the sound that vibrates, consisting mostly of an unmanifest imitation, is the phoneme. As it has been said:
"In that utterance which has been described, that which remains vibrating therein..."
A sound that primarily imitates the unmanifest is called a *varṇa*.

Thus, having raised the doubt—"Since its nature is the non-differentiation of all phonemes (*varṇa*), where can such an unmanifest (*avyakta*) phoneme be found?"—he says "of that" (*tasya*). Its primary form consists of the seeds of emanation and withdrawal; through the practice thereof, the attainment of supreme consciousness occurs. For instance, [it resides] in the series beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, whether accompanied by vowels (*sāccha*) or devoid of vowels (*anaccha*).
Whether it is uttered internally— [that is, remembered through the ascent of the vital breath (prāṇa) or remembered through the ascent of the intellect (buddhi)]—
or simply remembered, the touch of the vibration of consciousness (saṃvitspanda) is equal and distinguished; it is complete because it does not depend on ritual conventions (samaya),
even for one who does depend on such conventions [as those devised by the highest elders and so forth].

The convention (*samaya*) is that "this is the denotation of this [word]"; the words *ghaṭa* and so forth possess that [denotation], and they directly manifest it there for the sake of cognition, just as in the case of mental images and the like, words such as "beloved" manifest the state of a woman and so forth— even though she is not present— when intensely cultivated through passion, grief, or other emotions.

[They] directly realize [this]. Sounds, which bring about that object, like a daydream and so forth, through the touch of supreme consciousness (*anuttara-saṃvit*), one should unify the heart, throat, and lips, as well as the two *dvādaśāntas* and the heart; this is the secret of the phonemes (*varṇa-rahasya*).

Some maintain that the internal color— white, yellow, and so forth— which arises immediately after the inner vibration (vimarśa) flashing within, and which is being manifested, causes one to experience consciousness (saṃvid).
Due to the absence of the denotable [meaning "because of the non-existence of a separate denotable object"], through the vibration of consciousness,
by means of the cessation of the movements of the moon and the sun [meaning "by means of the inward-turning repose after having issued forth externally"].

But for whom, through the complete entry [into his own abode— this is the reading in manuscript *kh*], there is the fullness [fullness meaning free from desire because it does not look toward anything else] in the ritual procedure concerning the seed-syllables and clusters of the conscious principle.

Thus ends the intermediate verse. This concludes the rule regarding the phonemes (*varṇavidhi*). As for the instrument (*karaṇa*), we shall explain it in the section on the manifestation of the mudrās.

That immersion which occurs through the utterance [of mantras], the performance [of rituals], meditation, the recitation of syllables, and the visualization of locations,
is called the perfect *āṇava* [means].

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Surely, due to the diversity of means (*upāya*), there must also be a diversity of goals (*upeya*), just as there is a diversity of effects when there is a diversity of causes; therefore, the attainment of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) cannot be the single goal for everyone. To this he replies: "Not for these [beings] in the prescription of the supreme fruit. And if this is so, then how is there a diversity of means?

We say it is "due to the variety of the descent of power" (*śaktipātavaicitryāt*); the meaning is that just as there is a variety among the *śāmbhava*, *śākta*, and *āṇava* [initiations] due to the variety of the descent of power, so it is here as well. [The text continues:
"the sun, moon, and fire are void."
O friend, this is the true exertion;
by remaining here, the hero shall soon attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Individual Means" (Āṇavaprakāśana), in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now follows the external procedure (*bāhyavidhi*).
That very [procedure] is intended by the term "determination of the locations" (*sthānaprakalpana*) [in the passage beginning with *uccārakaraṇa*]. (Note: *k* reads *kamyate*.)
