In that context, the abiding of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) has been described as threefold. While "prāṇa" generally refers to the nature of vibration, it specifically takes the form of a designator (*vācaka*) in exactly three ways, as it has been said:
"Furthermore, this triad which precedes the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvan*)."

"This very path of time and space is clearly established in the vital breath (prāṇa). Thus, both the internal body and the external world are contained therein; for within that vital breath, there exists the entire sixfold procedure (*vidhi*)—all of which will be described below—and this path resides in the vital breath, which is of the nature of the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*).

It is measured (*kalyate*); for him, it is precisely the reckoning of succession and non-succession (*kramākramakalanā*). [The reckoning of entities by way of succession and non-succession is their delimitation; that itself is time. In this regard, [reckoning] occurs by succession in the case of cause and effect and so forth, and by non-succession in the case of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) and so forth. And thus it has been said:

"That very consciousness, moreover, manifesting through its unfolding both succession and non-succession which are internalized within its own self, is established as the activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti). Thus, time is that [consciousness]. [But surely, objects appear as being attached to consciousness; so how can the category of objects be dependent upon it?]"

He says "that [time] and so forth" because there might be a connection with time; having raised the objection that if this were so, then even the Supreme Lord would have a connection with time, he says "its manifestation and so forth. And it is the Supreme Lord alone who shines within, and that manifestation is the Goddess Kālī.
The capacity for the manifestation of the universe—consisting of the subject, the object, and so forth—as being of that very nature belongs to Him who manifests according to His own will;

however, within His own self, there is neither succession nor non-succession. For when fire possesses the power of burning, there is no emergence of a crackling sound or the like [independent of it]. Thus it is said: "The power named Kālī."

The power called *nāma* (name) is the manifestation of that [reality] through differentiation—that is, by way of its external emergence. However, the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) pertains to both succession and non-succession. For it is consciousness itself that, by virtue of its sovereignty, grasps a form differentiated from the objects of knowledge. And for this very reason:
Through association with limitations, it becomes an object of cognition, like the sky— as it has been said:
"That which is pure consciousness alone, whose ultimate reality is light, shines forth as the sky, distinct and having cast off the objectivity inherent in itself."

Thus, the statement that consciousness has not previously undergone transformation into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) would not be contradicted; for even when emptiness appears, there is no apprehension of any other form—this is what was meant by "previously. Therefore, due to its sovereignty, consciousness, falling [toward the object] with an eagerness to appropriate the object of knowledge—that is, through an outward orientation—is primarily characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
It is of the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇana*), as it has been said: "That very Self, eager to appropriate this object of cognition once it has been differentiated,
falls [into duality] while emerging upward, designated by the name of the wave of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*)."

Thus, there is a delimitation of the state of being identical with the universe by means of its transcendence of the universe; yet consciousness, being devoid of the universe and thus of the nature of the void, becomes once again such as it was, attaining the state of *prāṇa* through the acceptance of the universe.
Having the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), it fills the body through five forms, as it has been said: [citation].

"That function of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), by means of its fivefold forms beginning with *prāṇa*, makes the body its own through consciousness; therefore, this [body] shines forth as filled with consciousness. [The reading "it impels" (*prerayati*) is found in an alternative version of the text.]

Consequently, he appears as if endowed with consciousness. Within that power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), there is the path of time (*kāla-adhvā*) in the eastern portion, while in the northern portion is the path of space (*deśa-adhvā*) consisting of the diversity of forms (*mūrti*). Among these, the paths of phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, and words (*pada*) reside within the path of time.
[In the manuscript *kh*, the reading is "the paths of words reside in the path of time."]

Because it possesses subtle and gross forms. As for its abiding in space, it will be explained in its own proper context as consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*pura*), and kalās. In that regard, although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists within the body in a manner interwoven both internally and externally, nevertheless, the effort that is clearly perceptible—the vibration of the breath—is twofold.
It is both perceptible and imperceptible; these two are further divided into two types based on their being manifest or unmanifest.
This [state] begins from the heart. [The intended meaning here is: "However, those [energies] proclaimed in the heart-cakra are beneficial for practitioners."
"Prāṇa indeed moves through those [channels] according to the division of day and night;

thus I shall explain it to you by dividing it clearly. Thus, although this [prāṇa], whose effort is perceptible, exists everywhere in the body, it does not exist there with imperceptible effort, for that is not the case.
When effort is self-perceived, there is indeed some fruit, for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been set in motion by one's own will as the cause for various supernatural powers (*siddhi*);
thus, the conceptualization of divisions begins precisely from the heart. Therefore, this must be investigated from that very point.
In that regard, it is the power of the Lord (*prabhu-śakti*). And here, this doubt should not be raised: [text fragment].

To the question, "Since it is all-pervasive, how is it that despite its non-difference [from everything], it is manifest in some places and unmanifest in others? he says: "The power of the Lord. As it has been stated:
"In some cases the power of the Lord is primary, as in the movement of the limbs and the vital breaths."
The power of the self is, in some cases, like the contraction and vibration of the *kanda*.
In some cases, when the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the heart is clearly manifest,
two or three [powers] may become primary for attentive yogins.

"Due to attention, due to the unseen portion (adṛṣṭa), due to strength, and due to the movement of the support—there is even a reversal regarding the primacy of the vital breaths and the powers of the self.
Here, the "power of the self" refers to the power of the limited subject; these three constitute the exertion in the movement of the vital breath.

The reason is the predominance of the primary quality (*guṇa*). In that regard, for everyone—from Brahmā down to the smallest insect—the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) extends thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) from the heart to the limit of the twelve fingers (*dvādaśānta*), both during exhalation and inhalation, because everyone possesses a body characterized by its own appropriate strength and effort. In that context, there is the *ghaṭikā*.

The lunar day (tithi), the month, and the year—comprising a collection of years—thus constitutes the entirety of time. In this regard, according to the principle that one *caṣaka* consists of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) plus a fifth part thereof, there is the emergence of a *ghaṭikā*; for a *ghaṭikā* indeed consists of sixty *caṣakas*, and therefore it amounts to seventy-two finger-breadths.
Now, the arising of the lunar days (*tithyudaya*). Two fingers and a quarter is said to be a *tuṭi*; four such *tuṭis* constitute a watch (*prahara*).

Half a *tuṭi* and another half *tuṭi* therein are the junctions (*saṃdhyā*). Thus, in the outward movement it is day, and in the inward movement it is night; this is the arising of the lunar days, as it has been stated:
"The portion of the moon, which is the object of perception, is filled by the mass of rays from the sun, which is the perceiver;
to whatever extent it is filled, that lunar day (*tithi*) becomes manifest through the planets.
Now, the arising of the month: therein, the day is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), because of the waning of the moon of the downward breath (*apāna*) during the day.

The state of being the dark fortnight is night; therein, the first half-ṭuṭi and the final half-ṭuṭi are rest (*viśrānti*). They are not touched by time, because in the two half-ṭuṭis of the heart and the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), there is no calculation of time, as they consist of the nature of rest.

The fifteen intermediate *tuṭis* are indeed the lunar days (*tithis*). In each of those *tuṭis*, which take the form of a lunar day, there is both manifestation (*prakāśa*) and repose (*viśrānti*); these alone constitute day and night. As it has been said:
"Because consciousness, at every moment, is united with light and bliss..."

"As long as those two are cast forth, for that long alone are day and night. In this context, "day" is the manifestation consisting of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), while "night" is the dissolution or resting (*laya*, *rāti*) of the object of knowledge within the subject who discerns it. These two—the manifestation and the repose in light—possess infinite varieties due to the diversity of their durations, whether long or short.
But when there is equilibrium between those two, it is the *viṣuvat* (equinox), as it has been said:

"When there is an equilibrium consisting in the repose within the reality, that tasting within the Self is the equilibrium of the object of knowledge and the knower; that is the equality of night and day for the subjects. For the subjects...

Due to the gradation of the intensity of the object of knowledge, the primary focus, and so forth, the arising of consciousness occurs for some as a moment, for another as a kalpa, and for yet another as a mere blink of an eye; thus, there is a diversity of duration—long or short—in manifestation. Likewise, regarding repose, a greater degree of repose in the object of knowledge conduces to the lengthening of the day.
"In the same way, the state of resting in one's own self constitutes the expansion of the night.
In that regard, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the moon of the *apāna* breath bestows one nourishing digit (*kalā*) at a time upon the sun of the *prāṇa*,
until the fifteenth *tuṭi* near the *dvādaśānta*.

The moon, whose expansion of distinct digits has been exhausted, dissolves into the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa). Immediately thereafter, that half-tuṭi is the junction of the fortnights (pakṣasaṃdhi). Of that half-tuṭi, the first half belongs to the prāṇa, while the second belongs to the apāna.

Regarding the *prātipada*: when that *āmāvasya* portion enters into that *prātipada* portion due to the cutting of the lunar day (*tithi*) caused by the effort of coughing, straining, or focusing the mind, then there is a "seizure" (*grahaṇa*) therein.
[Because of that cough, there is the cutting of that lunar day at the end of the twelve-finger space; from that...]
"From the womb of power (śakti) below, emission arises; from that, the rain is produced.

According to this principle, due to the gradual expansion of the downward-moving breath (apāna) by virtue of exhalation, there occurs the emergence of the full moon through the increase of the lunar day (tithi) to its state of fullness. By the force of this growth, the portion of the full moon extends into the first day of the lunar fortnight (prātipada).

When [the shadow] enters the portion, then there is a lunar eclipse; according to the principle that "Ketu [occurs] in the sun and Rāhu in the moon," Rāhu is accompanied by Soma (the moon). As it has been said:
"The moon, whose motion is struck by the friction of the breath-sun..."
His own mother, longing for the nectar-essence that has been made to flow forth,
is indeed eclipsed by Rāhu;
yet, during this auspicious planetary conjunction, one who knows how to strike the three [centers] should savor that essence.
Thus it is said; likewise, the seizing of the sun is taught in the world. Indeed, the power that enters into the vital breath is what is prescribed as a *tuṭi*.
O fair-faced one, that should be known as the new moon (amāvāsyā) in the dark fortnight;
it is proclaimed as half a *tuṭi* located in the middle-upper portion of Śakti.
This junction of the lunar fortnights should be known as the half of the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the first day of the lunar day (pratipad);
indeed, it is at that point, through the cessation of the lunar day, that a solar eclipse occurs.
O Goddess, at that time the lunar orb appears within the solar orb;
within that, O fair-faced one, Rāhu resides, seeking the nectar.
"The moon flows with nectar, and Rāhu swallows it;
having drunk it, he releases that orb, and then he is said to be liberated.
And in that context, the Rāhu of the subject of Māyā, who co-exists with the Soma in the form of the object of knowledge, by its very nature—

Being incapable of dissolution and merely capable of concealment, he drinks the lunar nectar situated in the sun; because it effects the non-differentiation of the triad of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge, that auspicious time bestows fruits pertaining to the next world. Then, the solar consciousness enters into the vital breath one by one.
With a single *kalā*, one fills the moon of the *apāna*; that first lunar day (*pratipad*) is to be known as when the moon consists of a single *kalā*.
In this sequential manner, the moon is filled until the fifteenth *tuṭi*, which is the full moon (*pūrṇimā*); immediately after that is the junction of the fortnight (*pakṣasaṃdhi*).
"And the grasping" is as before; however, this bestows results pertaining to this life [due to the predominance of creation in this world].
This is the arising of the month. Now follows the arising of the year. Therein, the dark fortnight itself is the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), occurring at intervals of six finger-breadths each.

The transit of the sun of the vital breath (prāṇārka) is from Capricorn to the end of Gemini. Therein, for every finger-breadth, there are five lunar days (tithis), and therein also is the division of day and night. Thus, during the entry [of the breath], it is the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), which is the state of being in the womb (garbhatva).

The sixfold group of transformations beginning with birth— namely, the desire to arise (*udbhavet-chā*), the state of wishing to arise (*udbubhūṣutā*), the state of being about to arise (*udbhaviṣyatva*), the commencement of arising (*udbhavārambha*), the state of arising (*udbhavat-tā*), and birth itself— occur in sequence within the signs starting from Capricorn (*makara*) and so on, [in the case of] the sun of the vital breath (*prāṇārka*). In this very manner, the meditation (*upāsā*) is to be performed here, as has been stated.
Impregnation, desire, union, bliss, density, maintenance,
birth, existence, transformation, growth, decline, and destruction occur in succession.
Beginning from the month of Māgha, the established positions have been proclaimed;
they pertain to the accomplishment of success for practitioners as well as the arising of all states of being.

Thus, this mere desire, conjoined with the object of desire which consists of emergence, is the "desire for emergence" (*udbhavecchā*); its "emergence" (*udbhavana*) is its abiding within itself as an upward surging. It produces the appropriate fruit.
And herein are the Rudras, beginning with Dakṣa and ending with Pitāmaha, as well as their Śaktis. [In these months.]
The twelve presiding deities are as follows:
Dakṣa, Caṇḍa, Hara, Caṇḍī, Pramatha, Bhīma, Manmatha,
Śakuni, Sumati, Nanda, Gopālaka, and Pitāmaha.

Thus, by the sequence of transits (saṃkrānti), there are lords [of the months]. This is the arising of the year. Since there are sixty lunar days (tithis) for every finger-breadth (aṅgula), a year occurs in the course of a transit;
by this sequence, during both the entry and the exit [of the breath], there is the arising of twelve years, with three hundred lunar days for every finger-breadth.

When three hundred and fifteen *tithis* are assigned to each finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), there are sixty *tithis* in the fifth part of a finger-breadth; by this method, a year consists of one finger-breadth plus a fifth part.
This is according to the calculation where a "cup" (*caṣaka*) was previously stated to be a year.

"Five years at each transit"—by this sequence, in one period of the exit and entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is the arising of sixty years; here, the number of lunar days (*tithi*) is twenty-one thousand six hundred. Such is the number of lunar days within the arising of the sixty-year cycle.

Outside of that, the calculation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) constitutes a day and night; thus, the number of breaths in a day and night is not examined as exceeding sixty years of arising, because of its infinity. In that regard, regarding the calculation of external time: one human year is a lunar day (*tithi*) of the gods by this [reckoning].
[By the sequence of calculation consisting of fortnights,
months, solstices, years, and so forth,] the divine cycle of four yugas consists of twelve thousand years in succession; these are calculated as four, three, two, and one,
starting from the Kṛta age respectively.

Eight *saṃdhyās* consist of hundreds [of years]. Seventy-one cycles of the four ages (*caturyuga*) constitute a *manvantara*. Fourteen *manvantaras* constitute a day of Brahmā. At the end of Brahmā’s day, when the three worlds—characterized as *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*—are consumed by the fire of time (*kālāgni*), [the destruction occurs] in those three worlds and in other three worlds as well.
"The lifespan of those dwelling in the water-tattva is one day for those situated in the fire-tattva;

such is the sequence by which it increases by one hundred years at each stage. When [the world] is laid to sleep by smoke, all people, impelled by a forceful fire, become *pralayākala*s in Janaloka and remain there. But those who are awakened...

The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Hāṭakeśas, and others sport in Maholoka. Then, at the end of the night, the creation of Brahmā occurs. By this measure, the lifespan of Brahmā is one hundred years. That constitutes a day for Viṣṇu, and his night is of equal duration; his lifespan is also one hundred such years. That [period] is a day for Rudra, the lord of the world above that, and his [night] is of equal duration.

The night is as previously described; a hundred such years is the limit [of their lifespan]. Therein, at the conclusion of that period, the attainment of the state of Śiva for Rudra is mentioned as the limit of Rudra’s office. That is a day for the sustainers of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), namely the hundred Rudras; the night is of equal duration, and their lifespan is also a hundred [such years]. Upon the exhaustion of the hundred Rudras—

The destruction of the Brahmāṇḍa. Thus, from the water-tattva up to the unmanifest (avyakta), this very sequence constitutes the lifespan of the Rudras. The lifespan of the former is the day for those residing in the subsequent [tattva]; that is, the lifespan of those dwelling in the water-tattva is a day for those situated in the fire-tattva, and so on, increasing by one hundred years at each step.

Regarding the word "day": consequently, Brahmā [residing in the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*)], as well as the Rudras who hold authority over water and the other elements, remain in the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). And Śrīkaṇṭhanātha [residing in the principle of the individual soul (*puruṣatattva*)] is then the destroyer. This is the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*).
[Since the intermediate dissolution has been described: upon its exhaustion, there is creation.
In that regard, even those liberated according to other scriptures—namely, as proclaimed in the Sāṃkhya, Vedānta, and other systems—are also created.
As for the lifespan of Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, that belongs to those who dwell within the *kañcukas*.

A day of the Rudras is equal to their night; their lifespan is a day of Gahaneśa [the presiding authority over the womb of Māyā]. His night is of the same duration, and during it, everything dissolves into Māyā. Then Gahaneśa creates again. Thus, he who...

Having multiplied that unmanifest time by ten *parārdhas*, one should call it a day of Māyā; its night is of equal duration. That itself is the dissolution (*pralaya*). The time of Māyā, multiplied by a hundred *parārdhas*, [constitutes the time] in the Īśvara-tattva—since the sequence of causes will be explained [in the context of] the arising of the vital breath (*prāṇodaya*), it is indeed the Īśvara-tattva.

It has been stated that the reality of *vidyā* is contained within it; that which was previously described as being primarily the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and having the nature of vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is the day. Here, the vital breath creates the world for as long as it lasts, and the night is that period wherein the vital breath comes to rest.
Even when the vital breath has become tranquil within the abode of the *brahmabila*, there exists therein a sequential progression.

When a period of Īśvara, multiplied by a hundred *parārdhas*, has elapsed, that constitutes a day of Sadāśiva; his night is of equal duration, and that indeed is the Great Dissolution (due to the withdrawal of even the Pure Path). This is Sadāśiva.

At the exhaustion of its own time, the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and the *nirodhikā* are traversed and dissolve into the *nāda*; the *nāda* dissolves into the principle of *śakti*, and that [dissolves] into the *vyāpinī*, and she [dissolves] into the *anāśrita*. A day of the *anāśrita* is equal to ten million times the duration of *śakti*. The *anāśrita* resides in the state of the *sāmanasa*; that which is the *sāmanasya* is equanimity (*sāmya*).
When the dissolution of the universe has occurred, the entire multitude of atoms remains gathered together within *samanā* alone;
because the entire universe exists there without differentiation up to the level of *anāśrita*, this state is called "equilibrium" (*sāmya*). That is Brahman.
From this equilibrium—which is "akalya," meaning incapable of being differentiated—arises *kāla*.
The emergence of the revolving wheel that dissolves the expansion of all time— from the *tuṭi* onwards— as previously described, occurs in the mere twinkling of an eye. One, ten, a hundred,
a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, ten million, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, a hundred billion, a trillion, ten trillion, a quadrillion, and so forth.

The sequence of eighteen places, beginning with *śaṅku*, *samudra*, and ending with *madhya* and *parārdha*, each multiplied by ten, is the method of calculation. In this way, countless creations and dissolutions occur within a single Great Creation in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). [Since consciousness previously transformed into the vital breath, the vital breath...]

[He is] in the form of the Great Creation. That too exists in consciousness; that [consciousness] exists in its limiting adjunct (upādhi), and that exists in pure consciousness alone. This vibration of pure consciousness itself is what is called the emergence of time. Therefore, the diversity found in dreams, mental constructs, and the like is not contradictory for this [consciousness]. Thus...

Just as the emergence of time occurs in the *prāṇa*, so too does it occur in the *apāna* from the heart down to the *mūla-pīṭha*. And just as the six causes— known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Anāśrita— are located in the heart, throat, palate, forehead, the aperture [of Brahman], and the *dvādaśānta*, exactly the same applies to the *apāna*.

These are the presiding deities over childhood, youth, old age, death, rebirth, and liberation, located respectively at the heart, the bulb (kanda), the bliss-center (ānanda), the contraction and expansion, and the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta).
Now follows the emergence of time within the *samāna* breath. The *samāna* resides in the ten channels of the heart—namely, the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*.

Moving through the ten channels— namely Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, Yaśā, Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī— it transports the fluids and other elements with equilibrium throughout the entire body; therein, as it moves through the eight directions...

It imitates, as it were, the movement of the observer toward that direction. Moving upward and downward through the three channels—*iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*—it performs a coming and going. There, on the day of the equinox (known as the sun in Aries), at the time of dawn externally, [it moves] one and a quarter...

[Consisting of four hundred and fifty movements of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), a *ghaṭikā* measures sixty *caṣakas*. Since there are sixty *caṣakas* in a *ghaṭikā*, by calculating six breath-movements per *caṣaka*, there are three hundred and sixty breath-movements. It flows through the central channel (*madhyamārga*) for one *ghaṭikā*.

Then, by the calculation of nine hundred breath-discharges (*prāṇavikṣepa*), there are five transits (*saṃkrānti*)—from Taurus to Virgo—consisting of two and a half *ghaṭikās* each, alternating between left and right: left, right, left, right, left. Then, when those five transits have occurred, during fourteen [breaths] less a quarter.

When the *ghaṭikās* have elapsed, at midday during the southern autumnal equinox (*viṣuvat*), there are nine hundred breaths. Thereafter, there is a fivefold transition (*saṃkrānti*)— namely, right, left, right, left, and right [beginning with Scorpio and so forth]— with nine hundred breaths for each.

Thus, during the night as well, there are two and a half *ghaṭikās* for each [sign]. Therein, at the evening twilight known as the Aries transit (*meṣasaṃkrānti*), the *samāna* wind flows through the middle channel for one and a quarter *ghaṭikās* externally; the second and a quarter *ghaṭikā* is in the middle of the night.

[She has entered. Thus, on the day of the equinox and during that night, there are twelve transits (saṃkrānti) each. Consequently, with the increase and decrease of the days, there is the increase and decrease of the transits.
In this way, within a single [equal breath]—and not in a dual form like the prāṇa and apāna—in the equalizing wind (samānamarut).
For two years, there is an absence of the yoga of inhalation and exhalation; here too, it is indeed a single movement.

The arising of the twelve-year cycle and so forth is as before. In the case of the udāna, however, the movement extends as far as the *dvādaśānta*—that is, from the heart to the crown of the head and further to the *dvādaśānta*—consisting essentially of mere vibration.
Regarding time (*kāla*): here too, as before, the rule is the same.

However, in the case of the pervasive breath (*vyāna*), because it is all-pervasive, even though it is without sequence, the emergence of time occurs through its connection with a subtle state of surging forth.
Now, regarding the emergence of the phonemes (*varṇodaya*): therein, during the half-watch (*ardhaprahara*)—that is, during the internal half-watch of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

In each group (*varga*), there is an emergence (*udaya*) of four and a half finger-breadths. On the outside, however, the emergence of the groups consists of one hundred and thirteen and a half movements of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*). During the half-watch (*ardhaprahara*), the emergence of the groups is equal at the equinox; for each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), there are two hundred and sixteen external breath-movements.
The emergence of thirty-six cups is this effortless arising (*udaya*), which is natural;

it is the arising of the phonemes (*varṇodaya*). But the arising of mantra is effortful; like the driving of a water-wheel or a pulley, one who continuously joins together the manifold arising of mantra day and night by the power of a single continuous application—

One attains identity with the deity of the mantra. In that regard, the number of risings of the mantra—[the remainder being "of the mantra"]—is explained by the very count of the breath-movements [which consists of twenty-one thousand six hundred], which are perpetually arisen; [this is] when doubled. (kh:)

The reading is *tadviguṇite*. According to the sequence beginning with "half of that" (*tadardham*) and so forth, there is an emergence of two hundred [breaths] in a wheel of one hundred and eight; thus, for one who has come to rest in the nature of the movement (*cāra*)—both gross and subtle—the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) is exhausted, and when the devouring of time (*kālagrāsa*) has occurred, this single consciousness alone becomes complete.
It shines forth, replete with manifold powers. It is indeed the difference in time that differentiates consciousness, not the difference in the object of knowledge.

Anticipating the objection—“Let there be no difference produced by time, but might there not be one produced by the object of knowledge, such as in the sequence ‘this is the cognition of blue’ and so forth?”—he says: “not the difference in the object of knowledge. For, as for that which stands upon the peak...

Even though there is a difference in the objects of cognition such as houses and so forth, there would be only a single appearance of the city. Therefore, it is the time of the object of cognition that is the differentiator of knowledge; and that [time] is intended to consist of extremely subtle moments (*kṣaṇa*), by means of which the cessation of knowledge occurs immediately after its arising. But what is the use of a subtle moment?

The definition is stated as follows: "A *kṣaṇa* is the duration for which a cognition persists," and not a partless, indivisible fraction of time that cannot be defined; for such a thing is impossible to describe. Like a cognition situated on a mountain peak, the very duration of the persistence of a cognition is itself a *kṣaṇa*. [Regarding the arising of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is it not cognition...]
Regarding the question of how long [the state] remains, he says, "and at the arising of the vital breath" (*prāṇodaye*).

Since, according to the previously stated principle, there is a sequence of *tuṭis* and so forth within the vital breath, how can it be said that there is only a single cognition at the arising of the vital breath?
He says, "not so," and explains with the word "necessarily" (*avaśyam*): in one [moment], there is necessarily only a single cognition; otherwise, this would not be the case.
Conceptual cognition would not be unitary, because it is colored by sequential sounds, and even the *mātrā* (measure of time) is sequential. As it has been said:
"Of that [vowel], the first half is acute (*udātta*) for half a *hrasva*. (Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa 1.2.32)

Thus, as long as another vibration (*spanda*) has not arisen, there is only one single cognition. Therefore—[the word] "therefore" (ataḥ) meaning because it possesses the characteristic of unity despite the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of multiple attributes—as it has been said:
"In such and such a manner, the all-pervasive Lord of the wheel of the powers of reflective awareness..."
It is contemplated through the reflective awareness of the eighty-one gross words.
"Consequently, a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is complete in exactly as many [syllables] as it takes;

that is what is called a 'word' (*pada*), not something restricted by the rules governing nominal suffixes (*suP*) and verbal endings (*tiṅ*). Thus, at the moment of recollecting these eighty-one words, this very [consciousness], through the gateway of entering into various attributes (*dharma*), remains as one alone.
The conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) concerning the Supreme Lord— [conceptual thought being of the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*)]—

becomes non-conceptual in essence through the swallowing of time (*kālagrāsa*). Thus, perceiving the entire path of time (*kālādhvan*) as nothing but the arising of the vital breath (*prāṇodaya*), one perceives therein the manifold and innumerable processes of emanation and resorption.
By contemplating the supreme sovereignty of the Self alone and recognizing it, one becomes truly liberated;
for one perceives the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) of the Self, whose nature is consciousness, as well as its form and that which resides therein, beyond time.
Together with the cycles of creation, maintenance,
and withdrawal, he who is eternally diligent attains the state of Bhairava.
In this regard, this shadow is the vibration of the waves of perception of all forms of light; it is his vital breath.
Having fully understood the entire expansion of time established within the vital breath (prāṇa).
Just as the power of the wind manifests and just as it ceases, even so does Maheśvara;
having displayed creation and dissolution, he causes them to subside.
That Self is an ocean of the eternally conscious reality;
its surface is agitated by the shimmering waves of the ripples of perception.
Within the span of a breath, the entire expanse of time has passed away.
Just as the power of the wind surges forth and just as it subsides, so too does this Great Lord;
He bestows the fruit of righteousness when He emerges, and when He immerses Himself, [He takes it away].
Therefore, the self is not an object of thought or laughter.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Path of Time," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the seventh chapter. Now, regarding the path of space (*deśādhvan*):
therein, having described the path of time (*kālādhvan*) as being in the eastern part and the path of space in the northern part, [the text proceeds].
He begins to explain the path of space with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

This entire path of space—which arises from the power of manifesting the variety of forms (where "form" [*mūrti*] is the own-nature of an object)—rests within consciousness; by means of that [consciousness], [it rests] in that which is created by it through the gateway of consciousness.
The path is situated within the Void and so forth. As it has been said:
"This entire path is fully established within pure consciousness alone;
for that which does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky."

Thus: the entire path (adhvan) is established within the void of the intellect, the vital breath, the primary and secondary wheels of the channels, externally in the body, and as far as the linga, the sacrificial mound, the image, and so forth. That entire path—[as it has been said:]...

"Earth is proclaimed as a substance by virtue of its solidity, water [by its fluidity]," and so forth; according to this principle, the entire path is dissolved into the body. Having dissolved the body into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that [breath] into the intellect (*dhī*), and that [intellect] into the void (*śūnya*), one attains a consciousness that is intensely and perfectly full through that realization of the void.

One who knows the true nature of the thirty-six principles, perceiving consciousness—which transcends them—as being the form of Paramaśiva, should experience it as consisting of the entire universe; otherwise, one would grasp only some portion of the object of knowledge as supreme, such as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or others who hold office within the womb of Māyā. Therefore, necessarily...
One must be intent upon the knowledge of the *prakriyā*. As it has been said:
"Knowledge does not have the *prakriyā* as its ultimate goal...
and so forth. In that context, the *pṛthivītattva* (earth-principle) extends for a hundred crores [of yojanas] and takes the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍagolaka*).

According to the definition in the *Nirukta*—"the egg (*aṇḍa*) belonging to Brahmā is called an 'egg' because it is a mass (*piṇḍa*) of entities"—an "egg" is a mass or collection of entities such as bodies and senses; that very thing is also called a "sphere" (*golaka*).
The first is said to be made of gold, and the second is likewise golden (*raukma*).
Copper and iron are established in their respective order.

Such are the eggs (aṇḍas). Within them are the fire of time (kālāgni), the hells, the netherworlds (pātālas), the earth, heaven, and up to the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka). Outside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) are a hundred Rudras. And there is no limit to the number of cosmic eggs. Beyond that, the element of water (jalatattva) is ten times greater than the element of earth (dharātattva).

From that point, each subsequent element is ten times greater than the preceding one, ending with the ego (ahaṃkāra). That is to say: water, fire, air, ether, the five subtle elements (tanmātra), and the eleven organs contained within the ego. The principle of intellect (buddhitattva) is a hundred times greater than the ego, as it has been stated:

"In the teaching of Śiva, the cities of those beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra) and ending with the mind (manas) are located above the Ākāśāvaraṇa and below the Ahaṃkāra. Thereafter, the principle of Prakṛti is divided a thousandfold;
such is the extent of the Prakṛtyaṇḍa. And that, like the Brahmāṇḍa, is innumerable.

From the principle of Prakṛti, the principle of Puruṣa is ten thousandfold. From Puruṣa, Niyati is one hundred thousandfold. Beyond Niyati, each subsequent principle up to Kalā is ten times one hundred thousandfold; namely, Niyati, Rāga, Aśuddhavidyā, Kāla, and Kalā. From the principle of Kalā, Māyā is ten millionfold; this much constitutes the Egg of Māyā (māyāṇḍa).

From the principle of Māyā, Śuddhavidyā is multiplied ten-fold; from the principle of Vidyā, the principle of Īśvara is a hundred-fold; from the principle of Īśvara, the principle called Sādākhya is a thousand-fold. [Note: The reading "sādāśivākhyaṃ sahasrakoṭidhā" is found after "sādāśivākhyāditi pāṭhaḥ."]

The Śakti-tattva, multiplied by the group [of five] from that which is called Sāda, is the Śakty-aṇḍa. Because that Śakti exists pervading the entire path of the universe, both internally and externally, she is called Vyāpinī (the Pervasive One). Thus, these principles, existing as successive coverings, are such that each subsequent one is the pervader and each preceding one is the pervaded.
They exist by way of persistence. The entire path, up to the end of the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*), is pervaded by the principle of Śiva (*śiva-tattva*).
Furthermore, the principle of Śiva is immeasurable, transcending all paths while simultaneously pervading all paths.
Those worlds which exist within the intervals between these principles—their respective lords alone are situated here upon this earth.
In those abodes,
they bestow upon those who die there their respective destinies, and by means of the sequence of initiation, they gradually propel them higher and higher. For example:
Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Narakeśa, Hāṭaka, and then Bhūtalapa;
Brahmā, Munīśa, and Lokeśa.
Rudra is situated in the midst of the five eggs.
In the lower [direction] is Ananta; in the east are those named Kapālin, Vahni, Antanirṛti, and Bāla;
[and] Laghu, Nidhipati, and Vidyādhipa.
Śambhu, the lord of Vīrabhadra, [is] the end of darkness.
Thus, this circle of the earth, consisting of sixteen cities, is the power of withdrawal (nivṛttikalā) belonging to Lakulīśa Bhārabhūti.
And Ṛdiṇḍyāṣāḍhī, Puṣkara, and Nimeṣa.
Prabhāsa and Sureśa—
thus the eight [deities] belonging to each individual [center] have been declared in the water [element].
Bhairava, Kedāra, Mahā...
They are called Kāla, Madhya, Asra, and Jalpa.
Śrīśaila and Hariścandra— these constitute the eight secret [sites] within the Great Splendor (Mahas); along with Bhīma, Indra, and Aṭṭa, they are with Vimala.
Those known as Kanakhala, Nākhalā, Kurusthiti, and Gayā;
This group of eight, which is exceedingly secret, resides in the wind together with the subtle elements and the ego; indeed, [therein] are those known as Sthāṇu and Suvarṇa.
The Bhadra, the Gokarṇaka, and the Mahālayaka.
This sacred place, known as Avimukta, Rudrakoti, and Vastrapada, is situated in the sky;
[therein lies] Sthūlasthūleśa and Śaṅku.
Then Śrutikālā and Maṇḍalabhṛt.
The pair of *mākoṭa* eggs and the eight *chagalāṇḍa* eggs, however, reside in the *ahaṃkāra*;
others, moreover, end with the *ahaṃkāra*.
They say that the subtle elements and the sense organs [are derived from them].
In the intellect (*dhi*), there are eight divine origins;
in primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there are indeed the eightfold yoga beginning with *akṛta*.
Thus, there are the seven groups of eight worlds.
The foundation extends from the waters down to the root.
In [the principles of] Nari, Vāmā, and the others, there are eleven Rudras; in Vitkalā, Niyati, and the rest, there are two worlds for each.
At the time of the *matha*, there would be three *tantras* during the night.
This Vidyā consists of eight and twenty-eight worlds; it leads men to the end of night. [Sanskrit]
The perfectly pure path of all levels (adhvan), as well-defined by the teaching of the Supreme Lord,
[is established] within the intellect, in space, in the body, and in the vital breath.
Having perceived [the Self] within consciousness, one beholds the Supreme Lord.
Within Vidyā there are five; then, within Īśvara, there is the group of eight Vidyeśvaras. Thus is the enumeration of all the worlds.
Regarding that which was stated as one hundred and eighteen:
"Thus, among all the *tattvas*, one hundred and eighteen worlds are to be fully known in brief, but not in detail. [End of quote on *tattva*.]
In Sādākhya there is a pentad;
thus the Śāntā [tattva] consists of eighteen worlds. This entire path is [thus described].
In the body, in the vital breath, in the intellect, and in the great ether.
And perceiving the Supreme within consciousness,
one becomes Bhairava due to that fullness.
Having heard the command of the Supreme Lord,
the king set out on his journey,
his body burning with the fire of asceticism.
Having seen him, she, full of agitation and longing, approached her husband.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Path of Space," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the eighth chapter. Next, the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) is described—
that which consists of manifestation, [the expansion of absolute freedom].
The entire collection of worlds, containing within it the infinite variety of subjects and objects of experience,

is permeated by that which is of the nature of Great Light; for, according to the principle that "that which does not shine forth does not manifest," since the universe consists of the expansion of absolute freedom, that which is the underlying continuity is established through the impossibility of the manifestation of the world otherwise.

"Form shines; that alone is Śiva. That which is the form of Paramaśiva is like a great universal generality (*mahāsāmānyakalpa*). However, that form which is followed by only a few specific distinctions is a *tattva*, such as "earth," as it has been said:
For instance, the nature of Earth consists in the manifestation of stability, hardness, weight, and so forth, extending from the abode of Time (Kāla) up to the city of Vīrabhadra.
Thus, just as the designation "cow" is applied to a brindled cow, a hornless one, and so forth, due to their connection with the [universal] *gotva*,
so too the designation "earth" is applied to Kālāgni and other such entities because they manifest as support (*dhṛti*), hardness (*kāṭhinya*), grossness (*sthūlatva*), and so on.
Its name consists of the forms of support, hardness, grossness, and the like.
It pervades the entire universe, presided over by the Lords of the Worlds (Bhuvaneśas), beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Vīrabhadra.
Therein, the relationship of cause and effect among these principles (tattvas) is demonstrated; and that is of two kinds:
the ultimate (pāramārthika). [The meaning of "ultimate" is as follows: from the perspective of worldly view...]

Even during the manifestation of creation and so forth, because this universe consists of the expansion of the nature of independent light, it remains established through persistence— which is non-different from its own nature— and through withdrawal, which is rest within its own nature; thus, nothing whatsoever has arisen in it that is distinct from its own nature, and therefore there is nothing [new].

"Being conceptual" means being ultimately real. [Now, an objection: "If this is so, then how does this foundation of the universe, which appears with necessity, persist? Therefore, a conceptual relationship of cause and effect must necessarily be postulated for the sake of the universe's persistence. To this, he says: "Created."

[He] is created and established by *niyati*. In this regard, the ultimate causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is as follows: it belongs solely to the Lord, who is independent and whose nature is that of the agent, [manifesting] in such a form beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth—a form which is non-different from His own essence and yet rests within His own essence.
[This is] the expansion. However, the imagined relationship of cause and effect is constructed by the will of the Supreme Lord through the vital force of necessity (*niyati*).
And that [relationship] consists in the manifestation of a fixed temporal sequence for as long as and whenever [it occurs], even when other factors are present.
[For example], although there is a concomitance (*anvaya*) of the staff, the wheel, and so forth, clay alone is the cause; that [clay], however—

"Cooperative cause" (*sahakārī*) means "concomitance of essential nature" (*svarūpānugama*). By this, the [objection regarding] the rising of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī and so forth—which, despite the appearance of a temporal sequence between cause and effect, is excluded—is refuted; for in that case, there is no concomitance of form.
It is only to this extent that it is "concomitant with its own nature. By this [phrase "by this"],...

The manifestation of causality—which consists in a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority assisted by the continuity of form—occurs through the will of the Supreme Lord, and not as an objective reality; for even from the will of a yogin, a sprout may arise from a seed, or a jar and so forth may appear in dreams and the like. To this it might be objected: "But surely, in a dream, the notion that 'a sprout comes from a jar' is an illusion."
[The dream is not like this; rather, its manifestation persists until awakening. For this very reason it has been said:

"And that [manifestation] lasts only for that long. Even so, he says "nevertheless" (tathāpi) regarding the fact that the Supreme Lord's agency is never lost. Thus, even though it is unconstructed (akalpita), this ultimate reality remains established.

For when form, which stands as the basis for the ultimate truth, is present, all this—consisting of the imagined relationship of cause and effect such as clay, the staff, and so forth—is logically possible;
it would not be so otherwise. Therefore, by means of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), [the effect arises].

The causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is that single form which consists in the essential nature of the various factors resting within a single cognizer; it is not, however, the individual factors such as the staff and so forth taken separately. As it has been said:
"In every undertaking, whether it be the action itself or the instrument and so forth, [it exists] everywhere."
May the universe be independent; in that regard, you alone are the creator.
Thus; likewise elsewhere:

"I take refuge in that digit of consciousness which shines in whatever form, in whatever manner, and as whatever object—be it space, time, or substance. In this way, [it is established that consciousness is] the causality.

This is logical; for she consists of the entire web of existents, and by virtue of the greatness of autonomous consciousness, she possesses the nature of each respective mass of objects fixed in their own particular place and time.
At the moment of the production of the essential form of each individual thing, she is of such-and-such a nature; for otherwise, there would be a change in that which is already so constituted.
Just as [the consciousness] increases, so too does the heterogeneity of the object increase in proportion;

thus, the Supreme Lord, whose very nature is the sovereignty of consciousness, has the entire universe as His body—[the visible world being the "body" according to the principle stated in the *Śivasūtras*]. But one might object:
How could even that which is perceived through direct perception come to be the object of a contrary cognition?

For instance, in the making of a jar by a potter, agency is seen directly; it does not belong to Śiva, who is imperceptible, because it is the potter who is observed to be actively engaged in the process through direct perception. To this, he says:
Regarding "the consciousness of the potter," it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"The consciousness of a potter when he employs the wheel, the stick, and so forth, is indeed Śiva himself; for what distinction can there be in consciousness?"

Thus [it was said]. Now, one who is dissatisfied with the argument that "the potter's consciousness" is improper— on the grounds that the potter, as the agent of action, is indicated by the body alone, according to the maxim of moving the head, back, and hips— speaks again as follows, beginning with "of the potter's body," etc., just as:

There is no dispute regarding the agency of anything within the aggregate of existing things (*bhāvarāśi*); likewise, because the body is insentient, it is equal to the aggregate of existing things. Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between these two in terms of their existence, as both are dependent upon another. Enough [of this digression]. [The creator] of the jar and so forth—

If it is asked, "Since the consciousness of the potter is not distinct [from the Supreme Consciousness] and the potter's body is included within the aggregate of existing things, how can there be the potter's body’s conceit of being an agent?"— [the answer is that this is] brought about by the Supreme Lord.
[Like a surety, there is the conceit of being a debtor. In this very way, the conceit of agency belonging to the potter’s body—like that of a jar and so forth—will exist;
that is to say, there will be a similarity between the conceit and the jar. Therefore...
The theory of the causal complex (*sāmagrīvāda*) also applies only to consciousness whose body is the universe. As for the position of separate factors, it remains far removed from reality;
for clay, the wheel, the staff, and so forth, when separate, are never capable of producing a jar, whereas when combined, they cannot do so without resting within a single cognizing subject.

[They] are capable; this is beyond dispute. It is a corroborative factor for agency. In the phrase "on Meru" (*merau*), by the word *meru*, there is the quality of being difficult for the gods to attain, vastness, and uniqueness.
In the phrase "such a jar would not exist," by the word "such" (*tathāvidha*),...

The fact that [the world] must be abandoned by humans, its atomicity, and its multiplicity are implied. Having realized Meru as the Lord of the Vessel (Ghaṭanāyaka) because he possesses infinite power, and having accomplished [all things], O Śivā, what agency remains for you thereafter?
By this, it is stated elsewhere that even the act of creating Mount Meru brings no skillful benefit to Śiva, and so forth:

"The Sun, who moves in the center of the celestial sphere and assumes all forms—Śiva’s agency, which brings about his very existence by His own will alone," and so on. Indeed, [the power] does not reside there.
Such a jar would exist. Thus, when this state of being an effect is conceptualized,
regarding the causal relationship of the principles (tattvas) within the scriptures, [the nature of their] causality—
The reading is *prati*. Because it exists as having many modes precisely due to its ultimate reality consisting in appearing in such a way,
its relationship as cause and effect is described in both the world and the treatises.
In the *Rauravasaṃgraha*, it is stated that [the unmanifest arises] from Māyā and Kalā;
however, in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara), it is said that the Unmanifest arises from the principle of Kalā.

[The phrase] "and so forth" indicates its manifold nature. That too is consistent, just as a scorpion may arise from cow dung, from an insect, from the will of a yogi, or from a mantra and medicinal herbs. In that case, given such a manifold nature, which one possesses logical validity?
For when there is a multiplicity of forms, enough with the logic of the easily agitated camel!

To refute the great delusion that has arisen through the rejection of the arguments of others, he says "In that regard," and so forth. [By the view of our own system and by the view of previous scriptures. By the view of our own system, we shall demonstrate that [position] as it has been imagined. In that regard, the Supreme Lord is replete with five powers.
[He is] self-sufficient and complete. As it has been said:
"He manifests the state of the principles consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā through the differentiated manifestation of the five powers. Thus it was stated.

Manifesting that respective power as primary through His sovereignty— [for indeed, the presence of all five powers exists everywhere; thus, while one is primary, the others are secondary, but this does not mean they are non-existent].

In five ways: here indeed, the Supreme Śiva himself, whose nature is pure consciousness, though devoid of desire because of his perfection, by virtue of the majesty of his own sovereignty and with the desire to manifest externally,
through the gradations of the wonder of supreme bliss, first [appears] in the form of the reflective awareness "I."

Abiding in the state of power (*śakti-daśā*), He should manifest; immediately thereafter, through the nature of the two-fold reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I" and "this," He should cause that dual nature to appear. And therein, when the Supreme Lord causes the aspect of "this" (*idamaṃśa*) to emerge within the aspect of "I" (*aham*) which has pure consciousness alone as its locus, then—

Because its object is the mass of phenomena (*bhāvarāśi*) which, at the mere opening [of consciousness], is like a painting and thus indistinct, the Sadāśiva-tattva is characterized by the predominance of will (*icchā*).
When the mass of phenomena has become manifest as "I am this," and the aspect of "I" (*aham-aṃśa*) pours itself into the aspect of "this" (*idam-aṃśa*) within that very locus, then—

The category of Īśvara is characterized primarily by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). When the manifestation of the "this" aspect occurs within the mass of objective phenomena where duality has become firmly rooted—expressed as "this am I"—the "I" aspect shines forth as being grounded solely in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). This is the nature of Īśvara according to those who maintain the doctrine of non-duality-in-difference (*bhedādvaitavādins*).

The reflective awareness of "I am this," according to the analogy of the two pans of a balance scale being held equally, is the *vidyā-tattva*, which is characterized primarily by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); such is the fivefold division. [It remains thus: when consciousness (*cit*) is predominant, it is the *śiva-tattva*;
when bliss (*ānanda*) is predominant, it is the *śakti-tattva*; and when will (*icchā*) is predominant, it is the *sadāśiva-tattva*, for will— [...is indeed... (the text continues).

Because it consists in the acceptance of the state of equality between knowledge and action, the principle of Īśvara prevails when the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is predominant, and the principle of Vidyā prevails when the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is predominant. Up to this point,
although there are differences in states such as Śiva and the others, there is no [alteration] because one's own essential nature remains an indivisible and desireless reality.
"A certain distinction of state exists because it abides above *māyā* and because it is of the nature of the Fourth (*turya*);

thus, the pentad of principles (*tattva-pañcaka*) is characterized solely by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). And here, the Lords of the Principles—Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Ananta—are like Brahmā in the *nivṛtti* [kalā]. In the *nivṛtti*...

[In the context of the *nivṛttikalā* which is about to be described: Now, it has been stated that "the reality (*tattva*) consists in the persistence of a single form amidst the manifold"; how, then, is this so here? He says: "of these," etc.
The five particular instances (*viśeṣa*) which are the objects of the persistence of these general forms (*sāmānyarūpa*) are as follows: those belonging to Śambhu (*śāmbhava*).

The Śaktas, Mantramaheshvaras, Mantreshvaras, and Mantras constitute the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). Within this much, Śiva is the direct agent. Furthermore, Aghoreśa—whose other name is Ananta—creates the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), beginning with Māyā, by the power of the will of Īśvara.

For those individual souls (*aṇu*) who possess a craving for agitated enjoyment, that capacity for the desire to remain [in their state]— which is clearly the result of agitation known as craving acting as a cooperative cause— arises by the power of the Lord’s will.

Thus, when the karma-mala acts as a cooperative cause, its very orientation toward the future is what constitutes the longing for enjoyment (*bhoga-lolikā*), for the sake of accomplishing that enjoyment. [In this regard, one might object: "But even there, is it not the karma-mala alone that is the primary cause of transmigratory existence?"
Thus, in all cases, karma alone has been stated to be the cause of saṃsāra; yet, here again, what is this *lolikā*? To this he says:

"In that regard," and so forth. *Lolika* is a vibration (*parispanda*) consisting of the sense of being incomplete; it is merely a desire devoid of action, because it lacks the nature of actual activity.

It is merely a desire devoid of action because it lacks a specifically determined object; therefore, it is the delimitation of the future. For this very reason, impurity (*mala*) is not a separate ontological principle (*tattva*). Since it does not directly act as a substratum for delimitation, it is not some kind of real entity, but rather the mere non-manifestation of one's own full nature—this is the meaning.

The "capacity for future limitation" is not a distinct principle (*tattva*) from the person (*pums*); rather, the *rāga-tattva* is desire delimited by action. Action is the general form [expressed as] "may something happen to me," whereas *rāga* is a property of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*), variegated by the distinctions of various actions.
[It is variegated by way of specific forms such as hunger, thirst, and so forth. The distinction that it is variegated by the differentiation of karma will be explained later.
As for this [objection]: "But surely the established doctrine is that consciousness alone is independent and the ultimate reality; how then can there be anything other than that?"

Fearing that one might suspect "impurity" (*mala*) to be some kind of real entity, he says: "This very [impurity]. Impurity is nothing other than the Supreme Lord’s own will to conceal His own nature;
moreover, because its essence consists in such concealment, it exists even in the earth and other elements solely as the will of the Supreme Lord.
The meaning is that, just as earth and the other elements possess their respective forms despite being non-different from the Light of the Other (paraprakāśa), so too does impurity (mala). [Note:

The reading "of earth and the rest, which are essentially the will of the Supreme Lord" (parameśvarecchātmana eva dharādeḥ) is also found. This is because they are real entities (vastu). And that... [Now,] (Note: The provided text fragment ends with "And that" and "Now," indicating the sentence is incomplete.)
Furthermore, by reflecting upon his non-difference from Śiva through the will of Śambhu,
he gradually attains the nature of Śiva, appearing as the object of knowledge for the Mantreśvaras.

Since this has been stated, one might ask: "How can there still be impurity (mala) even for the *vijñānakevala*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that [impurity]. Impurity existing in the *vijñānakevala* is oriented toward destruction; thus, it does not nourish its own effect, which is karma.

But for the *pralayakevala* (the soul isolated by dissolution), karma— which remains as if yawning while being reinforced by impurity (*mala*)— is the instrumental cause for the experience of the manifold variety of saṃsāra; thus, it belongs to those individual souls (*aṇu*) who are permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that experience.

It is rightly said that the glorious Aghoreśa creates for the sake of the attainment of enjoyments; and the agitation of impurity (*mala*) occurs solely through the power of the Lord’s will (which thereby refutes the position that it arises from the inherent capacity of things). He confirms this very point with the words beginning "insentient," etc., as it has been stated:
"Since an insentient thing is nowhere capable [of acting] without being presided over by consciousness.

This is because an insentient thing lacks inherent capacity anywhere at all. [Regarding the so-called "atom": Now, enough with this talk of the supreme non-duality (*parādvaya*), since the Lord might simply employ distinct atoms as instruments.

Anticipating this objection, he says "the atom" (*aṇu*), and so forth. Therefore, because its nature is consciousness, the Great Lord alone is the essence of light; what is called the "atom" is simply the state of being insentient, which is the form of impurity assumed through His own sovereignty.
As it has been said:

"Śiva himself has assumed the state of the bound soul (paśu). Indeed, the manifestation of both the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit) is his very nature; his conscious form is sovereignty itself, while his unconscious form is impurity (mala). And for him who creates, that [impurity] consists of the will of the Supreme Lord, and from that very source it is eternal.

[Because they have come from the negation whose nature is destruction, which is denoted by the word *mā*, following the etymological meaning of the word *māyā*. Of the form belonging to the object that is about to be created [the reading in manuscript k is: "of the object belonging to the desired thing, because of its insentience"].

Because it is to be manifested as insentient (*jaḍatā*), and because it is measured—that is, delimited as something to be abandoned—by yogins, it is "insentient" (*jaḍa*). Furthermore, because it takes the form of pervading all effects and so forth, it is "all-pervasive" (*vyāpaka*) [it is called pervasive because it is subtle and thus measures everywhere]. This is the principle (*tattva*) known as *māyā*.
The material cause and that which effects its manifestation belong to the Supreme Lord—
who delights in the play of manifesting the entire universe; His sovereignty in the manifestation of duality,
and through that, the power which measures (mīnāti) or destroys (hinasti) by means of the projection of incompleteness, is called the power of Māyā.
Māyā is indeed a power that is entirely distinct from Him. [Now,
if it is accepted that the power of Māyā belonging to the Lord is invariable, then how can this [power] bring about the determination of difference?]

"In this regard, it is said that one should attain the state of reality (*tattvabhāva*): just as even the powers beginning with *kalā* are designated as *tattvas* when they belong to the Supreme Lord, so too is *māyā*. And thus it has been said:
'That which consists in the intensification of the limited agency of one whose power is obstructed...'"
The power of the Lord, which casts the individual soul downward, is called Kalā.

"Just as the power of Māyā attains a differentiated state of essential being, so too does the other expansion of principles (tattvas), beginning with Kalā. Thus, the twofold nature of the principles from Kalā down to Earth must also be described. And regarding this twofold nature:

The teachers of Abhinavagupta have also stated a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): that which appears in one's volition (*saṃkalpa*) exists externally as well, in a distinct and manifest form, like a jar. Therefore, the following formal argument is established here: the collection of principles beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) exists externally, because it appears separately in volition and the like; whatever appears separately in volition and the like [exists externally].

That which exists externally is distinct, as in the case of a jar or similar objects; and wherever something exists externally, it appears as distinct, as in the case of the Supreme Self (paramātman). Since the collection of principles beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra) appears as distinct, they must exist externally to the Supreme Self. Furthermore, although the appearance of distinctness persists in such passages as "this Self is once and for all manifest," [it is nonetheless established that the external world exists].

Like a flash of lightning, it would not undergo further growth; for, according to the principle expressed in such passages as "the Self is liberated in its sovereignty," there is no concealment of its nature as consisting of the fundamental, undivided *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (I-consciousness).
And thus, even [in the case of] Māyā, Kalā, and so forth, or like a sky-flower...

[Even for things such as a sky-flower, non-existence depends upon time and so forth; therefore, this very path applies, and thus no further deliberation is needed. "This very path" refers to the purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason.
And by this, those who resort to knowledge in the form of direct realization regarding objects such as Māyā, Kalā, Prakṛti, and Buddhi—

They too are established as accomplished [for they are also defined as being of the nature of the powers of Māyā and the rest]. This being the case, the manifestation of the universe proceeds from the principle of Māyā.

For since *māyā* abides as a universal commonality within all subjects; and although that [sequence] is indeed non-sequential [by way of ultimate cause-and-effect], nevertheless, by the aforementioned perspective [of the conceptual cause-and-effect], sequence appears. That too is thus described.

In this regard, the group of powers such as *kalā* and so forth is distinct for each individual (*pratyātman*), because their effects—such as the strengthening of agency—are perceived according to the distinction between individuals;

that is, because the collection of their effects, such as limited agency and knowledge, is experienced as being different for each individual. One person, having performed a certain action, knows it, while another, having performed something else, knows that.

"One knows" refers to the perception of individual distinctions. However, that group—the group of arts and so forth—may at times become unified [as in the case of watching actors or wrestlers], even by the will of the Lord, like the selves of the members of an audience; therein, this entire group of arts and so forth is pure.

In that context, the purity of *kalā* pertains to the worship and meditation upon the Supreme Lord; *rāga* generates an intense attachment directed toward the Lord; *vidyā* likewise produces discernment regarding Him; *kāla* effects the reckoning of time specifically for His instruction and so forth; and *niyati* governs the very process of His propitiation and the like.
Restriction (*niyamana*): That which, by virtue of having the Supreme Lord as its object,
performs its own function conducive to attaining His true nature—
because it stands in opposition to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)— and that [function] comes about through the power of the descent of the Supreme Lord’s grace (*parameśvara-śaktipāta*).

We shall explain this in its elucidation. Impurity (*aśuddha*), however, is the opposite of that. In that regard, *kalā* is born from *māyā*, which joins the individual soul (*aṇu*)—who is in a state comparable to deep sleep—with a limited capacity for agency.
For *māyā*, by effecting a separation of the soul from Śiva who consists of consciousness, brings about a state similar to deep sleep for the soul.

The utility of *vidyā* and *kalā* lies in their state of being devoid of seeing and acting. And that [utility] exists when there is a swelling (*ucchūnatva*) of both *māyā* and the *aṇu* (the individual soul), which is the seed of transmigratory existence. Now, one might object: "We must determine how it is that the connection between the *kalā*s and the *puruṣa* is the effect of *māyā*; for why should *māyā* alone be the material cause (*upādāna*) of *kalā*, and not the *aṇu*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "*māyāṇvoḥ*" (of *māyā* and the *aṇu*).
And so it has been said:

"This *kalā*, though born from the conjunction of *māyā* and the *aṇu*, does not make the *aṇu* its material cause (*upādāna*), but rather [makes] *māyā*, which is subject to transformation. [Thus it is] because of their conjunction.
Even when it has arisen, Māyā transforms itself, not even the slightest thing remaining untransformed; such is its nature as the effect of Māyā.
As it has been said: "Mala is the concealer, while Māyā is the material cause of objective existence."
Karma alone would indeed be the auxiliary cause for the arising of pleasure and pain.

Thus: for a material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa), having undergone a modification of its own nature, exists as that which follows the effect, as clay does in the case of a jar and the like; but the atom (aṇu) is not so, because it is eternal due to its being of the singular nature of consciousness (cideka-rūpa). Therefore, even though [the world] is born from the conjunction of both [the self and the atoms], Māyā alone is its material cause. Of this [Māyā]. Thus.

Due to their mutual interpenetration, there is no discernible distinction between the male and female principles. However, through the grace of a certain Lord— such as Ananteśa, who holds authority over Māyā and its womb— there occurs, upon the exhaustion of all karma, a discrimination between Māyā and Puruṣa, by which one remains forever as a Vijñānākala above Māyā.

Either there is the discernment of *kalā* from *māyā* and *puruṣa*, by which one remains above *kalā* [and does not transmigrate below *māyā*]; or there is the discernment of *prakṛti* (nature) from *puruṣa*, by which one does not transmigrate below *pradhāna*; or [if it is thus] the discernment of *mala* from *puruṣa*.
He explains when one goes beyond that *māyā* with the words "when the impurity of the person" (*malapuruṣa*). "But" (*tu*) refers to equality with Śiva.

When there is the vision of the fullness of the Person (*puruṣa-pūrṇatā-dṛṣṭi*)—that is, when the impressions of impurity have subsided and the firmness of reflective awareness known as autonomy (*svātantrya*) has been attained—then there is indeed Śiva-hood itself. Thus.

The principle of *kalā* alone bestows limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*), and agency does not belong to one who is ignorant. Limited knowledge is bestowed by *aśuddhavidyā*, which is born from *kalā*. [Now, it may be asked: what establishes this agency that was not mentioned by the Sāṃkhyas?

If it is argued that the *kalātattva* is sufficient for this, [the author] says "she" (*sā*) to address the question: "What is the purpose of the *vidyātattva*, which is said by them to denote the state of being a knower (*jñatva*) through the medium of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth?
And *vidyā* perceives the intellect and grasps with discrimination the pleasure and other qualities residing therein.

Regarding the intellect (*buddhi*), which possesses a form mixed with the qualities (*guṇa*): although the Sāṃkhyas hold that it is covered by *tamas*, which is of the nature of veiling, yet because *rajas* gradually removes that [covering], it is set in motion in certain instances; thus, even though *sattva* is of the nature of illumination without distinction, it would manifest pleasure and so forth in succession.

Although they say that the intellect (*buddhi*), though composed of the three *guṇas*, reveals its object—consisting of pleasure and so forth—by means of gradual discrimination, nevertheless, the intellect would only display the object consisting of pleasure and so forth like a mirror, and not through discrimination because it is intermingled with the *guṇas*. Therefore, he says: "of the intellect, whose form is intermingled with the *guṇas*," and so forth.

Because it is impossible to grasp [the Self] through discrimination; therefore, the object reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*) is discriminated by knowledge (*vidyā*). [Objection: Is it not the case that limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) exists only in some instances for the sake of establishing some part [of the Self], precisely by virtue of being a limited knower (*kiñcijjña*)?

Since even the state of being an agent of something has already been implied, for what purpose is the word "something" mentioned again in the phrase "being an agent of something"? To this he says: "only in certain cases. The operation of the *rāga-tattva* culminates in the sense of "agency," and its specific function lies in the portion expressed as "only in certain cases. [Is it not so?]
The Sāṅkhyas have stated that the cause here is a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by non-detachment (*avairāgya*).

To the question, "What is the use of this novel principle of passion (*rāga*? he says, "And not," and so forth. That [attachment] is not caused by non-detachment, because even in one who is non-detached, attachment is observed; for attachment is seen even toward virtue (*dharma*) and other such things when one is detached.

And because, even in one who is satiated with food and the like, there is no absence of non-detachment (*avairāgya*) due to the non-disappearance of the passion (*rāga*) residing within; for otherwise, it would follow that non-detachment could never arise again. Therefore, this is the very power of the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*) itself, that all qualities such as non-detachment and so forth appear in the intellect (*buddhi*) as external manifestations.

Regarding the phrase "especially the manifestation": Time, by measuring its effects—that which is delimited by it—also measures agency, since otherwise the cognitions "I have done," "I am doing," and "I will do" would be inexplicable. This is because, although the quality of being a knower (*kvacittva*) is equal [in all cases], agency belongs to this [consciousness] alone; such is the meaning here.
The operation belongs to *niyati*. Even regarding the relationship between cause and effect, its operation alone is at work; therefore, this tetrad arises from *kalā* alone.
This very [phrase "this very one," etc. is the sequential enumeration of *māyā*, *kalā*, *kāla*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, and *niyati*. Now knowing [only] a little, I am attached and act.

Consciousness of this kind, residing within the body, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth, is called the bound soul (*paśu*). This very group of six, beginning with *māyā*, remains firmly attached— like husks— to the Self, which is like the grain of rice.

The "six coverings" (kañcuka-ṣaṭka) are so called because, since consciousness has been cast aside by Māyā, the [principles] beginning with Kalā remain above it like coverings. Thus, regarding that limited agency which is the effect of Māyā, there is an agency characterized by "limitedness" (kiñcittva) which serves as the substantive (viśeṣya). In that regard—

It has been established that *kalā*, while active, is the cause for the production of *vidyā* and the other categories. Now, regarding the qualifying portion which was described as "something" (*kiñcit*): first, the definition of *kalā* is agency characterized by the nature of being "something"; therein, as for the agency which constitutes the substantive element within that qualified portion— [The text continues: ...that [agency]... [is what is meant].

Likewise, although the nature of the enjoyer and the agency itself are unconditioned, because they have only a partial object, they possess a partial form consisting of the aspect of the qualification; this remains strictly within the domain of the knowable.
Consequently, when [the Self] emerges by making that partial aspect its own motivator, it shines forth.
With respect to the specific objects of experience yet to be manifested, Pradhāna is that which consists of the general nature of the object of experience and has the form of the enjoyer.
As long as that Kalā separates him from his own self and brings about his manifestation in the form of an external state, so long is he precisely this [limited subject].

Of the principle of *prakṛti*— which is synonymous with the equilibrium of its qualities (*guṇasāmya*)— and which is the mere universal permeated by the specific objects of experience consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion (the meaning being that the principle of *pradhāna* is of the nature of equilibrium and undifferentiated, since a particular must be preceded by a universal).

Regarding "creation" (*sarga*): it is said that the dyad consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed is produced simultaneously— indeed, "for *kalā* produces both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer equally, inseparable from one another through the intention toward differentiation."

Thus, although there is non-duality due to the ultimate reality of non-duality— as expressed in such statements as "In truth, the enjoyer alone always exists everywhere in the form of the enjoyed"— nevertheless, with reference to the differentiation belonging to *māyā*:
Thus, inseparability has been shown to have the characteristic of mutual dependence. Emanation is dependent upon the *kalā*-tattva;
and here, according to the actual path, this [emanation] is indeed devoid of sequential order because of their mutual dependence.
