The meaning is: "of the sequence. It has been stated that there is creation (*sṛṣṭi*), and the particle *api* (also) implies that there is also the manifestation of sequence.

The sense of the word *api* is that "that single sequence is manifold," according to the maxim of "the enemy's prosperity" (*śatru-ṛddhi-makṣyāya*). The maxim "the enemy's prosperity" refers to the case where one and the same person is both an enemy and prosperous.

This has already been stated. Furthermore, the sequence of knowledge (*vidyā*), passion (*rāga*), and so forth, is observed to be diverse: some experience [passion] while knowing, others know while experiencing passion, and so on. Therefore, one should consider that even the presentation of a different sequence in scriptures such as the *Raurava* is not contradictory. That very same object of enjoyment (*bhogya-sāmānya*), when it has reached a state of agitation, is the *guṇa-tattva*.
[Now, one might object: "Surely, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, *prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;

how then can it be said that pleasure and so forth residing in *prakṛti* are objects of enjoyment? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this context," *sattva* is pleasure, which is the manifestation in the form of an object of enjoyment; *duḥkha*...

Rajas is of the nature of vibration consisting of both light and darkness, and for that very reason, it is of the form of action (kriyā). Tamas is delusion (moha), which is of the nature of the absence of light. All three of these are of the nature of the object of enjoyment (bhogya). Thus, [surely, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, the Pradhāna is only in a state of agitation...]

Anticipating the objection, "Let that [guṇatattva] be the cause of the group of effects; for what purpose was it said that the guṇatattva is produced through conceptualization (kalpanā)? he says, "In this way" (*evam*). As it has been stated:
"Indeed, a cause that has not undergone differentiation (*vaiṣamya*) is not capable of producing an effect. [This occurs] from the *pradhāna* when it is agitated.

The arising of another activity [the reading "kartṛvyāpārāntarodaya" is also found] does not occur from that which is undisturbed; therefore, a disturbance must necessarily be admitted in the interval. Thus, it is established that the principle of the *guṇas*, which is distinct [from the soul], exists—just as was stated by the Sāṃkhya.
That other agitation which does not obstruct the reflective awareness of the nature of the causal state is the effect; it is like the swelling of the seed and the sprout that follows it.
Thus, the sense is that one must also accept that the qualities (*guṇas*) possess the nature of reality (*tattva*).

[Now, an objection might be raised: "Since this [Prakṛti] is insentient (*jaḍa*), how can there arise in her an orientation toward producing effects, and consequently, how could there even be agitation (*kṣubdhatva*)? To this he says, beginning with "And that agitation," etc. The intention here is as follows:

For in the Sāṃkhya system, because the *puruṣa* is changeless, there is indeed no distinction between the states of bondage and liberation; thus, even toward one who is liberated, why would *prakṛti* not proceed to produce the entire collection of evolutes beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), since its inherent nature of activity has not departed? Nor does it [cease].
Because it lacks consciousness, there is no such reflection as "I have been seen by him" or "I shall act for this purpose";
therefore, there would indeed be no liberation. In our view, however, the agitation (*kṣobha*) is brought about by the independent Lord as the agent;
thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Furthermore, this agitation of *prakṛti* occurs precisely through the presiding influence of the Lord of the principles (*tattveśa*).

Otherwise, it would not be established that [the reflection] occurs necessarily with respect to the person (*puruṣa*). Therefore, from the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*), the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) arises, wherein both the light of the person and the object are reflected. For the reflection of an object is of two kinds:
through the gateway of the senses, as in perception and so forth; and without that gateway, as in imagination and so forth.
And because it serves as the substratum for the reflection of the light of the subject (*puṃprakāśa*), the intellect (*buddhi*)—despite its insentience (*jāḍya*)—is the illuminator of objects.
[This is] what is being imparted. From the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) [arises].

And the specific effect (*asādhāraṇa-kārya*) of the ego-sense is written here because of its utility in this context: the ego-sense itself, through its function (*vṛtti*) consisting of impulsive activity (*saṃrambhātmikā*).

It is that [ego] which effects the impulsion of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, by means of which one lives as long as there is the penetration of the experience of karma; and at its cessation, it effects their non-impulsion, by means of which one dies. As it has been stated elsewhere:
"The fivefold wind is produced by the ego through its form of agitation."

"Impelled, one may exist for the sake of life; otherwise, however, there is death. Thus, when the light of the person (puruṣaprakāśa) is defiled by contact with the object of knowledge reflected in the intellect (buddhi), there arises the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding that which is not the self, just like the conceit of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. For this very reason, its "artificiality" (*kṛtakatva*) is stated by the word *kāra*; however, for the Sāṃkhya...

That is not tenable; for he does not desire that the Self consist of the reflective awareness of "I," whereas we do desire even agency for it. And that [agency] is pure reflective awareness alone, without a counter-correlate; and thus, because this ego-sense consists of the sovereignty of pure consciousness—

Because its true nature is resting solely within itself, there arises from the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) that emerges by its own inherent force (*svarasa*) this specific distinction: namely, that it is fixed upon the intellect (*buddhi*), which is insentient and not the Self.
Thus, "I am" consists of the wonder of one's own Self. This is the functional aggregate (*karaṇaskandha*) of this ego-sense.
[The meaning is: the nature of the sense organs. The primordial constituent (*prakṛti-skandha*), however, [means:
the nature of the cause]; it is threefold due to the distinction between *sattva* and the others.
Among these, the *sāttvika* [is that which has *sattva* as its predominance, since even *rajas* and *tamas* are subordinate to it].

The meaning is "existence. Because the mind and the five sense organs—therein, with respect to the mind as that which is produced—the progenitor is endowed with the capacity to produce all the subtle elements (*tanmātras*). But in the case of the ear, it is distinguished by the capacity to produce sound. [All are mutual consorts; all are everywhere.]
By stating "going toward," because they function as mutual pairs, even though the ego (ahaṃkāra) is dominated by *sattva*,
the production of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) occurs from the ego that is dominated by *tamas*.

From the *ahaṅkāra*, which is superior to everything, the mind (*manas*) arises; from this it follows that the mind possesses the capacity to produce all the subtle elements (*tanmātras*). Consequently, there would be a relationship of perceived and perceiver between the mind and the objects such as sound and the rest.
In that regard, the specific qualities of the three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are known as desire (*icchā*), effort (*saṃrambha*), and cognition (*bodha*).

[Thus they have been defined elsewhere. This means that since the nose possesses the capacity to produce the perception of odor, it is composed of the elements (bhautika). Furthermore, the logical position (*tarkamata*) is that the sense organs are elemental because their status as apprehended object and apprehending subject would otherwise be inexplicable; and thus, because the nose is earthen (*pārthivatva*), it [perceives odor].

By the passage beginning with "being elemental" (*bhautikatva*), he demonstrates the incorrectness of the claim that [the sense of smell] is the grasper of odor alone and not of taste and so forth. Furthermore, because of the clear accompaniment of such expressions as "I hear," the nature of the ear and other senses as being derived from the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-principle) is evident, since they function as instruments (*karaṇa*).

"How is its status as an instrument (karaṇatva) possible otherwise? Why? To this he says "the instrument," and so forth. If it is argued that "otherwise" means [the instrument acts] through the very part of the agent (kartraṃśa) because it is the object of the action, [we reply] no, for then an infinite regress (anavasthā) would follow. Since it is derived from the ego (ahaṃkārika), it is logical that it possesses contact with the part of the agent, because the ego-function (ahaṃkṛta) is permeated by the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa). K. 1.22.3–4.

And as for the reading "kāraṇatve ca": the word "ca" (and) implies that [the sense organ] must necessarily touch upon the aspect of the agent; otherwise, if it were joined with another instrument, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress and so forth. And this aspect of the agent is indeed the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense); therefore, in the primary instrument...
As it has been said:
"For without *vidyā*, the other instruments have no inherent existence;
and without *kalā*, there is no agency or subjectivity in that [consciousness]."
"Therefore, they know that *kalā* and *vidyā* are the primary instruments for persons. Thus, there are two cognitions in a person:

*vidyā* with respect to knowledge and *kalā* with respect to action; for one who is blind and lame, because the cognitions and actions consisting of the form of "I-ness" have not departed [but upon their departure, toward external objects...]

Activity would not occur. As it has been said: "Therefore, when this [self] is deprived of the organs of cognition and action in certain cases, form and movement do not appear to an blind man or a lame man. [k: The state of the lame man is peaceful.]

The reading is "jñānarūpakriyā. However, from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*) itself, characterized by a predominance of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five organs of action arise. [The organ of] the feet is that which, characterized by the ego in the form "I go," is capable of performing its function.

The primary locus is external; since that [external locus] exists even elsewhere, there is no interruption of movement for one who is ill [the sense being that the action of walking is observed in the hands and so forth]. Nor is there a confusion of functions, because of the very reason already stated: action, instrument, and effect are primary and...
Movement and the like possess the nature of action (*kriyā*), whereas the perception of form and so forth does not, because the latter is classified as a quality (*guṇa*) in the system of Kaṇāda;
therefore, the group of action-faculties (*karmendriya*) must necessarily be admitted. And that group consists of five, because the corresponding functions are fivefold.
For instance, first of all, there is an external connection for the purpose of abandoning, or for taking up, or for both,

or for resting in one's own nature by being devoid of both— [wherein indeed this agitation that "this is to be rejected" and "this is to be accepted" subsides]. In that regard, they are respectively the anus, the hand, the foot, and the generative organ.
However, because of the continuity of the action that serves as the basis for the internal vital breath (*prāṇa*), the organ of speech [is so designated].
Regarding this, one might ask: "But since moving about is done with the hand and grasping with the foot, how can there be such a confusion of mutual functions?
To this he says, "By that," and so forth. For it is not the case that the hand performs moving about, nor does the foot perform grasping.
Rather, it is on a single substratum that both the foot and the hand perform the acts of moving and grasping;
because they pervade the entire body, they are perceived as functioning together, and thus there is no fault whatsoever. As it has been said:
"They perform this cycle of duties without any confusion."

"But the dull-witted perceive a confusion because the sense organs function together. [Thus it is said. One should understand that even the movement occurring in the hand is the action of the organ of the feet (*pādendriya*) alone; therefore, even the infinity of actions would not entail an infinity of sense organs. This much, they say, is the nature of *rajas* as a connector. Others, however, [say]:
They say that the mind arises from the *rājasa* aspect; others, however, hold that the mind arises from the *sāttvika* and the senses from the *rājasa*.

From the *ahaṃkāra* dominated by *tamas*—which conceals the subjective (*bhoktṛ*) portion because the objective (*bhogya*) portion predominates—there arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), which consist solely of the nature of objects of cognition.
For that which precedes the particular sounds—which are of the nature of agitation—is a single entity of the nature of non-agitation; as it has been said:
"Since the state of the particulars must necessarily be preceded by a non-particular state."

Thus, one should not think: "Why should we accept that only the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are perceptible, rather than these non-specific [subtle elements]? The universal, which consists of non-specificity, is the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*).
The same should be said up to the end of smell. Therein, from the agitated subtle element of sound—[from the agitated...]
The meaning is: "ready to produce its effect. Regarding the operation of providing space:
the meaning is that sound is the cause conducive to space because space possesses the operation of providing space.
This is because space is capable of accommodating the superimposition of the object denoted by the word "sound"; therefore, just as sound—

Because it is capable of supporting the superimposition of the denotable within itself, it provides space for everything; likewise, its effect, space (ākāśa), does so as well. The subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra), when agitated, becomes air (vāyu); however, sound remains present because of its non-separation from this space. Form (rūpa), when agitated, becomes fire (tejas); its two preceding qualities [sound and touch], however, remain as before. Taste (rasa), when agitated...

Water consists of the first three elements as before. When smell is agitated, earth arises from the first four elements as before. Others maintain that earth arises from the five elements in the sequence beginning with "wind from sound and touch," and so forth. Furthermore, earth is merely a collection of qualities (*guṇa-samudāya-mātra*); there is no other substratum of qualities (*guṇin*). As it has been said:
"A cognition never arises without the apprehension of smell and the other [sensory objects];
for even when water and the rest are not apprehended, a cognition of earth does arise.
Therefore, earth is not other than smell and the rest, nor is it distinct from water and the others. And in this regard:

In the collection of principles (*tattvakalāpa*), that which possesses a higher quality is the pervader (*vyāpaka*), while that which possesses an inferior quality is the pervaded (*vyāpya*). This very excellence of quality is such that, without it, another quality would not be possible; by this [principle], the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) [is established].
As it is said in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"Therefore, beginning from the state of Śiva, having taken up the nature of luminosity as being eternally established within one's own self..."
The earth shines brilliantly, completely pervaded by the entire collection of dharmas belonging to the series of all the principles (tattvas).
In this way, even for [the elements] beginning with water, there exists a body extending up to the abode of the principle of Power (śaktitattva) that is of such a nature; however,
each subsequent [element] exists as a principle precisely by virtue of being Power.
But previously it was "by way of its true nature (dharmatā)"; this is the distinction.

This has been correctly determined in the *Paratriṃśikā-vivaraṇa*. Beginning from the principle of Śiva, [the universe] is pervaded by the principle of water; likewise, water is pervaded by fire, and so on, up to the principle of Śakti.
The elements, the group of subtle essences, and the senses; the individual soul (puruṣa) together with its sheaths, and that which is utterly pure;
from Vidyā up to Śakti—this much is one's own consciousness.
The manner of the spreading of the river's waves.
Heated all over by the fire, emerged from the fire all over;
his very self was completely enveloped.
Equal to the Supreme Śiva.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Nature of Reality," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Next, the differentiation of the *tattvas* is investigated. That [differentiation] is sevenfold, as established by the Supreme Lord in the *Ṣaḍardhaśāstra* alone; [but surely it is not so in the Trika system...]

Having raised the objection—namely, that since the universe has been described as consisting of the nature of *nara*, *śakti*, and *śiva*, how can a differentiation of subjects (*pramātṛbheda*) appropriate to the Siddhānta system be asserted—he says "by the Supreme Lord," and so forth. As it has been stated:
"The [principles] beginning with Earth and ending with the Root [Nature], through the differentiation of the Possessor of Power and His Power..."
It is divided into fifteen parts, together with its own essential nature and the non-sentient.
The Pralayākala, like Rudra, is devoid of both Kalās and Bhedas;
likewise, Māyā is ninefold, while the Jñānakalā is sevenfold.
"The mantras, their lords (mantreśas), and the five other lords of the lords of mantras (mantreśapatayas) are threefold;

Śiva does not undergo division, being composed of dense consciousness consisting solely of his own self-luminosity. Thus it has been said. In that context, the Śivas are the Mantramaheshas, the Mantreshas, the Mantras, the Vijñānākalas, the Pralayākalas, and the Sakalas.

Seven. [The meaning is this: in the ultimate sense, the universe indeed consists of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul (nara), each of which is further composed of higher, intermediate, and lower aspects. As for the statement that there are seven types of possessors of power (śaktimat) and powers (śakti), that refers primarily to their internal subdivisions.

The possessors of power (*śaktimantaḥ*). They have exactly seven powers (meaning the powers beginning with Will, etc.; "due to their differentiation" means due to the differentiation between power and the possessor of power). Due to that differentiation, from Earth up to the primary principle (*pradhāna*), each assumes its own form through fourteen variations.

Fifteenth: therein, its own form is fit for being an object of cognition (prameyatā-yogya)—meaning it is insentient in nature—residing within itself, untouched by powers (śakti) and possessors of power (śaktimat); for if it were colored by them...
The meaning is that its very nature as such is what is reckoned.

And so it has been stated elsewhere: "In this context, the supreme aspect is the form of the subject (*mātṛ*), the intermediate aspect is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the inferior aspect is the object (*meya*), the possessor of power is the agent, and power itself is one's own nature. Thus it is said.

That which, through the grace of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), finds its resting place within subjects whose powers have become intensified—that is His very Śākta form, [attained] through the grace of the Illustrious Parāparā.
And that is sevenfold, because there are that many powers. However, when the nature of the possessor of power (Śaktimat) is primary—

That which rests within the group of subjects is the form of Śiva as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), by virtue of the grace of the venerable Parābhaṭṭārikā; and that too is sevenfold, because it has been stated that there are as many subjects as there are, beginning from Śiva down to the *sakala*. In this regard, [the distinction] arises solely from the differentiation of powers.
The distinction among cognizers is now stated in the sequence beginning with the *sakala* (the fully differentiated) for the sake of clarification.
In that regard, the power (*śakti*) of the *sakala* consists of *vidyā* and *kalā*; for, due to the diversity of their respective functions, the powers would be manifold.
Thus, they are generally reckoned as having *vidyā* and *kalā* alone as their essential powers, since these constitute its specific forms.
For the *pralayākala*, however, those very powers of intellect (*buddhi*), action (*karman*), and the senses (*akṣa*) are indeed indistinct because they lack an object;
the sense is that they exist in the form of a dormant serpent. Nor should it be thought:
"If these two are not manifest for the *pralayākala*, then how can he be situated above the *sakala*? For these...
Because it is the cause for the manifestation of an excess of impurity (*mala*), it is indeed the cause of falling downward; thus, the *sakala* [subject] is entirely at the very bottom.
For the *vijñānākala*, those same two [impurities], when their power is dissolving and accompanied by their residual traces (*saṃskāra*), awaken as *śuddhavidyā* for the *mantra*.
That same [power], when devoid of those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), is the Mantreśvara;

that same [power], desiring to assume the state of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), is the Mantramaheśvara; and that same [power], consisting of will and possessing manifest sovereignty, is Śiva—such are the distinctions of the powers (*śakti-bheda*).

The manifestation of powers occurs through internal subdivisions of the organs of knowledge and action; however, in reality, this property known as inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed one alone. As it has been said:
"This single property of his exists by encompassing everything."

"Therefore, in that case, the direct injunction is joined precisely with the power of autonomy (*svātantrya-śakti*). Thus, there are seven primary [powers]. And the differentiation among the subjects (*pramātṛ*) who possess these powers is produced by their coloring by those [powers], because the differentiation of instruments results in the differentiation of the agent, and because it is possible for the power itself—which is non-distinct [from the agent]—to be made into an instrument.

Not so for another, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress and other faults. As it has been said: "Therefore, by virtue of its autonomy, the agent, differentiating its own body, itself makes one of its own parts—which touches upon the objective aspect—into an instrument."

If it is maintained that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*), then how could that [agent] be an instrument at all? Rather, because it is the object of the action of impelling, the meaning is that it is simply the object (*karman*). Furthermore, since an action cannot exist without an instrument, another instrument must be sought; and since that too is distinct [from the agent], it too would merely be something to be impelled.

In that case, there would be another instrument, leading to an infinite regress. In reality, however, there is only one subject who rests in the bliss of the freedom of consciousness; when the earth is perceived as resting solely in its own essential nature, then that is its true nature.

Only the blue object perceived by Caitra’s eye shines forth. [In the cognition "I see what is seen by Caitra’s eye," does only the blue shine forth, or rather, the blue as qualified by its being known by Caitra?
In the first case, there would be no distinction between the two cognitions: "I know the blue" and "I know the blue known by Caitra."]

It might be argued that this is not so because it contradicts experience; however, in the second case, is the "knowability by Caitra" (*caitravedyatā*) of the blue an attribute inherent in the object itself, or is it inherent in the cognizer?

It cannot be inherent in the cognizer, because a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is impossible between two things residing in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*) due to their being of unequal status. But if it is inherent in the object itself...

It is established that the very nature (*nijam vapuḥ*) of an entity is its state of being knowable (*vedyatā*). Thus, in the cognition "I know what is known by Caitra," another essential form (*svarūpāntaram*) indeed shines forth, produced by the totality of powers (*sakala-śakti-kṛtam*) and consisting of the possessor of the totality of powers (*sakala-śaktimat-rūpa-kṛtam*). In this same way, it should be stated up to Śiva: the universe is grounded in Śiva and His power, and it finds its ultimate rest in the essential nature of Śiva.

Because there exists a distinct cognition in the form "I know. Now, if being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*) is the very nature of an entity, then it would be an object of knowledge for everyone; furthermore, if that state of being an object of knowledge were itself to be known, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[Now, what is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is indeed an action (*kriyā*), and that is inferred from its fruit (*phala*); and that fruit is what is termed "manifestation" (*prakaṭatā*).]

Anticipating the Kaumārila position that "the property of being an object" (*viṣayadharma*) is itself "knowability" (*vedyatā*), [the author] refutes it. The underlying point is this: just as properties such as blueness and so forth belong to an entity in a way that is indistinguishable for all [cognizers], so too would the property called "knowability" be; consequently, the extreme non-existence [of objects] would follow, and everyone would be omniscient.

[They] might say: "Furthermore, as for this property of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) that has been mentioned, is it itself cognizable or incognizable? If it were incognizable, then because it would not touch consciousness, it would not exist. If it were cognizable, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), whereby the cognizability of no object whatsoever could be established, and the entire universe would consequently end up as if in a state of swoon."

And by that [ignorance], the state of the world being blind and asleep is indeed clearly manifest; and by that, there is the conjunction of contradictory properties, namely being knowable and unknowable. Now, regarding existence (*bhāva*), it is twofold: essential existence (*svarūpasattā*) and inherent existence (*samavāyinī*). Thus, there is knowability through its own nature, as well as self-luminosity.

"Therefore, is there not the fault that the very same nature (svarūpa) possesses both the state of being the object of knowledge (vedyatva) and the state of being the knower (vedakatva), which is a superimposition of contradictory attributes? To this it is replied: "That is not its own body (svaṃ vapuḥ), because it has been stated separately from the essential nature (svarūpa); what then [is it]?"

That form which is the locus of repose within the power of the knower and within the knower himself is indeed self-luminous. [If it is asked: "But if the very nature of being an object of knowledge consists in resting within luminosity, then how can it be a property of an entity? [The answer is: True; just as by Śiva, through his sovereignty...
"In that very same way, the property of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*) appears as a differentiation. As it has been stated by Lord Śiva:

"Just as differentiation is manifested through [His] sovereignty, so too this property of being an object of cognition is said to be like blue and other such objects. That [differentiation] shines forth, but it is not...

The claim that it is "with respect to anything at all" is utterly discarded, because omniscience would be impossible and there would be a conjunction of contradictory properties. [In our position,] it is self-luminous and not illuminated [by another]; this is the conjunction of contradictory properties.
It is self-luminous alone; it does not manifest with respect to anything at all. Thus it stands in our view.

Since Śiva alone exists as the self-luminous Self, and because of the non-existence of any other object whatsoever, the statement that He "shines for another" is contradictory; thus, even omniscience is refuted. He shines by Himself and does not undergo the status of being an object (karmabhāva) in relation to Himself; therefore, knowability cannot be something distinct [from His nature].
[The refutation of infinite regress: Even though it is perceived by infinite subjects, it is one and the same—[the sense is that it is not distinct for each individual].

That is its nature, [determined by the relationship between power and the possessor of power], because within that [unity], they possess the form of a single manifestation; thus, [there is no infinite regress].
There is a certain obstacle to the inference of the cognition of another subject; and that nature of his is real because it performs a causal function,
just like a beloved woman being seen by another.

Having seen this, one feels envy toward her; [the sense is: if the quality residing in the beloved were something other than what is seen, then why would the husband feel envy? Beholding the jar of repose, which is the very nature of Śiva, one enters that reality in which all infinite subjects find their rest.

One becomes full upon seeing [an object], like the watching of a dancer [or wrestlers and actors]. This alone constitutes the "full" form: the reflective awareness (vimarśana) directed toward that very object, without any further desire for another object of knowledge because all other objects of knowledge have dissolved away. That very form of the blue object, which has come to rest within the subject, is likewise [the full form].

"Because of the arising of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) within that which is self-luminous," thus the fifteenfold nature [of the universe] extends from the element earth up to the *pradhāna* principle. This is because the *sakala* subject—one whose sheaths (*kañcuka*), such as passion (*rāga*) and the rest, are intensified to that extent—possesses the status of a knower; [even though, in the case of the *sakala*, the body and so forth, which are objects of knowledge, hold primacy].
Nevertheless, the point is that subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*) indeed exists due to the predominance of the sheaths (*kañcuka*) such as *kalā* and *vidyā*, which stimulate knowledge and action.

[Objection: "But surely, since the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*) is predominant, it is logical that even for the *sakala* [subject], there should be fifteen levels just as in the case of the earth and other elements; so how can it be said that [the *sakala* extends] only up to the primary principles (*pradhānatattva*)?"
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even for the *sakala*," and in the *Tantrāloka*:

"In the *sakala* who is situated within [the levels] beginning with Earth, there is indeed an internal *sakala*; for even here, among the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), there is a subject (*mātṛ*). Thus is the fifteenfold nature (*pāñcadaśya*).
Because that too is indeed an object of cognition (*vedyatva*). This has been determined in detail in the *Tantrāloka*:
"When the state of being an object of knowledge is attributed to the person (*puruṣa*) ending with the category of *kalā*... [as stated in the *Śrītantrāloka*].
"The portion of the *kañcuka* (veils) arising from that is the object of measurement; it is not his state as a subject (*pramātṛtā*).

Therefore, for the one known as *sakala* (the conditioned), subjectivity does not exist. [Thus it is said. Therein, up to the *kalā-tattva*, there are thirteen [categories] belonging to the *sakala*; because of the connection with subjectivity therein, they consist of the nature of power and the possessor of power (*śakti-śaktimad*).
Due to the complete subsidence of the two-fold division, there remains only the essential nature (*svarūpatva*) of the *sakala* [limited subject].
When the *pralayākala* is the essential nature and the five [senses] are the subjects (*pramātṛ*), there are eleven divisions.
When the *vijñānākala* is the essential nature and the four [senses] are the subjects, there are nine divisions. [In the case] of the *mantra*...

If the three [Mantras] are the essential nature [of the subject], there are seven subjects; if the Mantreśvara is the essential nature, there are five subjects when the two [Mantra and Mantreśvara] are the subjects; if the Mantramaheśvara is the essential nature, there are three due to the distinction between Śakti and Śaktimat when the Lord alone is the subject; but as for Śiva—

For that which is filled with the absolute freedom of the single consciousness of light, no differentiation exists because of its perfect fullness. Thus, this very differentiation of the *tattvas* has been described according to the singular doctrine of the Supreme Lord and the Anuttara;
the wonderful variety of the differentiation of the *bhuvanas* is [also] stated as follows:
"From that very source, this manifold arrangement of the worlds and so forth is said to arise.
Likewise:
"In this same way, the garland of worlds is clearly divided by these various distinctions."

He creates the hells, heavens, and the worlds of Rudra within the earthly realm—as it has been said: "Even in their status as earthly beings, there is no equality between the worlds of Rudra and Viṣṇu;
what then can be said of other matters, whether in terms of enjoyment or essential nature?"

The phrase "elsewhere" (anyatra) means within the self consisting of the earth and so forth, or in the world-realms and so on; for although [the nature] is the same, a more remote difference in essential nature has been stated. And here, one who is curious to know the intermediate distinctions through the perception of mutual differences—[for indeed, such knowledge of intermediate distinctions belongs to everyone].
Because [the Self] is the essence of all, even in the *sakala* state, the emergence of the powers such as *layākala* and so forth exists in reality;
therefore, by multiplying the identical powers of the subjects— beginning with the *sakala*— by seven,
the emergence of forty-nine forms occurs, and this very possibility is the proof here.
It should be understood that there is no fault even if they possess such characteristics. As it is stated in the *Tantrāloka*:

"Let that [consciousness] be manifest in its own nature; it is capable of providing the aspect of differentiation. In this way, the differentiation of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) must also be accepted, as these too are differentiated from one another.

There are one hundred and twenty-four types [of powers] increasing by one, and there is likewise variety in other ways as well; because the particularities of the universal are produced through transformation, the infinity of distinctions arising from the emergence and disappearance of the powers of the eyes and so forth is quite evident. Nor should it be thought that this is sufficient merely through the distinction of the objects of cognition (*vedya*).

Since the very beginning and end of the powers of the eyes and so forth consist in their manifestation and concealment? There is indeed a distinction characterized by immersion (*āveśa*), submergence (*nimajjana*), expansion (*vikāsa*), and whirling (*vighūrṇana*): *āveśa* is becoming identical with that; *nimajjana* is entry into its interior, consisting of attachment; and *vikāsa* is the outward flow toward it.

The "whirling" (*vighūrṇana*) is a vibration consisting of an upward surging due to that orientation; for one whose power is unmanifest, even what is seen is as if unseen, whereas for one whose power is intensified, there arises a supreme wonder when looking at an object after having applied [the gaze]. Thus, the meaning is that the distinction is indeed produced by causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

One should focus precisely on the *Tantrāloka*. Thus, even by following each individual jar and so forth, the differentiation of the principles (*tattva*) such as earth and the rest has been described; likewise, within a single principle that possesses many states, there is again the state known as a single jar.
The intention is this: who indeed could possibly state how many divisions there are? And it has been said elsewhere:
"In this same way, whatever state exists among the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth—even that which is called a 'jar'—a division is demonstrated therein."
In this case as well, what is called "knowability" is identity with the knowers;
therefore, this jar, being knowable by all, is indeed the Sakala [the Fully Manifested] himself.
As long as this [reality] is knowable solely by Śiva, so long does Śiva alone manifest;
for as long as that consciousness exists, it shines forth as having a single body.

Thus: "In that very way, O Beloved, as long as these are not knowers, how can they be objects of knowledge? This is to be understood according to the principle stated here. Identity (*tādātmya*) is non-difference that tolerates some degree of difference.

Now, having indicated the entire earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*), which consists of both the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the object (*prameya*), it is described through its non-difference from the earth-principle.
First, he shows the seven subjects therein with the words "yo dharātattvābhedena" and so forth. [An objection: But surely, Śiva is so called because he nourishes (*bṛṃhaṇa*) all the principles?
Raising the doubt as to how that which is called *brahman* is established with necessity, he says "yathā" and so forth.

That Light is Śiva. Just as the Śruti says, "This *brahman* is indeed the earth," he is the Great Lord of the Earth-mantra (*dharāmantramaheśvara*) who impels [the soul] toward the attainment of the earth-principle (*dharātattva*), and he is the one to be impelled.
The Lord of the Earth-mantra (*dharāmantreśa*) is the expressive mantra (*vācaka*) consisting of the very nature of his conceited body (*abhimānikavigraha*).

Having transcended the fettered sciences (*pāśavavidyā*) such as Sāṃkhya and others, through the sequence of Śiva’s science (*śivavidyākrama*), he has practiced the yoga of the earthly element (*pārthivayoga*) but has not yet attained the fixed state (*dhruvapada*); that is, having failed to achieve the perfection of contemplation (*bhāvanāniṣpatti*), he remains in the intermediate state.

The meaning is: one who has not attained the stable state due to dissolution; that is, a *vijñānākala* belonging to the earth. One who has practiced the yoga of the earth through the sequence of the fettered (*pāśava*) knowledge, at the end of a kalpa or at death, becomes a *pralayakevala* of the earth—meaning there is a dissolution of the earth, but not of water and the other elements, for when a lower principle is destroyed...
Likewise, the yogin [experiences this] through the penetration (*āveśa*) of the higher principles (*tattva*); he illustrates this with the words "for in deep sleep" (*sauṣupte hi*), and so forth.

For one who has been penetrated by the water-principle (*jala-tattva*), there occurs a dream-creation consisting of crossing the ocean and the like. Deep sleep, which invariably precedes it, is the cause of the dream; for it is precisely by virtue of the penetration of the principle during deep sleep that the manifold [dream] arises.
The emergence of the dream state occurs when one possesses the conceit of being the earth; yet even here,
through the predominance or subordination of power (*śakti*), there is a sevenfold power consisting of functions such as obstruction, creation, and so forth, just as described elsewhere.
The agitation that occurs when this very group of seven is engaged in its respective functions is clearly said to be the [manifest] group of seven powers.
Thus it is said. Regarding this, the specific detail is as follows:
"In that very place, within the earth which appears as differentiated, whatever pillar or other object is perceived separately—that on earth is the power of Śiva."
In this very [state], she who exists in manifold conditions performs emanation, dissolution, maintenance, grace, and withdrawal, extending from the level of the Sakala up to Śiva.

This power of the Great Lord of Mantras (Mantramaheśvara) is the sovereign over the principles (tattvas); for she is the power of Maheśvara who, by sheer force, impels individual souls (pudgalas) toward the various groups of principles and mantras. That power which has reached the ground of awakening is indeed this one.
That by which one may perceive the true nature of reality, such as yellow and so forth,
and which protects one from its opposite, is considered the power of mantra.

That state of impurity which consists solely of that [limited] measure, bestowing a correct orientation toward the experience or non-experience of those respective principles, is indeed the power of the *vijñānakevalin*.
Due to the orientation toward various specific karmas corresponding to the various awakened and expanded realities,
the power directed toward the experience thereof belongs to the *pralayākala*.
"But that state which exists during the immersion into the manifestation of the impurities of illusory action (māyākarma),
produced by the external and internal senses and following through various conditions—
that power which is the means of experience resides in the *sakala* individual souls. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the state of being fourteen: these are the divisions of the *dharātattva* (earth-principle) which has attained the status of a subject (*pramātṛ*), whereas its pure nature is the object (*prameya*). [This means it consists of humans, because of the predominance of knowability (*vedyatā*).
As it has been said:]

"But that which is devoid of contact with the consciousness whose form is the subject, pure and insentient—that is its own nature; thus the universe consists of the three. Thus, and likewise elsewhere [the meaning is "in water and so forth"]. Now, in a single cognizer...

Because everything is established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—according to the reasoning already stated that "this entire path belongs to the *prāṇa*"—the subject's establishment is in the *prāṇa*. Regarding the determination of division (*bheda*), such as the fifteenfold division and so forth: for one perceiving blue here, the *prāṇa* consists of sixteen *tuṭis*.
[It should be understood that two and a quarter finger-breadths constitute one *tuṭi* of the movement of the vital breath.

Therein, the first *tuṭi* arises as having a single nature of non-differentiation up until the immersion into the object of knowledge (*vedya*); the second has the form of the emergence of the subject (*grāhaka*); and the final one is non-distinct from the object, consisting of it [consisting of the object].

The penultimate [tuṭi], however, has the nature of the manifest grāhaka (subject). Within that group of twelve tuṭis in the middle, the first six have a non-conceptual nature and conceal conceptualization;
their state of being sixfold constitutes, by its very essence, a single tuṭi, while the fivefold nature of the conceptualization to be concealed is the desire to emerge.
And this state of "unfolding" (unmiṣattā), because its nature is a manifest activity, consists of two moments (tuṭi); since vibration does not consist of a single moment,
there is both the state of unfolding and the performance of its own function— thus, due to the fivefold nature of the conceptualizations to be concealed.

From its own nature (*svarūpa*), there are six moments that are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*): thereafter, the state of the non-conceptual being destroyed (*dhvaṃsamānatā*), its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), the desire to emerge of the conceptual (*vikalpa*) (*unmimiṣā*), its emerging (*unmiṣattā*), and its having emerged (*unmiṣitatā*). These constitute six *tuṭi*s.
However, the capacity to perform its own function, which is the nature of the subject (*grāhakarūpatā*), has already been mentioned and is not counted again.
Thus, the meaning of the word "iti" is that the earth, as indicated by the word "blue," has been explained as residing within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Those whose wealth is discernment (*viveka*) and who practice the instructions of the Guru distinguish the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) everywhere— meaning throughout everything up to the primary principle (*pradhāna-tattva*)— by means of analysis.
Regarding the deficiency of conceptualization (the meaning being "on the thirteenth breath-unit, etc.");

according to the view that it is a deficiency in the very nature of the conceptualization, there is a deficiency of the *tuṭi* (unit of time) due to its being cast into the state of the subject, which results in a slackening of this [conceptualization] as a subject,
but not an absolute destruction of its essential nature within the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) consisting of thirty-six finger-breadths.

For in that case, the count of *tuṭis* is not lost. But as for the deficiency in *tuṭis*, what is the result of such deficiency, as in the case of the perception of pleasure and so forth? He says "pleasure" and so on, as it has been stated:
"Just as one who has long been afflicted by suffering, and subsequently attains a state of pleasure..."
One indeed forgets that suffering by means of the path of resting in happiness.

"Likewise, even though they are established in consciousness where conceptualization has ceased, people do not recognize that existence due to the power of resting in conceptualization. Thus, it is non-conceptuality itself; yet worldly people, through the repose of conceptualization, [perceive] that which consists of "I-ness" (ahantā).

Those who are resting in bliss consider that state of non-conceptual reflective awareness (*vimarśabhūmi*)—which is free from the expansion of the conceptualization of "this-ness" veiled by the sense of "I"—to be as if unmanifest;
however, through the diminution of conceptualization, it indeed becomes manifest. This is that very [state].

Regarding the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, there must be attentiveness; that is, one should be focused on that from which the grasped and the grasper arise or in which they find rest, by means of which all desired fruits are accomplished. As it has been said:
"The consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings."

"But for yogins, this distinction lies in their attentiveness toward the connection. Thus say the teachers of Abhinavagupta. And so, while the fifteen-fold state remains, as long as there is a diminution of duality—which is essentially the "I-ness" (idantā)—the pairs [of moments] decrease until the immersion into Śiva consists of two *tuṭis*.

[Because the two *tuṭis* consisting of the final and penultimate moments are deposited within their own essential nature: therein, the first *tuṭi* is entirely full, while the second, when practiced while permeated by the instruments of all knowledge,
conduces to omniscience and omnipotence, but not the first [because of its universal sameness— this is the sense].

As the venerable Kallaṭa has said: "At the falling away of the *tuṭi* [at the falling away of the *tuṭi*, there is the attainment of omniscience and omnipotence; this is the aphorism]. Here, the word 'falling away' (*pāta*) refers to that very same Blessed Goddess, the illustrious Kālī—meaning the falling away, the diminution, the decrease, of the first *tuṭi*, which is to say, the second *tuṭi*. In this context, the term *pāta* denotes that very Goddess Śrīmatkālī.
Bhairava is the true being of the Mother; he is intuitive flash (*pratibhā*). Enough with this [discussion of] the secret and the non-secret [meaning:
the disclosure of that which was secret]. Thus, from the moment of the *tuṭi* of Maheśa... [thus]...

Having raised the doubt as to whether the attainment of omniscience and other powers mentioned in relation to the second *tuṭi* might likewise occur in the third and subsequent ones, he says, "In this way, [one becomes] a Mantramaheśa," and so forth; for it has been said:
"For one who fixes the mind upon those [states], characterized by exclusive concentration..."

"The immersion into those respective accomplishments arises of its own accord. From this point onward, through the practice of each respective [method], there arise those various accomplishments (*siddhis*). These various *siddhis*—such as the heaviness of the body and so forth—are described in the chapter on *dhāraṇā* and elsewhere in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra) and other texts. Now, in this very context:
In the path of the principles (tattva) and so forth, which is taught as having the nature of the sequence beginning with the fifteen-fold [division],

the states such as waking are described; therein lies the manifold variety of the object of knowledge— which is indicated as being the very nature [of consciousness]— and of the consciousness directed toward that object, which is spoken of as the respective subjects.

That state exists as a mutual dependence; it belongs neither to the object alone, nor to consciousness alone, nor to the two separately. Therein, when there is an appearance as an external form by way of being the object of presiding [consciousness], that is the waking state, occurring with respect to the object, the subject, and the means of knowledge. But when, in that very same state...

When there is an appearance in the form of the object of superimposition (adhiṣṭhāna)— meaning, in the form of the means of knowledge— that is volition (saṃkalpa), and that is the state of dreaming. But when, in that very same state, there is an appearance in the form of the subject of superimposition (adhiṣṭhātṛ)— meaning, as one with the knower— [that is the waking state].

The manifestation [of the universe] as being essentially of the nature of the seed—meaning that the seed is the cause because it is connected to the future effect through its very essence—is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). [Now, it was said that there is the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the knower (*mātā*), the means of knowledge (*mānam*), and the substrate; how then can one be the knower?]
He says, "These very [three]," meaning that these three states—
the object of cognition (*prameya*), the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the cognizer (*pramātṛ*)— are each said to be fourfold according to the divisions of waking and so forth.
However, when, within that very state of resting in the cognizer, there arises the cognizer's orientation toward fullness (*pūrṇatā-unmukhya*):
At that time, the manifestation through that door by way of being oriented toward fullness is the state of the Fourth (turyāvasthā). [If it is argued:

"But surely this is a cognition consisting of the fruit of the means of knowledge, which is established by the triad of the object of knowledge and so forth; therefore, the object of knowledge and the rest are its very lifeblood," he says "And that...
etc., to show: "It is not so. And its form is precisely of this nature: "I am the Seer."

The state of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*), whose essence is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), does not transcend the three parts [of the sphere of manifestation]— proximity, intermediacy, and distance— in the sense that one might think, "I see [it] beyond [those parts]"; for such a view is without means (*anupāyikā*), meaning it lacks a functional, logical, or possible means.

Bestowing the consecration of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, she is threefold because she favors those three states. This very fourfold state is *piṇḍastha* (the "abiding in the body"), so called because it abides in the *piṇḍa*, that is, the body;
it is the station (*pada*) or place of all the paths (*adhvan*), namely the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and moreover, it is that which is reached (*padyate*).
That by which something is known is a "foot" (*pada*), namely, volition (*saṃkalpa*). One who stands upon that [volition] is "standing on the foot" (*padastha*).

That which makes things visible—rendering the various objects of experience possessed of form through the act of assimilating them into one's own self—is "form" (*rūpa*), meaning the subject (*pramātā*). Identity with that [subject] is "standing in form" (*rūpastha*). Although form is limited, it is called *rūpastha* because it transcends even the limited subject.
That which transcends form (*rūpātīta*) is thus described.

Yogis conversant with the wealth of *prasaṃkhyāna* employ the terms "abiding in form" (*stharūpa*), "abiding beyond form" (*stharūpātīta*), "all-auspicious" (*sarvatobhadra*), "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), "great pervasion" (*mahāvyāpti*), and "accumulation" (*pracaya*). [This is like the universal manifestation of the hand.]

It is called *pracaya* (accumulation) because it is seen as being accumulated [by the preceding levels]. This is shown by these words, and its literal meaning is demonstrated in the *Tantrāloka* and the *Ślokavārtika*. Furthermore, they define that which is contained within all, whose form is complete, as the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), transcending everything, and the Great Accumulation (*mahāpracaya*). Moreover, whatever form belongs to anything at any time becomes manifest...

That which is stable and continuous is the waking state; its opposite is dreaming, which is the experience of the *layākala*. Deep sleep is the non-perception of everything, which is the experience of the *vijñānākala*. The fourth state (*turya*) is the non-differentiation from the object of experience, which is the experience of the *mantras* and others regarding all entities.

Non-difference from Śiva is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which transcends all. Within that, there are five states across fifteen divisions: 1) *svarūpa* and *sakala*, 2) *pralayākala*, 3) *vijñānākala*, 4) the group consisting of *mantra*, *mantreśa*, and *maheśa*, and 5) *śiva*. In the thirteen-fold division, these are arranged in the sequence beginning with *svarūpa* and *pralayākala*.
In the elevenfold division, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of the *vijñānākala* and *śakti*;

in the ninefold division, the essential nature consists of the *mantras*, their lords (*mantreśas*), the *maheśas*, and *śiva*; in the sevenfold division, the essential nature consists of the *mantreśas*, the *maheśa*, *śakti*, and *śiva*; and in the fivefold division, the essential nature consists of the *maheśa-śakti* and the *maheśa*.

In the fivefold division, Śakti is Śiva; in the threefold division, they are the essential nature, the power of action (kriyā-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of will (icchā-śakti), which are Śiva.
Thus, although the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is non-dual, it is conceived through the arrangement of the forms of action, knowledge, will, bliss, and consciousness.
Those whose wealth is the yoga of higher discernment speak of the state of the five stages.

In the network of principles beginning with Earth, there is indeed no such body for the knower that remains devoid of repose in consciousness; rather, his state as a subject manifests in manifold ways.
Therefore, within this network of objects of knowledge, non-conceptual *ahantā* (I-consciousness) [perceives] the sequential arrangement of the succession.
Dwell upon the ground whose essence is the awareness of freedom, and attain the reality of your own self.
Send forth the power of the inner essence of both [the self and the other]; enter within the tranquility of the minister of truth; here, in this very moment, wipe away the sleep of the ignorant.
This is the path of peace, wherein the power of the inner essence has ascended through spiritual awakening.
Filled, seen, heard, and again filled. ||1||
The sword of the light of the intellect, joined to the handle of the fourfold states,
is sharpened by the process of fulfilling all that is possible.
May the five-faced one, who has the appearance of a serpent with a curved hood, protect you. ||2||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Divisions of the Tattvas," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the tenth chapter.

The path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) has already been described; now the path beginning with the limited powers (*kalādyadhvan*) is being examined. In that regard, just as it was stated that a principle (*tattva*) is a certain pervasive form within the worlds (*bhuvana*), so too, that which is the pervasive form among the principles according to their respective groups is [the *kalā*].

The *kalā* [is as follows]: For some say, "Furthermore, that power which is internal and extremely subtle is called the *kalā* of the principles (*tattva*s), just as it is the supporter of the earth."
In these two positions, the object does not appear as distinct,
because a persisting universal is not accepted [by us] in the manner of the Naiyāyikas and others.

This and more has been stated elsewhere. Just as the sustaining power (*dhārikā śakti*) is inherent in the earth, so too there is the power called *nivṛtti* (the power of cessation), which, by turning one back from the extroversion that has reached the ultimate limit, acts as a restrainer; and there is the power known as *pratiṣṭhā*, which acts as a restrainer through stabilization. In this same way, the other [powers] are also to be understood as such restrainers. Thus:
And it has been said:
"Cessation occurs within the earth-tattva; Pratiṣṭhā extends to the realm of the Unmanifest;
Vidyā reaches the end of Night; and Śāntā reaches the end of Śakti—this constitutes the fourfold Egg."

"Beyond the tranquil [state] is the supreme reality; beyond the *kalās* is the highest station. This is because it cannot tolerate the conceptualization of even a single form. For example, *nivṛtti* resides in earth, since from it the creation of the principles (*tattva-sarga*) recedes. *Pratiṣṭhā* resides in the group beginning with water and ending with *pradhāna*.

Because it performs the functions of causing, nourishing, and filling; because from *puṃs* up to *māyā*, there is *vidyā* due to the concealment of the object of knowledge and the predominance of consciousness; and because from *śuddhavidyā* up to the end of *śakti*, the waves of the sheaths (*kañcuka*) have subsided into tranquility—this very group constitutes the fourfold egg (*aṇḍacatuṣṭaya*), known as the earthly (*pārthiva*), the material (*prākṛta*), the illusory (*māyīya*), and the empowered (*śākta*).

Since the elements such as earth and the others reside here within the Śakti-tattva, and as long as mutual contact exists—given that contact implies resistance—it is logical that there is an "egg" (aṇḍa). As it has been said:
"And what is called an 'egg' is the cause for the maintenance of the division of the worlds."

They say that this obscuration (āvaraṇa) exists as far as the level of Śakti. In the Śiva-tattva, there is the state beyond tranquility (śāntātītā), because it is being cultivated through instruction, meditation, worship, and so forth. But the supreme reality is independent;
even therein, that which is immeasurable is beyond the kalās, because it is devoid of all constituent parts (kalā).

[The state of being. Thus, there are exactly five *kalās*, which constitute the thirty-six *tattvas*. To explain: the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is twofold, by way of being gross and subtle, making ten; the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is twofold, as pure and as touched by agency (*kartṛtā*), making ten; and because the state of agency is made manifest through its subordination to the state of being an instrument, there are five.

Due to the state of being a pure agent, when the five [elements] are oriented toward expansion through the dissolution of their divisions, there is the thirty-sixth Śiva-tattva, which is devoid of all limitations. As it is said elsewhere:
"When whatever is knowable appears, that which shines forth upon its cessation [is Śiva]."
That reality has been determined; it shines within the heart as the thirty-sixth principle.
When it is taught that "That" is of the singular nature of consciousness, bliss, and absolute freedom,
the thirty-seventh [tattva] shines forth there, and no further expectation remains.
"Even that [consciousness] in which this established knowability appears is composed of consciousness (cinmaya).
It is taught as the thirty-eighth for the sake of contemplation;
yet, if one were to do so, it would again become the thirty-seventh. Thus it is taught. When that is taught...

Or, that which is cultivated is the locus of its establishment; that is the thirty-seventh. Even when that is being cultivated, there is the thirty-eighth, yet there is no infinite regress, because that which is being cultivated possesses uninterrupted sovereignty (*anavacchinnasvātantrya*). [k: "the sovereignty of the yogin is uninterrupted"].

[The reading: Since the process of making known (*vedyīkaraṇa*) culminates precisely at the thirty-seventh [tattva], the thirty-sixth is considered to be free from limitation because it transcends all *tattvas*; such is the rule for the five *kalās*.
The *ātma-kalā* extends up to the *vijñānākala*, the *vidyā-kalā* extends up to Īśvara, and the remainder is the *śiva-kalā*.
The procedure for the three principles (*tritattvavidhi*). Likewise, there are also nine principles and so forth; as it is said elsewhere regarding the nine principles:
"Primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), necessity (*niyati*), and time (*kāla*)."
Māyā, Vidyā, as well as Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva;

Thus; by the word "etcetera," there is the state of being eighteenfold. Regarding the term "one should infer": the division of the paths (*adhvan*) consisting of worlds (*bhuvana*), principles (*tattva*), and limited powers (*kalā*)—which pertains to the object of knowledge—is threefold because it possesses gross, subtle, and supreme forms;
likewise, through its repose within the subject (*mātṛviśrānti*), it is threefold in that same way.

Regarding that state of being a means of valid cognition, it is said elsewhere as well: "That form of the path which consists of the nature of a means of valid cognition and reaches the portion of the cognizer is called a 'word' (pada), because it is permeated by the nature of comprehension."
"And that very state is the mantra when it has fallen away from agitation;

for the Mother speaks in secret, remaining established in silence. Thus, the path of the word (*padādhvan*) belongs to the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) itself when the waves of agitation are subsiding, while the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*) occurs upon the complete cessation of that [agitation].

In the state of the perfect subject (*pūrṇapramātṛtā*), that very path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) attains its true nature through resting within that [state]; thus, it is logical that a single entity possesses a sixfold nature.
[The compound *padamantravarṇam* is a collective singular; "one" refers to the aggregate of words, mantras, and phonemes.]
The form of the letter *kṣa* consists of sixteen puruṣas, from Kālāgni up to Vīrabhadra.

"Sixteen puruṣas, O Earth" refers to the *nivṛtti*-kalā. The number of syllables for the *tattvas* is thirty-three (three fires and two eyes); by this, the elements beginning with earth up to the unmanifest (*avyakta*) are indicated.
The principles (*tattvas*) are twenty-three, beginning with *ha* and ending with *ṇa*; the *rasas* are six; and the *śaras* (arrows) are five—thus there are fifty-six cities.

The weapons (*astras*) are the five arrows; therefore, there are two words of four syllables and three words of five syllables, making five word-mantras (*mantra-padas*). Furthermore, *anyā* is a synonym for *āpyāyinī*.
The installation [is performed];
the other [consists of] the syllables of the mantra for the weapon, which are the city of the essence and the arrows. ||1||

"Muni-tattva-arṇam": the sages are seven; by that, the principles (tattvas) beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā, as well as the phonemes (varṇas) beginning with 'ma' and ending with 'gha', constitute two. By that, there are two words and mantras—one of five syllables and the second of two syllables—and the Vasus are eight and the eyes are two; thus, there are twenty-eight worlds.
The "later digit" (*aparakaletī*) is the *vidyā* which is another synonym for *bodhi*. The mantra of two words consists of eight syllables and the world;
the later digit consists of the element of the fire-syllable (*agnyarṇatattva*), which is singular—[since there are three fires, the phonemes are *ga*, *kha*, and *ka*].

Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva are the principles (tattvas) that constitute the "one" (eka); thus, the word and mantra consisting of three syllables refers to the eighteen *akṣauhiṇī* divisions of the army and worlds. "The fourth" (*turyā*) is another synonym for *utpūyinī*, which is *śāntā*. "Sixteen" refers to the sixteen vowels beginning with the visarga and ending with the letter *a*; thus, it is a single word consisting of the nature of the sixteen vowels.

And the Mantra-tattva is that which is called Śiva, the thirty-sixth; and although it possesses Śakti, it is considered one because of its predominance, for the sense is that Śakti cannot be distinct from the possessor of Śakti (Śaktimat).
However, since worlds do not exist within the Śāntyatītā [Kalā], there is no mention of them here.

Thus, the summary meaning is that the sixfold path (*ṣoḍhādhvan*) consists of one hundred and eighteen worlds, thirty-six principles (*tattva*), five kalās, ten steps (*pada*), an equal number of mantras, and fifty phonemes (*varṇa*).
The fourth [state] is the world of the army, which is the *pada-mantra*. 2.
There are sixteen phonemes, one word-mantra, and one reality; this is the Śāntyatītā [Kalā].
Thus [says] Abhinavagupta in the Āryā.
These three have been taught for the sake of summarizing [the doctrine] for the disciples. ||3||
The cry of the swan remaining as the sole survivor in the vicinity of the lake of the world-net;
the intense longing for that very state.
The form of a swan with five parts, having the head of the four-faced one (Brahmā).
This [self] is the five-fold digit (pañcakalāma) of Maheśvara; it is here abandoned as something extremely subtle, like the tip of a hair.
A great river with waves that are difficult to awaken from their fullness.
The entire multitude of beings, appearing as those very [beings], is like a net of half-strands.
He who removes the great disease of sin and the affliction of the senses.
This [world] is filled with those who have not yet attained the state of being supported by the Self, whose minds are not fixed on the jewel of the Self,
and whose vital breaths are driven by the winds of the mind.
The throat of the sage was completely filled with the *dhī-sāman* chant.
Desiring to seize him, he struck the body of the lord of the enemy army with his fist, causing it to tremble.
He then summoned his pride.
The new moon has appeared, closely following [the full moon].
In all cases, the elision of the final vowel occurs when the suffixes *addhakaraṇa*,
*nirbbāhāra*, *etilaḍeci*, *a*, *eha*, and *itattva* follow.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Paths of Kalā and the Others," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.

Regarding that, the intention behind saying "as far as" (*yāvad*) is this: due to the variety of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), there is indeed a difference in the causes, but not a difference in the effects. As it has been said:
"Wise men should not conceive of any difference in the fruit here within consciousness.
This means that for all [practitioners], beginning with those on the *āṇava* level, the attainment of the unsurpassed state (*anuttarapada*) alone is the fruit.
This has been stated as being for the sake of some person's direct attainment of liberation (*apavarga*).

[For the sake of cultivating the nature of self-luminosity: according to the aforementioned method of summary, since it serves as a prerequisite for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) to be described for certain individuals—[the reading in manuscripts *k* and *kh* is "because of the arising of the knowledge of its removal"]—initiation and so forth must be explained. In that regard, who [is such a person]?

The descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is examined for the purpose of defining the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*). Regarding this, some say that because of the absence of knowledge, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is rooted in ignorance; when that [ignorance] is removed, knowledge arises. As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"Knowledge, O Arjuna, reduces all actions to ashes."

Thus it is said. In that regard, the experience of karma is also twofold: gradual and simultaneous. Among these, if the experience were gradual, the consequence of further karma would be unavoidable; thus, there could never be a total exhaustion of this [karma]. On the other hand, if it were simultaneous, there would be no experience of these [karmas] at all. For such is the nature of karma: the giving of results in a sequential manner.

[If one were to say that the nature itself would be abandoned, this is not the case; thus, in both ways, the destruction of karmas would not be established from this. And therefore, it has been stated: "from the arising of knowledge. "The descent of power" (*śaktipāta*) refers precisely to the arising of perfect knowledge in them.

It must be stated: what is the cause? For that [cause] was said to be the investigation of the sixteen categories (*ṣoḍaśapadārtha*) and so forth; among those, which one is the single cause? If it were produced by karma, then—just like the fruit of karma—it would follow that it is itself an experience (*bhoga*);
the point is: what indeed is the difference between these two? And regarding that which experiences...
If one accepts the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) as being caused by the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*), there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [To this, one might object:

"But surely, even though there is no difference in their being the fruits of karma, it is by the force of the Lord's will that knowledge alone burns away other karmas, whereas karma such as [the attainment of] heaven or cattle does not. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The will of the Lord," and so forth.

Furthermore, there is mutual dependence regarding the arising of knowledge; for when knowledge has arisen, it is inferred that the cause is the will of God, and when the will of God is inferred, knowledge has arisen—thus, because of this mutual dependence, both would remain unestablished. Moreover, there is futility.

There would be the consequence of attachment and other passions in God; for when two opposing actions of equal strength mutually obstruct each other, there is an equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*). Indeed, here, when many karmas have been exhausted through the power of the sequence of experience, at some indefinite time, that which remains unripened—though it has reached maturity—[is obstructed].

Because they are mutually opposed by equal power, the two conflicting karmas remain obstructed with respect to their fruit; they remain indifferent toward ordaining their respective fixed experiences. Furthermore, the karmas that follow immediately after them do not turn toward the path of experience because they are not yet matured. Such is this state.

The equality of karmas is said to be characterized by the contradiction between two opposing actions. If it is argued that "therefore there is a descent of power (*śaktipāta*)," we say no; for if there were succession, contradiction would be impossible. Furthermore, it is logical that karmas occur only successively, because they cannot exist simultaneously since their very natures are mutually exclusive. And therefore—
Since each [cause] bestows its own fruit only in due sequence, what mutual obstruction could there possibly be among them regarding the fruit?
For it is impossible for them to act simultaneously at any single moment.
Even if there were an obstruction, it would be in relation to one thing while another remains unobstructed.
If it is argued that because karma has the tendency to grant experience (*bhoga*), when non-contradictory karma does not proceed,
there would be the consequence of the body falling at that very moment; therefore, the karma that bestows birth and lifespan (*jāti-āyuṣ-prada*) is not obstructed,
but rather only the karma that bestows experience (*bhoga-prada*) is obstructed— then from what [source] is this known?

If power (*śakti*) were to descend when that karma exists, then why would it fear the bestower of experience (*bhoga*)? Furthermore, regarding the ripening of impurity (*mala*): there is no dispute on the point that ignorance (*ajñāna*) toward the eternal, self-luminous reality is itself the impurity that causes the sprout of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). In this regard, the teacher Kheṭapāla has stated concerning it as follows:
He speaks of maturation: through the cessation of impurity (*mala*), there is the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). For it is the power *Raudrī* that causes cessation;

when she withdraws from her activity known as "cessation," then this [individual], through immersion in manifest knowledge and action, becomes a recipient of the descent of Śiva’s power. What is the nature of that descent of power?
[Here, he raises an objection with the words] "Of what nature... and so forth: First of all, the destruction of impurity (*mala*) is not possible;

for if impurity were one, it would be destroyed even for other souls, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of universal liberation. Alternatively, if there is no destruction but rather a "cooking" (*pāka*), which is the state of being obstructed by its own power—that too, like poison or fire, is indistinguishable for everyone, and thus that same [consequence follows].

A further objection: if it is argued that [the world] has a cause, then it must be stated whether that cause is karma or the will of Īśvara. In this regard, karma is not such a cause, because its sole purpose is to bring about experience (*bhoga*). Nor is it the will of Īśvara; for is that [will] independent or dependent? If it were dependent, on what would it depend? If, on the other hand, it is independent, then [it belongs] to him.

If it is argued that because he is free from passion and hatred, they would arise without cause due to the resulting lack of distinction toward all beings, then destruction would occur even earlier, and thus its stability would not exist at all. Furthermore, what is its cause?

By this, it is shown that dispassion (*vairāgya*), a specific quality of merit (*dharmaviśeṣa*), [as well as] service to the virtuous (*satsevā*) and the occurrence of adversity (*āpatprāpti*) [are the causes].

[The reading: Discrimination, service to the virtuous, association with the virtuous, worship of the deity, and so forth—these causes have been refuted; thus, everything asserted by the proponents of duality is inconsistent.
However, this is logically established in the non-dual doctrine of the independent Supreme Lord, for just as the Supreme Lord...
As it has been stated elsewhere:
"Just as the Supreme Lord, concealing his own nature with his own essence,
is called a 'bound soul' (paśu) by worldly people, even though his body consists of supreme non-duality."

In the very same way, when that [consciousness] again does not conceal its supreme luminosity, which is the nature of the stainless mind, it is called "Śiva" by the yogis. Through the play of concealing its own nature, it becomes the bound soul (paśu), the individual (pudgala), or the atom (aṇu); yet there is no contradiction regarding the distinctions of space, time, or essential nature for it.

In the same way, by the cessation of the obscuration of its own nature, the individual soul (aṇu)— which is the recipient of the descent of power (śaktipāta)— is said to be one whose essence is solely autonomy, whether it attains the restoration of its own nature instantaneously (by means of the "no-means" and so forth) or gradually (by means of the initiation and other rites to be described hereafter).

That Supreme Śiva is the one who causes the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) independently—meaning, he does not depend on karma, yoga, or other such factors. This *śaktipāta* has the manifestation of one's true nature (*svarūpaprathā*) as its fruit;
however, for one who is eager for worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), it depends upon karma, as in the case of one eager for enjoyment in a supramundane form.
"Supramundane form and unsurpassed enjoyment"; [in the manuscript *kh*, the reading is "supramundane form and enjoyment"].
However, that very descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs through Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others who hold office within the womb of Māyā, impelled by the will of the Supreme Lord.

Bestowing as its fruit the nature of the mantras and so forth, the discernment between Māyā and the person (puruṣa), the discernment between the person and his qualities (kalā), the discernment between the person and primordial nature (prakṛti), the discernment between the person and the intellect (buddhi), and other results, [it grants] the enjoyment of the lower principles (tattvas).

For one who is eager for both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), [the descent of power] obstructs enjoyment; it depends on karma regarding enjoyment, but regarding liberation, it is independent of that—thus it is "dependent and independent. Nor should it be asked why the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs in only a certain person, for it is the Supreme Lord himself who manifests in such a way; what then is this "person" (*puruṣa*) in its true nature?
That by which an injunction is made with reference to an object is called a "name" (*nāma*). And this descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is ninefold.
(In order to confirm what was stated here—that the descent of power is ninefold—the teaching from the *Mālinīvijaya* is now elaborated.)
Thus, at a certain time, by virtue of his own fitness,
this self becomes connected with the peaceful power of Śiva, which bestows the fruit of liberation.
Due to that connection, someone may be liberated from that very moment;
