for some, their identity with ignorance ceases.
Pervaded by the power of Rudra and desiring to depart by the will of Śiva,
he is led toward a true guru for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having propitiated Him and received from the gratified Lord the initiation of Śaṅkara,
one shall go to Śiva either at that very moment, through enjoyment, or upon the fall of the body.
Having received the initiation into yoga and understood it, one should practice yoga;
one attains perfection in yoga and, at its conclusion, the eternal state.

In this very context, the author of the *Laghupañcikā* states that one's identity with and absorption into a certain ignorance— characterized as incomplete manifestation (*apūrṇākhyāti*)— is reversed; through the casting off of that [ignorance], complete knowledge (*pūrṇajñāna*), which is characterized by the direct realization of one’s own Self, arises, because he has been permeated by the intensely powerful energy of Rudra.
It is recognized by the arising of its respective characteristics; he will explain this in the second chapter.
And when that exists, one should observe these signs of his:
among them, the first sign is unwavering devotion to Rudra.
The second is the accomplishment of mantra, which produces immediate conviction;
and the third characteristic for him is mastery over all sentient beings.
They say the fourth sign is the completion of the task already begun;
the fifth should be known as poetic skill, charming and adorned with figures of speech.
"The knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises for him spontaneously.

For this very reason, because he does not depend on a guru or others here, he is taught elsewhere as "one who is initiated and perfected by the goddesses of his own self-awareness" (*svasaṃvittidevībhiḥ*). And thus, for him...
Even when knowledge arises spontaneously and is not conceptually constructed, for one who requires corroboration— wondering "Is this exactly so, or not?"—

when the desire to approach a teacher arises, then that [desire] is led toward a true teacher, whose characteristics will be described hereafter, by means of the Supreme Lord’s power. Thus it is said:

By the mere attainment of that [state], such firmness arises within him that his supreme knowledge may reach fullness; by virtue of which, for others, enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) would occur effortlessly. For this very reason, although it is unconstructed (*akalpita*), its "having a foundation" (*sabhittikatva*) is stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*; otherwise, however, it would be "foundationless" (*nirbhittika*) for him alone.

And by the repetition of the three quarters [of the verse], he— being one whose own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*) has been awakened by Śiva’s power (*śivaśakti*) in a form that is either dull or intense—

desiring to attain the realization of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), wishes to go toward a true Guru. Once he has gone and reached him, from that Guru, who is pleased by various modes of propitiation (*ārādhana*), [he receives grace].

Having attained a certain method of initiation belonging to the Supreme Lord, one may, immediately thereafter, while still in the body, go to Śiva; by means of the intensification of perfect knowledge and action,
one attains the direct realization of one's own self as being of that same nature, whereby the previously mentioned collection of characteristics is attained.
He shall become liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Alternatively, having experienced his remaining enjoyments, when death is imminent, he shall go to Śiva at the very moment the body falls.
[The teacher should act] upon seeing a disciple seized by old age and tormented by diseases.
Then, having caused him to ascend, one should unite him with the supreme reality.

The meaning is that, according to this principle, one should be immediately joined to the supreme reality (para-tattva) by means of the initiation for immediate liberation (sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā). For this very reason, the two words "or" (*vā*) indicate an alternative: however, one who is bound by an intense-moderate power (*tīvramadhyamā śakti*), even after receiving initiation as before, remains in the same state because of the persistence of the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties which are not the Self.

Because he does not know his own nature as being of the single form of Śiva due to a lack of firmness regarding the Self, he must experience for some time this karma that initiated the present body; then, with the remaining traces of activity exhausted upon the fall of the body, he shall go to Śiva,
whereby there will be the manifestation of identity with Him— this is the meaning of the entire passage beginning with "he" (sa).

The phrase "or at that very moment" (*tatkṣaṇāt*) is set aside, and by way of returning to the point, this is the meaning: since yoga is indeed the sole means for enjoyment (*bhoga*), it is logical that for those who desire enjoyment, initiation should primarily consist of yoga;
thus it is called "yoga-initiation. For this very reason, in the initiation described previously, knowledge (*jñāna*) was primary.
Since the action that brings about liberation follows both [desire for enjoyment and desire for liberation], it is not mentioned separately; therefore,
although one is connected with the power of the "middle-middle" nature and possesses a longing to attain the state of Śiva,
because of the very fact of being a seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), one is joined by the Guru to some specific reality as desired by the intellect, and from that very [point].
Having understood yoga by means of hearing, reflection, and so forth, one should practice it through the successive stages of the respective *dhāraṇās* and other methods;

by the majesty of its accomplishment, having enjoyed the experiences of the various *tattvas* with this very body, at the conclusion thereof, one attains the eternal state—this is the connection [of the text]. This applies to the case of a middling-intense descent of power (*madhyamadhyasaktipāta*).

The distinction here is that at the end of the body, one attains perfection through yoga (*yogasiddhi*). As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, in the section on the medium descent of power (*madhyama-śaktipāta*): "Even though one is eager to attain Śiva, if one is intent on enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), then upon the destruction of the body after having experienced that [enjoyment], one becomes Śiva."
But one who is joined there in the center of the mandala by means of the reality (tattva) as well,
shall enjoy that excellent experience at the end of the body and thereafter go to Śiva.

Thus, this twofold division concerns the *śivadharmiṇ* and the *sādhaka*; however, the first [division] concerns the *putraka*. This is the distinction. By repeating this very verse—excluding the second quarter—for the *lokadharmiṇ* *sādhaka*, there is the attainment of the form of enjoyment (*bhoga*) through yoga, by means of conjunction (*yojanā*) with whichever desired principle (*tattva*) or other state is intended at the end of the body.

Since attainment occurs precisely through the intense, middling, and mild forms of perfection (*siddhi*), it would follow that power (*śakti*) itself is of such a nature. This has been stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* itself:
"In the intense-mild, the middling-mild, and the mild-mild [degrees], there is the desire for enjoyment (*bubhukṣutā*)."
Ultimately, through the method of the supreme [state] alone, one gradually reaches Śiva.

Thus [it is said]. And all of this has been analyzed by us in that very *Tadviveka*; however, there is this much deficiency therein, namely that the reading of this final verse is absent. Although we have provided it as a plausible restoration, we did not include it [in our edition], because it is generally not seen in other manuscript copies.

Furthermore, due to the fear of the base and foolish people of this day who are mostly wicked, and because it is explained as being the author's own discovery through the logic of the matter, it is indeed the supreme [explanation]; so enough of further elaboration. In that regard, there is again a threefold division according to the intensity, mediocrity, and mildness of its excellence, neutrality, and deficiency.

At that very moment, upon the falling away of the body, supreme lordship results from the most intense [degree of practice]; from the medium-intense degree, there arises for one who is independent of scriptures and teachers an intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*) based on self-realization—the arising of which makes him known as an "intuitive teacher" (*prātibho guruḥ*), who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation even without external refinement. For such a person...

There is no conceptualization here of [distinctions such as] the initiate (*samayin*) and so forth; yet even here, there exists a gradation due to the variety of individual desires. Thus, although intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) is present, it may still require recourse to scripture and other means for the sake of corroboration. Consequently, there are many divisions, such as that between the "wall-less" (*nirbhitti*) and the "with-wall" (*sabhitti*).
It is stated in the scriptures that for the *prātibha* (intuitive) teacher, the intuitive portion (*pratibhāṃśa*) is in every respect more powerful;
in his presence, others have no authority, just as in the presence of the beginningless Śiva, there is no perception of duality.

For those who are liberated Śivas, through a mild or intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*) regarding the tasks of creation, dissolution, and so forth, there arises a desire to go toward a true Guru; however, if it is directed toward an untrue Guru, there is only concealment (*tirobhāva*). Indeed, going from an untrue Guru to a true Guru occurs only through the descent of power. As for the true Guru:
The venerable Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka himself is directly full of the knowledge of the reality of this entire scripture;

for even in the case of a yogin, since liberation occurs through the very fact that his knowledge is well-practiced, the state of being a yogin is of no use there, just as possessing good fortune, beauty, and so forth is irrelevant.
[The reading is also: "the service of beings such as Lāvaṇya is useful," and so forth.

Any other [teacher] whatsoever is a false guru. Thus, one desiring to go [to liberation] receives from the guru initiation characterized by knowledge (*jñāna-dīkṣā*), by means of which one becomes liberated immediately even while living; this is because of [the power of] the gaze and the teaching here.

The distinctions [of initiation] include being awakened by the scriptures, witnessing the conduct [of the Guru], the offering of sacrificial oblation (*caru*), and so forth. Alternatively, for one who possesses constant practice (*abhyāsa*), he obtains at that very moment the initiation that effects the immediate separation from life-force (*prāṇa*). We shall explain later that this [initiation] must be performed precisely at the moment of death. The intense [descent of power] (*tīvra*) is threefold, according to whether the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is superior, middling, or [inferior].
Even one who has received initiation may not yet possess such firm conviction regarding his own Śiva-nature;

however, through the gradual ripening of that conviction, he becomes Śiva himself at the end of the body. Yet, even while eager for Śiva-hood, there may be one who still desires worldly enjoyment from the midst of his existence; such a person is likewise a vessel for knowledge through that very initiation.

"Having experienced enjoyment with this very body obtained through the practice of yoga, one becomes Śiva at the end of the body; however, for those of inferior or middling [capacity], having experienced enjoyment with another body, they attain the state of Śiva. As for the middling [type], it is threefold; when the longing for enjoyment is predominant, then there is dullness.
Since the practice of the mantras and yoga of the Supreme Lord culminates in liberation, it consists of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).

Even within that, there is a threefold division due to differences in degree; this is the primary [threefold] descent of power. As for the followers of Vaiṣṇava and other traditions, however, their [attainment] does not culminate in liberation—just as a king’s favor [may lead to various worldly ends]—and thus they are not analyzed here.

It has been stated that the presiding presence of Śiva’s power (śivaśakti) exists everywhere; however, that [power] is not always the supreme Jyeṣṭhā, but may instead be Ghorā or Ghoratarā. This descent of power (śaktipāta), though diverse, is so due to its varying degrees of intensity—that is, by way of internal gradations.

Someone established in a Vaiṣṇava or other tradition, having reached full maturity through the sequence beginning with the *samayin* stage within the fivefold stream (meaning within a specific tantra among the five streams),
attains the supreme authority over the Lord’s transcendent *Ṣaḍardhaśāstra* (Trika); but another...

Through the process of transcendence (*ullaṅghana*), which possesses infinite divisions, there is a certain "non-sequential" (*akrama*) state; for this very reason, even those gurus who abide in the lower and lower teachings are here non-qualified even for the mere sight of the mandala.
Conversely, a guru who abides in the higher teaching not only qualifies but rather enlivens the lower and lower teachings due to his fullness.
Thus, he is the one authorized for all [levels].

And he—the spiritual guide (deśika), the teacher (guru), the preceptor (ācārya), the initiator (dīkṣaka), and the "kisser" (cumbaka)—is indeed the most excellent of all only when he possesses complete knowledge, because without him, initiation and the like cannot be successfully accomplished. However, if he is eager for the fruit [of practice], he may be fit to be a yogi.

Through the instruction of the means (upāya), one is capable of bestowing the fruit immediately; however, through the instruction of the means, one is properly engaged in knowledge itself, for even regarding liberation, there is a desire for the perfection of knowledge by means of the practice. And [as it has been said]: "One should seek out many gurus."
"Just as a bee seeking fragrance might go from flower to another flower, so too a disciple seeking higher knowledge should go from one guru to another. Thus he should act.

However, depending on the distinctions between the various levels of knowledge—such as the highest of the high—one may remain with them; yet, in the case of abandoning a guru who possesses complete knowledge, [one must proceed further].
It is indeed a penance. Now, one might ask: "Should he not also be abandoned for speaking falsely or contrary to the truth? We say: "Certainly not.

For, because he possesses perfect knowledge, there is an absence of passion and the like; thus, his silence and so forth are due solely to some condition pertaining to the disciple. (Note: The reading *śiṣyagataṃ naiva* is found in manuscript *kh*.)
Since it might occur due to causes such as unfitness or lack of confidence, the disciple should strive for its attainment through worship and not for its abandonment.

Thus, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which has grace as its cause, is indeed independent—because it does not depend on karma, necessity (*niyati*), or other such factors. [Note: *k* reads "due to non-dependence on necessity" (*niyatyanapekṣaṇāt*).]
Regarding *tirobhāva* (concealment): concealment indeed has as its fruit the experience of intense suffering and delusion dependent upon karma and other factors.
As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"When, by means of necessity (*niyati*) itself, through the process of veiling one's own nature..."
At that time, one experiences suffering, delusion, and so forth; such is the sequence of the fruits of karma.

"Having abandoned the rule [of karma], he remains intent on desire, though enveloped by suffering and delusion; yet, wishing to illuminate [all], he dwells without partiality even in concealment. [The reading "independent of karma and so forth" (karmādyanapekṣa) is found in manuscript k.
For just as one who is awakened acts like a fool through the heart due to the sovereignty of light, so too does he act.

And he censures the conduct of the deluded; likewise, even the deluded person might perform the conduct of the awakened, such as the propitiation of mantras and so forth, and might censure it. As it is said by the venerable Vidyādhipati:
"Those who have received initiation into your path of instruction..."
Driven by delusion, they fall into error;
surely the light of your splendor does not reach them— for can the rays of the sun ever cause the day-lotuses to close?
Even those who have known what is to be known and occupy the position of a protector, if they follow a wrong path other than your way in their mantras, they are not correct;
for their [knowledge] generally arises from inferential cognition and the like.
"False awakening is like a lamp made from snake-fat. Just as his deluded actions,
even while being performed, come to an end for one who is awakened, so too do his awakened actions [come to an end],
yet they are censured because they consist of the performance of prohibited acts.
And because he himself is suspicious of that very [state],

he causes him to sink into the mire of suffering and delusion; however, for one upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred, there is no concealment (*tirobhāva*), and even here there is dependence on karma and so forth, as it has been said:
Nor was his karma so great that he remained in such a state;
for what indeed was that karma, or why was the destiny here not equal to that of the former?
Therefore, by that will of the Supreme Lord, he is so deluded that he seeks to become a vessel for suffering to be experienced throughout infinite time.
"In that case as well, due to the diversity of desire, it consists of three types: pertaining to this world, the next world, or both. As before, this [consequence] is to be negated there as well;

for, due to the diversity of desire, there may be the result of suffering to be experienced solely in this body, as in the case of those previously mentioned who are prone to both serving and reviling the teacher, the deity, the fire, and so forth, during initiation, the observances, and ritual conduct.
Just as for those established in the teaching of Śiva and for those who have abandoned it, even in that case, due to the variety of divine will (*icchā-vaicitrya*),

one who has become concealed may either be joined with grace (*śaktipāta*) spontaneously, or after death, through the mediation of the compassion of relatives, gurus, and others; thus, there is the participation in the fivefold cosmic act (*pañcakṛtya-bhāgitva*).
As it was said by the venerable Śrī Somānanda:
"If it is asked, 'How could that which is unblemished be directed toward that which is contemptible?', [we reply:
because of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the expansion of form, its being contemptible is illogical."
"Since he possesses the nature of Śiva through the expression of the fivefold activity for his own purpose,
where is there any need to search for other causes for one who is thus engaged?
Thus, by reflecting within himself that he is indeed the Supreme Lord, he should not view his own self as fragmented.
Just as the Supreme Lord, through his own unimpeded freedom,
may conceal his own nature, so too may he reveal it.
Or, even when his own abode is not yet awakened, he should act as if awakened;
or he may awaken again—this is that descent of power (*śaktipāta*) which is independent of external means.
Just as Maheśvara, though possessing no wealth, remains free from the thirst of desire,
so too does he remain when his nature is understood.
Her form is like the clear, stainless autumn sky.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Descent of Power," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

It was stated that initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other matters must be explained; therefore, for the purpose of defining the essential nature of initiation, the preliminary bath (*snāna*) is taught. Furthermore, bathing is said to be purity (*śuddhatā*), and purity is...

It is the immersion into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord. For purity is indeed the removal of turbidity—this is a general statement. And turbidity is the conceit that there is a commingling with another form whose nature is not that [of the one], even though it is of that very same nature. Regarding this, he states the specific detail:

By the words "tadiha" and so forth: impurity (*aśuddhi*) is the conceit (*abhimāna*) that there is a mixture of a form other than that [pure self] within one's own Self—which consists essentially of independent bliss and pure consciousness—or even within the universe; [the phrase "a form other than that" means a form that is dependent and non-luminous]. And that [impurity]...

That [obstruction] too is removed by means of the intense immersion (*samāveśa*) into Mahābhairava; for some it occurs instantaneously, while for others it depends upon looking toward other means. In that regard as well—meaning, in the case of depending upon other means—it occurs for someone, somewhere, and at some time, according to the distinctions of one, two, three, and so forth, whether in their entirety or individually.

The variety of distinctions is obtained through consolation (*āśvāsa*), and that is eightfold, consisting of the forms of earth, water, wind, fire, ether, moon, sun, and the Self. As it is stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
"For these eight forms, whose nature is grace, are essentially Śiva."
"By meditating on them as having the nature of Svarūpa-Śiva and Śiva-rūpa, they bestow their respective fruits. Thus,

when the forms have been contemplated as being of the nature of the Supreme Lord through the power of the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), and when the body has been entered by the Supreme Lord through identity with Him, the functioning of distinctions such as "body" and so forth [ceases].

The reading is *śarīrāvibhāgavṛtteḥ*. Even consciousness (*caitanya*) attains immersion into the Supreme Lord; however, because it generates satisfaction through bathing, clothing, and so forth, it becomes a means (*upāya*) to the Supreme Lord. And it has been said in the venerable *Ānandatantra* and others, as stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
And in the venerable *Ānandaśāstra* it is said: "For the wise man, there shall be no impurity;
rather, bathing while clothed serves to generate contentment. [Thus:
steadfastness, nourishment, vigor, the burning away of impurities, pervasion, the capacity for emission (*sṛṣṭi*), and the capacity for maintenance (*sthiti*).

And non-differentiation—these are the primary fruits in those respective [cases], meaning in those various [elements] such as earth and so forth. This is because the mantra, being "superimposed" (upāhita)—meaning established through contemplative connection—assumes each of those specific forms. However, there is a distinction regarding the Hero (vīra), as follows:

The dust of battle is the water for heroes, the great wind is the ash of heroes, and the sky of the cremation ground is the moon and sun placed therein; the Self is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). Furthermore, regarding the external and internal [aspects], [the external bathing procedure is as follows]: while recollecting the desired mantra in the heart, [one should walk] three steps within the dust of cow-hooves.

One should go [to bathe] in the royal [pool]. Likewise, having washed from the head down to the feet with water consecrated by the five-limbed mantra, one should immerse oneself while reciting the root mantra along with its limbs. Then, having consecrated the ash raised up with the *astra* mantra, one should apply it to the crown, heart, secret place, and feet; thereafter, one should place on the crown a handful of ash consecrated with the root mantra along with its limbs.
One should cast [the breath] three times into the *hlādini* wind; having performed the movement of coming and going, one should perform the *vāyavya* (wind) bath.
Likewise, when the sky is clear, fixing one's gaze upon the single fire, one should recite the mantra—this is the *ākāśīya* (ether) bath.
Similarly, the meditation on Śiva within the splendor of the moon and sun is called the [lunar and solar] bath.
The Self alone is the Supreme Lord, the great ocean free from all ritual conduct;
having submerged the universe therein, He remains as both the pure and the purifier.

Thus ends the eighth [practice], the bath of the self. It has been stated that "duality" refers to immersing oneself here and there within [the deity] by means of identifying with the mantra that is worshipped externally. The specific detail, however, is as follows: having rendered the substance of bliss—which resides in the vessel of the *vīra*—consisting of Śiva through gazing, one performs the worship of the circle of mantras (*mantracakra*) right there. Then...
The primary bath is the satiation of the wheel of deities residing in both the body and the vital breath by means of that very [fluid].
The internal [bath] is the state of identification with those respective wheels, such as the earthly and so forth, through the assumption of their forms, beginning with earth.
They say that bathing is the immersion into Supreme Bhairava; however, as to how that occurs,
even that is merely external bathing.
It is not primary, but rather figurative; however—
The knowledge of those whose thirst has ceased is immersed in supreme bliss;
there, night and day are spent.
He who knows another as himself.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Ablution," in the *Śrītantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.

Then, with a serene heart, he should go to the place of sacrifice; and that place is wherever the heart becomes endowed with serenity and fit for immersion into the Supreme Lord, and not merely any other location.

Even though other characteristics have been mentioned, the cause is indeed identity with the object of meditation (*dhyeya-tādātmya*); and since that too arises solely from the clarity of one's disposition (*bhāva-prasāda*), there is no other means of establishing it. As for the mention of locations in the scripture, such as "the seat and mountain peak" (referring to the Pradyumna-pīṭha and so forth), this is merely an enumeration of sites.

One must understand that this alone is the supreme [reality], because in those various locations such as the *pīṭhas*, by the will of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the powers (*śaktis*) possessed by the Supreme Lord assume bodies; thus, these places are like the "Land of the Aryas" (*āryadeśa*)—the sacred land situated between the Vindhya and Himalaya mountains—as they are for the righteous.
(As the lexicon states: "The Land of the Aryas is the sacred ground, the middle region between the Vindhya and Himalayas.")

Like the lands of the Mlecchas belonging to the unrighteous, the mountain peaks and similar solitary places constitute a state of one-pointedness due to the avoidance of distraction; as it has been said:
"Therefore, for the sake of accomplishment or liberation, in worship, recitation, and meditative absorption..."
"That place where the heart becomes beautiful through rest. [Note:

"The reading is *aikāgryapradatvam* (the state of bestowing one-pointedness). Thus it is said. There, one should perform the general placement (*sāmānyanyāsa*) outside, in front of the sacrificial hall, first on the two hands, and then— [Note: "The reading is *pūrṇam* (full) in manuscript G. Then—]
In the body: *hrīṃ na pha hrīṃ hrīṃ ā kṣa hrīṃ*.
With these two mantras of the *mālinī* and *śabdarāśi*, which denote Śakti and the Possessor of Śakti (Śaktimān), [the *śabdarāśi* is the *mātṛkā-tantra*; the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* is as follows].

On the forehead, the face, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the two cheeks, the two rows of teeth, the two lips, the crest-lock, and the tongue— these sixteen locations are occupied by the vowels ending with the visarga.

One should assign the *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group respectively to the right and left shoulders, the arms, the fingers and nails of the hands, and the armpits; and the *ka*-group to the hips, thighs, and so forth.
The labial consonants (pavarga) on the two sides, the back, the belly, and the heart—thus, these nine [syllables].
This is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.

Thus [it is said]. The *mālinī-nyāsa* is specified in the *Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa*. In that context, the *mātṛkā* is well known as the sequence beginning with *a*, *ā*, and so forth. As for the *mālinī*, it is as follows: *na, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, tha, ca, dha, īṃ, ṇ, u, ū, ya, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, i, a, va, bha, ya, ḍa, ḍha, ṭha, jha, ña, ja, ra, ṭa, pa, cha, la, ā, sa*.

[AH PA KṢA MA ŚA AṂ TA E AI O AU DA PHA. At the beginning, by means of a single [syllable], there is first the Power (śakti) and then the Possessor of Power (śaktimān). In the case of liberation (mukti), [the sequence proceeds] from the tips of the feet to the end of the head; however, in the case of worldly enjoyment (bhukti), all is the reverse. For the Goddess Mālinī is the primary form of Power (śākta-rūpa), which grants all desires through the union of the seed-syllables (bīja) and the womb-syllables (yoni).
As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"From the agitation of mutual seed and womb, and from the arising of emission,
what accomplishment would it not bestow, or what deficiency would it not fulfill?"
"Although the intermingling of the letters of the *yoni* and the *bīja* exists in many ways,
nevertheless, this sequence beginning with *na* and ending with *pha* is proclaimed as the primary one.
Furthermore, for another purpose, this [alphabet] is joined with the garlands of Rudra's powers (*rudraśaktimālā*) and is in bloom with fruits.
She is the female bee of the sound that destroys the coolness of saṃsāra, the bearer of supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mokṣa), and endowed with the power of giving and taking—
this is because of the traditional teaching on the identity of the letters *ra* and *la*. For this very reason, even a mantra whose ritual procedure has been lost [is effective].

By this placement (*nyāsa*), even one who is "with stain" (*sāñjanaḥ*—meaning accompanied by the impurity of *māyā*) becomes full. Having attained the state of being "without stain" (*nirañjana*), the [mantra] of Garuḍa, Viṣṇu, and others becomes the bestower of liberation.

This very placement is to be performed in the *arghapātra* (offering vessel) immediately after the placement on the body. For here, [it serves] the functions of the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*).
[Its definition is as follows:
Whatever, whether established or unestablished, is designated as that which is to be accomplished (sādhya),
is called "action" (kriyā) because it possesses a nature characterized by succession.
Likewise:
"A collection of parts that arise in succession,
whose unity is mentally constructed by means of their subordinate components, is designated as 'action' (*kriyā*)."

Thus it is said: "Likewise, the factors of action (kārakas) are indeed only six: the agent (kartṛ), the object (karman), the instrument (karaṇa), the recipient (saṃpradāna), the point of departure (apādāna), and the locus (adhikaraṇa)."
The act of worship has been presented as an illustration for the sake of establishing the firmness of the realization of non-difference from the Supreme Lord.
[Regarding "presented as an illustration":
for instance, just as a horse, having attained the autonomy of the delusion that it is a bracelet...]
Even when mounted in battle, a horse does not transgress that training.
Likewise, one whose factors of action (kārakas) have been transformed into Śiva through the practice of the rite of worship casts off the duality of those factors, whether walking or standing still.
In the same way, for one steadfast in practice, this entire universe gradually and forcefully manifests as if dancing in the unshakeable, perfect state of Śiva.
Thus it has been said by the venerable Utpalabhaṭṭa:
"Oh, what a most excellent and great festival of Śiva’s worship is this,
wherein the agitation of even the thirty-six principles abounds in splendor!"

And in that regard, all the agents (kārakas) attain the state of the Supreme Goddess in this manner: through the purification of the place and the performance of the placement (nyāsa) on the vessel of honor (arghapātra)—which serves as the support for the sacrificer—and through the placement upon the body of the sacrificer, and through the placement upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), etc., of the object of sacrifice. Thus, it is also by means of the sequence of ritual action.

Having made all the causal factors (kārakas) into the Supreme Goddess, and perceiving all actions through that very vision, one becomes the Supreme Lord himself even without the primary practice of knowledge and yoga. Having thus deposited [the deity] into the vessel of offerings (arghapātra) and worshipped it with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should sprinkle the essence of the sacrifice, the flowers, and other materials with its droplets.
[As it has been said:
"Indeed, everything touched by droplets of water from the *argha* vessel becomes pure;
what other purity could there be than that which comes from contact with the rays of the Sun of Śiva? Thus. Then:
Regarding the *prabhāmaṇḍala*: "One should proceed to the trident, the sun, the bull, the Mothers, and the Kṣetrapāla; this is the sequence for worship there.
The mantra for worship consists of the *tāra* (OM), the name in the dative case, and 'namaḥ'."

"Or, by a single utterance, he is called the 'External Retinue' (bāhyaparivāra). Thus, one should worship on the ground or in the sky with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the External Retinue. Then, at the location of the door—in this regard, the detailed sequence for the door-location is as follows:
Above the door, one should worship Lakṣmī and Gaṇeśa; to their right, Diṇḍin, and to their left, Mahodara;
in the center, Vāgīśvarī; likewise, to its own right, Nandin, and to the left, Kāla; in the center, the Trimārgagā (Gaṅgā);
and similarly, on the two door-posts to its own right, Kālindī, Cchāga, and Meṣa.

Below the threshold, one should worship Ananteśa and the Ādhāraśaktis; in the middle of the door, one should worship [the deity] along with Sarasvatī and the thousand [others]. All are to be conceived as situated upon the lotus-base, and the mantra is exactly as before.
In brief, it should be understood as: *namaḥ dvāradevatācakrāya*. Oṃ.

One should worship with the mantra: "Obeisance to the circle of the door-deities. However, if the place outside is not concealed, having entered, one should perform the worship of the outer retinue and the circle of door-deities right at the front of the mandala's sacrificial ground, as stated in the *Tantrāloka*.

"If one performs the secret worship (rahasyapūjā), then one should worship the external retinue and the door-keepers inside, before the deity, according to the sequence of visualization. Thus, one should perform the previously mentioned rites such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth, but not externally. Then, having cast flowers consecrated with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), reciting "phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ," [one should proceed].

Having visualized the obstacles as dispelled, one should enter within and look all around the sacrificial hall with a gaze ignited by the rays of the Supreme Lord. [In this regard, there is a further distinction: one should perform the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra and its covering with the Kavaca-mantra. Therein:

One desiring liberation should stand facing north, so that by the fierce splendor of the Lord, his bonds may be instantly scorched. In this regard: "Even though here there is no such thing as a direction called 'east,' 'west,' and so forth..."
For there could be no cognition of that single, unconditioned [entity].
If it is argued that priority and so forth are designated by an adventitious condition (*upādhi*), then that [priority] is already accounted for by direction.
But how could a mere adventitious condition alone produce such diversity?
Internalizing this doubt, he says "therein" and so forth: the very sovereignty of the Supreme Lord,
through the manifestation of forms— and that manifestation of forms,
by virtue of the variety of forms, causes the succession of space to appear.

Thus, according to the principle established in the *Pratyabhijñā* and other works, the reality of Space (*diktattva*) manifests. In that context, the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) alone is the center, because from it the differentiation of "other" things proceeds. That which is accepted by the light is "above," while that which is not so—that is, not accepted by the light—is "below."

That which is oriented toward manifestation is the "east" (pūrva); the other is "west" (apara) [meaning subsequent]. Because it is the state of having become manifest, that which is the place for ascending the stream of its manifestation immediately thereafter is the "south" (dakṣiṇa) due to its favorability; however, that which faces it is the "north" (uttara) because it is the object of illumination—thus is the quartet of directions.

Therein, in the center is the Blessed One; above him is the Īśāna face, below is the Pātāla face, and in the four directions starting from the east are the faces known as Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāma; in the middle of these four directions are the other four [faces].

Thus, it is the very majesty of consciousness (*saṃvit*) that manifests the differentiation of directions produced by form; therefore, direction (*dik*) is not a separate reality. And just as one's own shadow—[as it is said in the *Trika-hṛdaya*:
"Just as one desires to overstep the shadow of one's own head with one's own feet"—]...

"Just as the head would not be at the location of the feet, so too is this Vaindava-portion. Thus, when she desires to transcend, she appears further and further ahead, and in that way she attains the state of being the center of the Supreme Lord. It has been stated that "being the presiding authority over all" is precisely what constitutes the state of being the center (mādhyasthya).
Just as the Blessed One is the one who establishes the divisions of the directions—as it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"The division of directions arises from that [central face], due to the four faces;
when joined with the fifth, those two [the left and right] abandon their own individual natures"—so too is the Sun. For he...

It has been stated in various places—such as the *Parātriṃśikā* and elsewhere—that the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is indeed the supreme sovereignty (*pārameśvarī*). In those instances, it is prior to manifestation;
and wherever that is so, it is precisely there, for even though it is dependent upon its own self, it stands before the space facing itself.
"In this way, the discussion regarding the directions is based on the contemplation of the unification of the triad consisting of one's own self, the Sun, and the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara)—
so say the teachers of Abhinavagupta. This being the case, one faces north [regarding 'facing north,' it has been said as follows:]"

"To grasp the southern light of the Lord situated in the center, they should face north; to grasp the western light, they should face east. Having sat down, [one performs] the purification of the body, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth, by which [the purification of the *puryaṣṭaka* body occurs].
Having projected the self, situated in the heart-lotus— subtle, resembling a firefly, and flickering like a spark—
upward through the piercing of the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by means of the upward breath-retention (ūrdhvarecaka),
and having dissolved the mind, ego, and intellect into the Supreme Reality, [one perceives] the void.

"One should meditate on the body": by abandoning the sense of "I," one should burn away the state of being a body, as it is said in the *Vijñānabhairava*: "With the fire of Time that has arisen from the station of Time, one should burn one's own city."

"One should contemplate it as consumed at the end; then a state of peaceful radiance arises. Thus, even while in proximity, because of the absence of a body—just like another's body—for one who has ascended to the firm, waveless abode, there occurs that which is indeed the primordial [state], due to the very nature of vision.
That very [power] is the form of the vibration (*spandakalā*). Above that is the placement (*nyāsa*) of the circle of deities to be worshipped (*yājyadevatācakra*), as taught;
and here, primarily, it is the *śaktis* that are to be worshipped, because the Lord’s ninefold self (*bhagavannavātman*) and so forth reside upon them.
As for their being ninefold:
Primordial Nature (prakṛti) and the Person (puruṣa), as well as Necessity (niyati) and Time (kāla);
likewise Māyā, Vidyā, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva.

Thus it has been taught that [Śiva] is worshipable precisely because of His power (śakti). Herein lies the intended meaning: since reflective awareness (vimarśana) alone is indeed worship in every respect, even Śiva requires it for the attainment of His own self-luminosity. [The reading is "bhagavati"].

And because it is power (*śakti*) alone that is worthy of worship, so say the Gurus. In this context, one should contemplate the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhā nyāsa*), which consists of the five states beginning with waking and the sixth, the state of essential nature (*svabhāvadaśā*) called the Absolute (*anuttarā*). Therein, for each of the causal deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śakti—[the following applies]:

Because of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—that is, the placement (*nyāsa*) in which the entire collection of thirty-six principles, transcending worldly principles, functions as non-different from the venerable Lord Bhairava—the state of Bhairava is attained due to its fullness; therefore, this objection has no place. As they say: "Once the ascent into the waveless [state] has been achieved, what more remains?"

"By means of the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the emission of the principles (*tattva-sṛṣṭi*), etc."— for that very form of Bhairava is "waveless," consisting of the infinite variety of the cycles of emission and withdrawal manifested within its own self. Thus, having contemplated the vital breath, body, intellect, and so forth as having become the Supreme Goddess through the yoga of mutual fusion, [one should contemplate] both externally and internally.

One should worship with flowers, incense, libations, and so forth, as far as possible. Therein, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the trident and lotus upon the body, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the intellect (*dhī*), according to the respective sequence. For example: at the base of the *ādhāraśakti*—meaning within the four-finger space at the end of the *ādhāraśakti*-trident—is the root (*mūla*), the bulb (*kanda*).
From the base to the tip of the uvula is the stalk ending in the *kalā*-tattva; the knot consists of *māyā*;

the lotus of *śuddhavidyā* is of the nature of a fourfold crossroads; and therein resides the venerable Lord Sadāśiva, who is himself the Great Corpse (*mahāpreta*) because he is profoundly dissolved (*prakarṣeṇa līnatvāt*).

Because of its predominance as awakening, because of the dissolution of the body which consists of the object of knowledge, and because it consists of the reflective awareness of *nāda*— thus, that [power] has arisen from the navel and emerged through the three apertures at the crown of the head.
The triad of spokes consisting of Nāda, Antaḥśakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā, ending with the twelve [tattvas], and above that the three pure lotuses of the Unmanā state—
when this differentiated [universe] composed of all things has been made into a seat by virtue of its being the pervading substratum; [in this seat...]
[The reading is *vyāpakābhāvena*. Having visualized the deity as the object to be contained,

exactly as intended, the offering of all phenomenal existence (*viśvabhāva*) right there into that self which is filled with the nature of the All (or, according to the reading in *k* and *g*, "filled with the contemplation of the All")— that alone is worship.

That which is the becoming one with that [reality] is meditation (*dhyāna*); that which is the oscillation arising from the presence of such internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is recitation (*japa*);
and by the very power of the great splendor awakened through the sequence of such reflective awareness, [the goal is attained].

The universalization of all things— that is the fire-oblation (homa). Having performed it in this manner, one should meditate upon the retinue as emerging from that very mass of fire like sparks, and worship them in the same way.
Meditating on this trident from its base up to its tip at the *dvādaśānta*,
having transcended sequential order and reached the forefront of the circle of goddesses, one attains the state of moving through the void.
This Khecarī consists of filling the space from the Mūlādhāra up to the tip of the sky at the end of the twelve finger-breadths;
she is so called because of her own movement and abiding, and because of her consumption of her own nectar.

Thus, in reality, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done arises from the internal sacrifice alone. Even so, for one truly possessed [by the deity], the external sacrifice must also be performed for the sake of removing limitations (*avaccheda*). For even he who does not possess such immersion (*samāveśa*), the external sacrifice is primary; because through its practice, he too attains immersion.

The internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) is for the purpose of concealing the state of being a bound animal (*paśutā*); even when that [state] has not yet been ascended, it bestows purity through the power of its intentional resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Now, when one wishes to perform initiation (*dīkṣā*), then for the sake of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), one should perform the appropriation of the ground (*bhūmiparigraha*), the worship of Gaṇeśa, the worship of the two jars (*kumbha-kalaśa*), and the worship of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

And one should perform the oblation (*havana*). However, for the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, there is only the worship of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth, and the oblation. In that context, "preparation" (*adhivāsana*) is the conferring of fitness through purification upon the disciple, like the acid treatment of teeth.

The reading is *kartavyā*. [This refers to] causing the deity to become oriented toward the performance of the rite (*kartavyonmukhatva*), and the Guru’s taking hold of that [orientation]. Furthermore, by means of the presence of the sacrificial materials within the temple, there is the conferral of fitness for the articles of worship through the nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇa*) provided by the splendor of the Supreme Lord (*parameśatejas*). In that regard, the sacrificial hall is filled with all the necessary implements.
Having performed the ritual for the goddess Mālinī or the Mātṛkā, and contemplating that [the vessel] has been taken and filled with a mass of light from their syllables,
one should cast a handful of flowers. Then, having recited the previously mentioned mantras of the weapons as appropriate, [one should proceed].
Having scattered grains of *siddhārtha*, unhusked rice, parched grain, and so forth—which possess a radiant form—one should sequentially strike [the ground] in the northeastern direction;
this is the ritual of seizing the site (*bhūparigraha*). Then, having offered a seat ending with *śuddhavidyā*, one performs the worship of Gaṇapati;
thereafter, one should worship the jar (*kumbha*), which is filled with the substance of bliss (*ānandadravya*) and adorned. Then...

Having placed the assembly before the one to be consecrated (*yājya*), he should empower that pitcher with one hundred and eight recitations of the principal mantra, while remembering it as the presiding deity over all according to the prescribed rite.
In the second pitcher, he should worship the *astra* (weapon-mantra) for the pacification of obstacles. Then, he should worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their respective directions.
One should worship the weapons (*astra*). Then, one should place the weapon-vessel (*astrakalaśa*) into the hand of the disciple who has previously been initiated.

The Guru himself should take up the water-pot (*kumbha*). Then, while the disciple pours a stream of water along the boundaries of the house to pacify obstacles, the Guru, accompanied by the vessel, should follow him, [reciting] this mantra:
O Śakra, reciting this, you must [place it] in your own direction for the pacification of obstacles.
One must perform one's work with vigilance, by the command of Śiva.
In the three-syllable name, "bho" is the only one [to be used], because otherwise there would be the risk of violating the meter.

Then, one should place the water-pot (kumbha) in the northeastern direction. Upon the scattered offerings (vikiro), one should place the weapon-vessel (astrakalaśa)—the meaning is that they are placed upon the pot in mutual alternation. This is the intended sense for the pacification of obstacles.

When the identity of Śiva and Śakti has been accomplished through the power of immersion (samāveśa), then follows the worship of both. Then follows the worship of the Supreme Lord in the center of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). Then, having contemplated the fire-pit as the form of the Supreme Lord’s Śakti, one kindles the fire therein.
Having unified [the mantra] with the fire of consciousness within the heart— visualizing the blazing fire of Śiva through its conjunction with the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the mantra—

and having deposited [the mantra] therein and worshipped it, one should satiate the mantras with clarified butter (*ājya*) and sesame seeds, as well as with the vessel of the offering water (*arghapātra*).

The consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other substances is indeed sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is precisely the vision of their non-difference from the Supreme Lord. Then, having offered oblations according to one's capacity, one should position the *sruk* and *sruva* facing upward and downward respectively—representing Śakti and Śiva—as they turn toward one another.
Rising with both feet together,
while reciting the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [he visualizes] a stream of supreme nectar falling from the full moon of Śiva risen in the sky at the end of the twelve [fingers].
And the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) should remain until the exhaustion of the clarified butter (*ājya*). As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"That awakening which indeed exists above is reflected in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*);
the fire is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are the same, and the oil is the essence of consciousness consisting of volition."

Having thus understood from the beginning the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva), the clarified butter (ājya), and the mantras, one should cast the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire of awakening at the *dvādaśānta*.
This is the "Satisfier of the Mantra-Wheel. Then, having brought the consecrated sacrificial porridge (caru):

Having offered a portion to each of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the jar (*kalaśa*), the pitcher (*kumbha*), and the fire (*vahni*), and leaving one portion remaining, he should give that portion to the disciple. Then [he gives] the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*). Regarding its casting, there is a reading stating it should be done with the *astra-mantra* [in the directions] of Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Vāyu. Then, avoiding any distraction, [the ritual continues].

Having led the disciple— who has his eyes bound for the sake of becoming fit to behold the future mantra— into [the mandala] and having placed him with knees on the ground, one should have him cast a handful of flowers. Then, his eye-bandage suddenly removed,
because his faculties have been graced by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), he perceives that place where the mantra resides through direct realization.

Beholding it, one becomes absorbed in that; for those whose faculties have been graced, the presence of the mantra becomes manifest, as if all beings were trembling before it. Then, having worshipped the wheel of deities—filled with all the paths—with his own right hand shining brightly, [he does so] with the left hand.
[The remainder: Having worshipped that hand, one should place it—burning away the bonds (pāśas) of the disciple—upon the head, heart, and navel of the disciple.
This is the ritual of the Śiva-hand, as stated in the Tantrāloka.
Having performed the rite of Śiva’s hand, he should cause the disciple’s bonds to be consumed by it,
and then, through the yoga of meditation, lead the disciple to the state of ultimate rest.

Then, he should cause that child to perform a prostration toward the water-pot (*kumbha*), the weapon-vessel (*astrakalaśa*), the fire, and his own self; thereafter, he should cast the offering (*bali*) for the spirits (*bhūta*) and the Mothers (*mātṛ*). Then, having worshipped on the left with gentleness, he should then perform a prostration toward the one who nourishes the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*). Then...

One should offer the *bhūta*, *devatā*, and *dig-bali* outside, filled with liquor, meat, water, and so forth [the reading "filled with meat and so forth" is found in manuscript *k*], and then perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*). Thereafter, having personally partaken of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*),
one should remain with one's mental activity awakened, having attained identity with the disciple’s self, even while sleeping.

At dawn, if the disciple has had an inauspicious dream— [as it is said in the chapter on dreams regarding the consideration of the auspicious and inauspicious nature of dreams: "Devas, fire, gurus, their worship, ritual implements, and so forth..."]
A woman who is pleasing to the heart, the drinking of wine, and the eating of raw meat.
Drinking blood, having one's head cut off, being smeared with blood, feces, and urine, and mounting mountains, horses, elephants, or delightful vehicles;
Whatever generally leads to one's pleasure is declared to be auspicious;
one should proclaim that for the increase of satisfaction, for joy is indeed the supreme fruit.
Thus, this [result] pertains to one who harbors doubt; for another, however, there is nothing—neither auspicious nor inauspicious—as it has been said:
"But for those whose doubt has dissolved, [the result] arises by the power of their dream."
There would be nothing, whether auspicious or inauspicious... [etc.]

Thus it is said: "Even therein, the sattvic self clearly perceives the distinct particularity through the subtle body (liṅga); the rājasic [perceives] from the mere signs; the tāmasa perceives nothing at all—neither pleasure nor pain, neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious. One should state that.

One should not explain this to him, for otherwise he would be seized by doubt and anxiety; rather, one should effect the expiation for that solely through the *astra* [mantra]. Then, having worshipped the Supreme Lord in that same manner, one should enter before Him through the sequence of the disciple's vital breaths (*prāṇakrama*) into the six locations: the heart, throat, palate, forehead, the aperture (*randhra*), and the *dvādaśānta*.

Performing the contact with the six causes while contemplating eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for each one, he should cause the disciple’s vital breath to rest there for a short time and then descend again.
In this very way, having brought about the attainment of the portion of Rudra (*rudrāṃśāpatti*) through the forty-eight purificatory rites performed above, [the initiation is complete].

The forty-eight sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are as follows: conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), parting the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*), the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), and the initiation into the vows (*vratabandha*). Within this very category is the vow of binding the girdle (*mekhalābandhavrata*).

The seven vows—namely, the vow of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha-vrata*), the vow of the deerskin (*ajina-vrata*), the three-life-span vow (*tryāyuṣa-vrata*), the twilight vow (*saṃdhyā-vrata*), the vow of fire-worship (*vahnyupāsā-vrata*), and the vow of mendicancy (*bhikṣā-vrata*)—are included herein. These very same [vows] are designated by names such as Bhauteśa and others in the Tantric scriptures. Likewise, the *aiṣṭika* and *pārvika* [rites].

The domestic rites, the Soma sacrifices, the Godāna ceremony, and marriage; the Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, Āgrayaṇī, Caitrī, and Āśvayujī offerings; the Āgneya sacrifice, the Agnihotra, the Darśa, the Paurṇamāsa, the Cāturmāsya, the Paśubandha, the Sautrāmaṇī, and the Agniṣṭoma.

The Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Āptoryāma. He has golden feet; [these are its internal subdivisions]: Guhyahiraṇyadhṛt, Hiraṇyameḍhra, Hiraṇyanābhi, Hiraṇyagarbha, Hiraṇyaśrotra, Hiraṇyatvak, and Hiraṇyākṣa.

"Hiraṇyajihva" and "Hiraṇyaśṛṅga"—these are the names of the nine Citra-sacrifices. [The other nine are: Aśvamedha, Vānaprastha, Pārivrājya, Compassion (dayā), Forbearance (kṣānti), Absence of Envy (anasūyā), Purity (śauca), Lack of Exertion (anāyāsa), Auspiciousness (maṅgalya), Absence of Miserliness (akārpaṇya), and Absence of Greed (aspṛhā).
These have been successively indicated and enumerated in other scriptures; and likewise in the venerable Svacchanda,
it is stated that there are forty-eight qualifications for a Brāhmaṇa.
The impregnation rite, the rite for the birth of a male child, the parting of the hair, and the birth ceremony;
Naming, the rite of departure, the first feeding of solid food,
and the tonsure ceremony— by this alone, O lady of excellent hips, eight [purifications] are proclaimed as being purified.
O Goddess, when these have been completed, he is then born as a twice-born;
this ninth stage is proclaimed to be the "binding of the vow" (vratabandha), which constitutes his full physical form.
I shall now duly explain the constituent parts in their proper sequence:
the girdle, the tooth-stick, the deerskin, and likewise the triple weapon.
They know the twilight rites, the worship of fire, and alms-gathering as the seventh;
these are seen as the restraints at the time of initiation, O fair-faced one.

According to the Vedic ritual tradition (*vaidikakalpa*), these [rites] must necessarily be performed so that there may be no lapse in the observance of the first stage of life (*prathamāśrama*). However, according to the Tantric tradition (*tāntrika*), they are as follows:
Bhauteśa, Pāśupatya, Gāṇa, and likewise Gāṇeśvara.
And they know Unmattaka, Asidhāra, and Ghṛteśa as the seventh.
These seven vows of the religious students (brahmacārins) have thus been described.
These have been seen in the Pārameśvara Śāstra—that is, in the Tantra. Thus they are indicated. The observances of conduct (caryāvratas) are to be understood as being proclaimed as auxiliary limbs;
for together with these, there is indeed one ninth bond of observance.
This group of seven vows has been described as being included within that;
thus, O fair-faced one, fourteen vows are to be offered.
Thus it is said: likewise, the four Vedic vows must undoubtedly be offered as oblations.
He states them as follows:
The *aiṣṭika*, *pārvika*, *bhautika*,

and *saumika* [observances] are mentioned in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-śāstra*) as vows to be performed at specific times through the recitation of Vedic texts that prescribe the *iṣṭi*, *parvan*, *bhūta*, and *soma* sacrifices. However, in the *Yajñasūtra*:
The threefold knowledge, the fourfold officiating at sacrifices, the gift of a cow, and the ceremonial bath—
these are the four Vedic vows.
Thus these have been described; however, in this context, the gift of a cow (godāna) shall be treated separately.
One should understand that up to this point there are thirteen such sacraments (saṃskāra).
And he says that by performing these [rites], one becomes qualified for the Vedas:
"Therefore, indeed, [he] is a vessel for the Vedas."
Furthermore, O beloved, what follows from that? That "gift of cows" (godāna) consists of fourteen items;
it is characterized by the gift of a pair of cattle to the preceptor at the conclusion of Vedic study for oneself.
The shaving of the hair and so forth is the *godāna* rite.
Then, having been authorized for the householder’s life by his gurus, the initiated one, having become perfected in knowledge, should marry a maiden as his wife.

One who has attained purity through the study of the Vedas is called a *snāta* (one who has performed the ceremonial bath). For it is with this very intention that the ritual bath at the conclusion of study is prescribed in tradition; therefore, he is perfected and complete by means of the knowledge consisting in the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas. Alternatively, it is because of the injunction: "One should renounce even from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*)."
Desiring to go forth into the religious life immediately,
one should fashion a wife out of darbha grass and perform sacrifices together with her.
The fifteenth [topic] to be known is thus the sacrament consisting of marriage, which takes the form of the obligatory and occasional rites enjoined for the householder stage of life;
by this very [means...]
The five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) are indeed: the satiation of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings; likewise, the satiation of all living creatures, and the study of the Veda.

Thus, the obligatory sacrifices (*nityayajña*) as set forth in the *Yajñasūtra* have been summarized. Furthermore, there are five slaughter-houses (*pañcasūnā*) for the householder: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar, and the water-pot; by using these, he is bound [by sin].
For the sake of expiating all of these in due order,
the high-souled ones have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day.
And therein,

study is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), while libation (tarpaṇa) is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña); the burnt offering (homa) is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña), the bali-offering is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).
Thus, the intention is that these obligatory sacrifices (*nityayajña*) are included within the context of marriage.
He now states the occasional sacrifices (*naimittika*):
... [omitted] ... thereafter, the animal sacrifices (*paśumakha*) in sequence.
They call those [omens] indicative; I shall describe them in due order.
The Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrāyaṇī,
as well as the Caitrī and the Āśvayujī— these are the seven cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas) in their proper order.

The *aṣṭakās* named after vegetables (*śāka*) and so forth are those occurring during the dark fortnights beginning with the month of Pauṣa; they are so called because they are intended for the satiation of the ancestors with vegetables, meat, cakes, and greens. The *parvanī* [aṣṭakā] occurs on the first day of both the bright and dark fortnights; the sacrifice performed on that occasion is likewise called *śrāddha*.

The rite to be performed on the anniversary of the death of one’s father and others, the procedure for the *upākarma* and other rites to be observed on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the *śrāvaṇī*, the *āgrayaṇī*, and the sacrifice of the new grain (*navānnayāga*); the ritual for the ancestral *śrāddha* and so forth to be performed on the full moon of Caitra because it is the beginning of a *manvantara*; and that which is to be performed on the full moon of Āśvayuja—the *āśvayujī*.

The rites of the *vrīhyāgrayaṇa* and others, such as the obligatory offering of oblations (*havirdāna*), constitute the seven domestic (*gṛhya*) cooked offerings (*pāka*) thus specified. One should understand that, together with these, there are twenty-two [rites] in total.
Together with these seven, one should perform the fifteen previously mentioned sacraments (saṃskāras). Then, the Āgneya, the Agnihotra, and after that the Dārśa;
likewise, the Paurṇamāsī and the Cāturmāsya are to be known.
The animal sacrifice (paśubandha) has been specified, and after that, the Sautrāmaṇi;
these seven oblation sacrifices (haviryajña) have been taught, O beloved, as they purify.
The production of fire by means of the fire-drill (araṇi) according to the Āgneya method; the Agnihotra, which is the offering of oblations both evening and morning;
the Dārśa, which by way of figurative indication refers to the sacrifice performed on the new moon when the moon is visible;
the Paurṇamāsī, the general sacrifice to be performed on all full-moon days; and the Cāturmāsya.

Starting from either the month of Phālguna or Caitra, at the end of the four-month period on the full-moon day (paurṇamāsī), one should perform the distinguished sacrifice known as Paśubandha, a specific type of sacrifice in which the flesh, fat, and other parts of an animal are offered; and the Sautrāmaṇī, a liquor sacrifice dedicated to the deity Sutrāman. He summarizes these as well:
Together with these, one should understand the twenty-nine formative factors (*saṃskāra*).
Now, [the Soma sacrifices are]: the Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, and likewise the Ṣoḍaśin.
The Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and likewise the Āptoryāma.

Thus, these specific sacrifices are designated as *somasaṃsthās* (Soma-terminuses). The ritual actions characterized by the form of sacrifice (*yajña*), which consist of drinking Soma using a vessel (*gṛha*) as the instrument, are the *somasaṃsthās*.
One should perform these aforementioned formative factors (saṃskāras), numbering thirty-six, according to the sequence of mantra-offerings; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Now...
Hiraṇyapāda, Pathama, as well as Guhyahiraṇyadhṛt,
Hiraṇyameḍhra, Hiraṇyanābhi, and Hiraṇyagarbha.
Hiraṇyaśrotra, Hiraṇyatvak, and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa,
Hiraṇyajihva, and Hiraṇyaśṛṅga— these are proclaimed as the ten sacrifices.

The embryo is the heart; these are the parts beginning with the wings, which are specific types of fire-altars (*agnicityā*) for which gold is placed in the locations of the feet and so forth, according to the various shapes of those respective wings and other parts.
Furthermore, each one here is supported by a hundred [pieces of gold].
Regarding the specific requirement for the *homa* (fire-offering) for the sake of attaining this [result], he says:
"All these are purified by a thousand [offerings]...
This very *citrayajña* (variegated sacrifice), beginning with the "Golden-footed" (*hiraṇyapāda*) and so forth, is to be accomplished by means of a thousand *homas*.
...the thirty-seventh.
Furthermore,
after that, one should perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) in due order;
this horse sacrifice is also for a Brāhmaṇa who, by virtue of his karma, has attained the status of a sovereign monarch (sārvabhauma-bhūpati).
This must indeed be done. Thus, from the time of marriage onwards, by performing all these rites with the aforementioned number of offerings, one then becomes a householder (*gṛhin*);
a householder is one who stands in the second stage of life (*āśrama*).
The meaning is that one should know that thirty-eighth [chapter] to be the ritual known as the Aśvamedha;
thereafter, one becomes a forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
Then, by undertaking the life of a wandering mendicant and performing the final rites, one thus attains the status of a true Brāhmaṇa.
The two stages of life consisting of forest-dwelling (*vānaprastha*) and wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) constitute two purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*);

the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) is prescribed for one established in the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) for the purpose of purification through expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in case it is not performed, but not for one who has become a forest-dweller or has resorted to wandering mendicancy.

Therefore, he is not counted separately as "thus. In this way, according to the sequence of the fire-offerings (*homa*) for the Pārameśvara mantra, although the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) pertaining to the bound soul (*pāśava*) exists, because of the presence of defects such as the consumption of seeds and so forth, true Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) does not arise. However, they recognize this forty-first sacrament, characterized by the state of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), along with those previously mentioned.
This is to say, it is calculated together [with the following].
Therefore, I shall briefly describe the eight qualities of the self:
compassion toward all living beings, patience, and freedom from envy.
Likewise, serenity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, and furthermore,
freedom from miserliness and lack of longing— these are remembered as the eight qualities of the self (ātma-guṇas).

Compassion (*dayā*) is empathy for others; forbearance (*kṣānti*) is the absence of retaliation even when one has the power to do so against those who cause harm; freedom from envy (*anasūyatā*) is the capacity to endure the virtues of others; purity (*śauca*) is the cleanliness of mind, speech, and body; lack of exertion (*anāyāsa*) is the performance of actions that do not bring distress;
and auspiciousness (*maṅgalya*) is [the possession of] auspicious objects.
Beholding, touching, and thinking, lack of miserliness, giving according to one's ability, lack of craving,
and contentment with what is obtained— these are the qualities of the self;
they are qualities of the internal organ, the elements, speech, and so forth, which are closely connected to the self, but not qualities of the self itself.
"Because its nature is consciousness (cidrūpatva). In this very manner, forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāra) have been enumerated.

Thus he becomes a *samayin*. Then, one should entrust him with the venerable mantra along with flowers and other offerings. Thereafter, one should explain the *samayas* to him: devotion toward the Guru with one's whole being, as well as toward the scripture and the deity.

One should understand that turning away from those who are the opposites of such [teachers] constitutes a form of disrespect; likewise, one must show reverence toward the teacher’s son and others, as well as toward those with whom one has a connection through sacred knowledge (*vidyā*)—such as those initiated by him previously—even if they are unrelated by blood, provided it is for the sake of honoring them and not out of personal attachment.
This should be understood as applying to those connected through marriage as well, but only for the purpose of their veneration and not out of self-interest.

One should not harbor loathing toward women who are barren. One should not utter the names of deities, the names of one’s gurus, or mantras, except at the time of worship. One should not use a bed or other items that have been used by one’s guru.
Whatever [else...].

One should not engage in worldly play and the like in the presence of the Guru. Apart from that, one should not harbor thoughts of superiority toward others. In all matters, such as at śrāddha ceremonies and the like, one should worship the Guru alone. During all occasional rites, one should not utter words such as "śākinī" and so forth. One should observe the sacred festival days (parvan).

One should not associate with those of inferior vision, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others. One should not look upon those established in this teaching with the notion that they belong to a lower caste. When the circle of one's gurus has arrived at one's home, one should perform a sacrifice according to one's ability. [One should not look upon] any Vaiṣṇava or other follower of an inferior path...
Out of curiosity for that scripture, one may even treat it with respect, yet one should not abandon [one's own path]; even then, one should not look upon it with a sense of superiority.
One should not engage in common conduct or association with those who bear sectarian marks (liṅgin); rather, one should honor them solely according to one's ability.

One should abandon doubt. Abiding in the *cakra*, one should not conceptualize the divisions of the final and foremost [parts] as being produced by birth. Apart from the body, one should not regard any other abode, sacred site (*tīrtha*), or the like with great respect.
One should [recite] the heart-mantra (*mantrahṛdaya*) without ceasing.
Having heard "You should remember [this]," the disciple should bow down, accept the teacher,

satisfy him with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) extending even to his wealth, wife, and body, and then gratify those previously initiated, as well as the poor, the helpless, and others, according to the procedure for future [rites]. And by the rule for what is to come...

One should satisfy the circle of forms (*mūrticakra*). In this way, one becomes a *samayin*. One is qualified for the practice of mantra, daily worship, listening, and study; however, regarding occasional rites (*naimittika*), one should always request the Guru alone in every case—this is the rule of the *samaya*.
Having surveyed the entire path within and then beheld one's own Self as full,
one should look upon the group of twelve with a mind intent on bestowing grace.
In this way, the initiate disciple shall reach the ultimate limit.
Having become a leader among those who have attained the supreme burden of the highest realization, he is one whose own self is uplifted and whose essence is free from all worldly attachments;
through this initiation into the discipline of the path, he has bathed in the fire of the supreme sound.
Thus spoke the Jina, who is the abode of modesty and the destroyer of much humiliation.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation for the Samayin," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Next is the procedure for the initiation of the *putraka* (spiritual son). [The term *putraka* means "like a son"; the suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of a representative.
That procedure is extensive and should be understood from the *Tantrāloka*. Here, however, it is stated in brief. The ritual up to the stage of the *samayin*...

Having performed the worship on the third day upon the trident-lotus— [the description of the trident-weapon mandala here is for the purpose of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) in the case of the initiation of a *samayin*, whereas here the distinction is that it is by means of external visualization (bahiḥ-kalpanā)— one should perform the collective sacrifice (sāmudāyika-yāga) there in the mandala.
One should worship the outer retinue and the circle of door-deities outside; then, on the eastern side of the maṇḍala,
beginning from the northeast corner and ending at the southeast, one should worship in successive rows Gaṇapati,
the Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parameṣṭhin, the former teachers, the circle of Yoginīs, and Vāgīśvarī.

One should worship the Guardian of the Field (kṣetrapāla). Then, having obtained the appropriate command, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) and worship the entire path, beginning from the base of the trident up to the white lotus. Thereafter, in the central trident, on the middle spoke, is the Blessed Lady Śrī Parābhaṭṭārikā together with Bhairavanātha.
Likewise, on the left spoke is the venerable Aparā; on the right spoke is the venerable Parāparā;

in the center of the right trident is the venerable Parāparā; and in the center of the left trident are the two venerable Aparās, each according to its respective place. Thus, in the Lord’s presiding over all locations, everything [is pervaded].

"It becomes complete through that empowerment. Therefore, one should worship the entire circle of deities, from the central spike to the outer spokes, up to the world-protectors and their weapons, as non-differentiated from that [central deity]; by virtue of that empowerment, everything is worshipped everywhere. Then, [one should worship] in the pitcher, the jar, the mandala, the fire, and in one's own self.
Through the contemplation of non-duality, there is the pentad of substrates:

"Just as the pentads consisting of Hrasvā, Ākāra, Viriñci, Jagarā, Dhāriṇī, and so forth, as well as Śakti and the others, likewise belong to the praise of Śaṅkara, whose nature is the full reflective awareness."

I constantly remember that Pañcapraṇava, which is renowned throughout the universe and whose names beginning with Praṇava have been attained by Kuśa, Lava, and others, for the sake of reaching the abode of absolute freedom.

"Having known the *praṇava* in its fivefold form—short, long, protracted (*pluta*), subtle, and extremely subtle, which is supreme auspiciousness—one pierces through [the knots] and attains liberation; of this there is no doubt. Then, one should perform the special worship with flowers and other offerings, nourished by the flavor of non-duality with the Supreme Lord.

One should perform [the rite]. Why say more? One should prepare the sacrificial site, fully provided with libations and offerings, free from stinginess regarding wealth. However, if one lacks wealth, the Great Maṇḍala Sacrifice must certainly not be performed. Furthermore, one should offer living animals; for they too are thus graced, out of compassion.
One should have no doubt regarding the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice. Then, having gratified the Supreme Lord in the fire with sesame seeds,
clarified butter, and other offerings, one should prepare another animal before it for the offering of the omentum (vapā), and satisfy the circle of deities with that omentum.

Then one should worship the maṇḍala again; thereafter, having made a request to the Supreme Lord and having contemplated oneself as being entirely non-different from and complete with all six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), one should place the disciple standing before oneself.

In the case of initiation by proxy (*parokṣadīkṣā*), whether for one who is living or deceased, one should first meditate upon that person, or place an image of them made of *darbha* grass, cow dung, or other materials before oneself. Having thus prepared the disciple—
