sprinkled with drops from the vessel of honor (*arghapātra*) and worshipped with flowers and other offerings— one [should purify] the entire path (*samastamadhvāna*).
One should place [the mantras] upon his body. Then, one should reflect as follows: for one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), one should not purify the auspicious;

however, for one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*), both the auspicious and the inauspicious must be purified. In the case of the seedless initiation (*nirbījā*), one should also purify the bonds of the rules (*samayapāśa*); and this [initiation] should be performed even for one whose death is imminent or for one who is utterly ignorant.
The command of the Supreme Lord applies even to him, yet his success comes solely from being steadfast in devotion to the Guru, the Deity, and the Fire.

And in all these cases, the distinguishing factor for the mantras is precisely the grasping of their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because they perform their specific functions in accordance with those impressions. Thus, having considered this difference in latent impressions—
Through the specific contemplation of the primary mantra, one should contemplate the entire path situated within one's own body as non-dual with Śiva,
proceeding in this sequence from the big toe up to the *dvādaśānta*.

Having approached the disciple— whose body and consciousness have been made non-different from his own body and consciousness— right there in that lake of infinite bliss, which is the essence of the sovereignty of freedom,
the Lord of the entire wheel of deities who is replete with all the powers of will, knowledge, and action, [he bestows] the entire multitude of mantras...

Having become one with the self of the disciple, he should attain rest; thus, he becomes non-different from the Supreme Lord. Then, if he should desire enjoyment (*bhoga*), wherever his desire for enjoyment arises within a particular *tattva*, there he [should remain] in both its collective and individual aspects. (*Samasta* refers to...)

One should apply [the visualization] by means of the conceptualization of the egg (*aṇḍa*) and the conceptualization of its internal divisions. Immediately thereafter, for the sake of his remaining activities, one should contemplate for him a body consisting of pure principles (*śuddhatattva*), which has issued forth instantaneously from the nature of the Supreme Lord, so that his remaining activities may be accomplished.

Thus, this is the initiation (*dīkṣā*) which severs all fetters (*pāśa*). Thereafter, the disciple should worship the Guru with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) as before. Then, he should perform the ritual for the disciple in the fire using the *Śrīparā-mantra*. The definitive explanation of this is very clear in the *Parātriṃśikā-vivaraṇa*.
[It should be observed: "I purify such-and-such a principle (*tattva*) of such-and-such [a person]," ending with *svāhā*.
For each principle, there are three oblations; at the end, there is a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending with *vauṣaṭ*.

Thus is the purification of the principles up to Śiva. Then, according to the sequence stated for the rite of union (*yojanikā*), there is a full oblation for one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*).

One [initiation] is for the purpose of union with the station of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*), another for the purpose of the emission of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*). Then follows the worship of the Guru with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); this is the initiation of the "spiritual son" (*putraka*), by which past and future karma are purified, with the exception of that one [karma] currently being experienced.
Having internally unified his own existence— which consists of the entire path— with that which is external, [the Guru], free from all differentiation,
[establishes] the disciple’s intellect, vital breath, and body within his own [powers].
The awakened one should unify them within those [energies].
Having instantly attained the state of being one with the disciple, while he rests within that [state] which is full of the awakening of great bliss— just for that long.
The bound soul attains the nature of Śiva.
This ocean of worldly existence remains without the union of the virtuous;
that beast of ignorance becomes even more formidable without it.
Thus, it remains facing inward within the boat.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Initiation of the Spiritual Son," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Furthermore, when death is imminent—as it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"Having seen the disciple overcome by old age and tormented by disease..."

"Then, having caused him to ascend, one should unite him with the Supreme Reality. When the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs either spontaneously or through the mediation of a kinsman, then one should perform for him the initiation of immediate departure (*sadyaḥ-samutkramaṇa-dīkṣā*).
Having projected the entire path (*adhvan*) onto the disciple and having purified it in due order, [one should worship] the Blessed Lady...

Having placed the *kālarātri* mantra and the *kṣurikā*, which possesses a luster equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*), one should sever the bonds of the vital points (*marmapāśa*) one by one in sequence with it, having pierced those bonds of the vital points.

Having meditated on the fire-dhāraṇā by means of the radiance emerging from its vicinity, one should meditate upon the scorching of all the vital points (*marmas*) by that [fire]. Then, one should meditate on the body being filled with wind from the big toe up to the crown of the head; thereafter, one should [meditate on] that [wind] from the big toe.

"Having drawn it upward to the limit above, one should cut it with the Night of Time (Kālarātri). Thus, one should cause the consciousness of the disciple residing in the *brahmarandhra* to emerge. Then, according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the sake of unification (*yojanikā*), so that at the end of the final oblation, the individual soul (*jīva*), having emerged, becomes non-different from Paramaśiva. [For him...]
The sense is that for someone who possesses faith and so forth, there is utility [in this].
For one desiring enjoyment (*bubhuksu*), however, the second full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) serves to join him to the place of enjoyment;
and at that time—[that is, at the moment of departure]—there is the dissolution of his life-force (*jīvalaya*), and no remaining course of existence here.
Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyām*)—meaning the entire [knowledge] interwoven with the partless [reality]—here this is the reasoning:

this initiation of immediate departure (*sadyaḥsamutkramaṇadīkṣā*) is to be performed only for a yogin; for one who has not practiced the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) could by no means perform it. Therefore, it is said that "one should recite the knowledge of Brahman."
One who has not practiced this [mantra] should perform this initiation after having recited it. Regarding this, he states the reason: "For that," and so forth.
It should also be understood that, by virtue of the causative sense being implied (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), one should have [the disciple] recite it. Or, one should recite it into the ear;
for that [mantra], being of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-svabhāvā*), [penetrates] the consciousness of the unawakened *paśu*.
[The reading: It immediately produces awakened reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the consciousness of a bound soul (*paśu*) who has been awakened.
Even for those such as the *samayin*, as it is said in the *Tantrāloka*: "Whether he be a *samayin* or a *putraka*, he should likewise recite this Vidyā."
"By reciting that [mantra], one attains the state of being a portion of Rudra arising from the *samaya*.

And this is the qualification for the recitation of this [mantra]. If, however, one should show the initiation—whether with seed (*sapratyayā*) or without seed (*nirbījā*)—to a fool who has received the descent of power (*āyāta-śaktipāta*), then this is the procedure at the time of the bestowing of the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*).

Having visualized in the right hand a triangular mandala belonging to Agni, formidable with flames, emitting sparks of the letter *ra*, and being fanned by a whirlwind outside, one should place therein some seed— such as betel nut and the like.
By means of successive *phaṭ* sounds awakened by the upward and downward *repha* (the letter *r*), [as stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
"The seed-syllable, scorched and tormented by the fierce series of *phaṭ* sounds ignited by fire,
becomes seedless and incapable of producing its own offspring."]

By that very same conviction, the impurities known as *mala* and *māyā*, along with karma, are heated [but not yet consumed] for the sake of their subsequent growth; however, through the power of mantra, meditation, and ritual action, they are [transformed].
"Once burnt, they are no longer capable of their own function; rather, this condition is one of seedless causality.
Thus did the illustrious and most gracious Śambhunātha explain it to me.
[Thus,] one should burn that power of its generation; performing it in this way, one should place that hand upon the head of the disciple.

For both of these, this seedless initiation (*nirbījā dīkṣā*) results in the destruction of the capacity to perform one's own functions, since it has been stated that even immobile beings (*sthāvara*) are eligible for initiation. The disciple, having become lightened and remaining within the interior of the wind, is shaken about. [In this regard, the following is the intended meaning in the *Tantrāloka*:]
"For the body, which is taught to be primarily composed of earth, then relinquishes its primacy;
one should join it to the supreme state by means of the mantra that brings about future lightness. Thus one should contemplate by which [means] it becomes light as if on a scale.
It is seen thus:
"If the mantra [is applied] during the procedure of cutting the vital points (marmakartana), in the state of lightness, and in the dissolution of the seed-state (bījabhāva)."
The Supreme Lord, being directed by that very appropriate path, swiftly accomplishes each respective task.
Having grasped whatever specific object they desire, they utter the mantra, their life-force being the power of their will.
That very mantra will certainly bring about its effect.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation with Empirical Signs," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.

Now follows initiation for one who is absent (*parokṣa-dīkṣā*); it is of two kinds: for the dead and for the living. Among these, the "dead" refers to one who has performed service to the Guru, or one who has been removed [from life], or one killed by malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the like, or one killed by a child [in a fit of rage], or one whose such inclination arose at the very moment of death.
Or, one whose descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has arrived through the mouth [of the teacher] is likewise to be initiated; such is the command of the Supreme Lord (the remainder of the sentence).

And here, in the initiation of the deceased (*mṛtadīkṣā*), the preliminary rites such as *adhivāsa* are not required. For the presence of specific mantras in the mandala, where much ritual action is involved, the best instrument is [the best...].

The meaning is "endowed with the characteristics. The site consists of flowers and so forth; the mandala consists of the seats and so forth—since, even when the mantra-mandala has not been invoked, it accomplishes the state of being a *samayin* (one bound by the pledge).
The form consists of the trident, lotus, and so forth, which is a specific object of meditation; and the mantra is itself self-luminous.

"The connection between a yogin devoted to meditation, one possessed of total absorption through single-minded devotion, and a man of knowledge—these have been described as causes for proximity in ascending order. What need is there to mention the case when all are present together?
Thus it was said by the Supreme Lord. Then, having worshipped the Deity, [one should fashion] His image out of kusha grass or other materials.
Having placed it at the forefront, one should behold it through the sequence of instructions on the knowledge obtained from the Guru; and that [power],

having risen from the *mūlādhāra* and forcefully traversed the staff-like path of the infinitely extended and well-distributed channels, reaches the space of the nose and, casting itself forth, is able to pervade all.

This is the great ritual application named "The Net" (Mahājāla), which brings about the desired living beings by completely covering the circle of the paths with a mass of flames that have become dense and beautiful with smoke.
By this, that which was to be concealed comes under the control of another; first it is brought face-to-face, and afterwards, if all of it is brought forth,
then from the middle of the path, it is led wherever one desires.
Whether for the purpose of attracting or raising up a deceased person, or for drawing forth one who is still living,
I have described this yoga called "The Net" (*jāla*), as received from the tradition of Śrī Śambhunātha;
this has been determined with supporting examples in the *Tantrāloka*.
Just as when two armies that have been long separated meet again, the horses,
elephants, and chariots rush toward their own respective kinds with delight;
so too, when the channels (*nāḍī*) and the wheels of the vital winds (*prāṇa*) come together through the winds of the *karaṇas*.
"Having unified [them] through their respective essences by those who have brought them under control through their own net. Thus it is said.
If it is asked, "Why does this not occur externally as well in acts such as attraction and so forth, even without practice? [the answer is:

because when those [external acts] proceed by the power of the connection with passion, hatred, and so on, there is no possibility of an immersion into sovereignty (*aiśvaryāveśa*). Therefore, due to being constrained by necessity (*niyati*), there must indeed be a dependence upon practice and the like. In this context:

However, such a state occurs through the immersion into the nature of the Supreme Lord, whose essence is grace. For it is the Supreme Lord alone who, by means of presiding over the body of the Guru, bestows grace upon those to be graced. And that [Lord] possesses inconceivable majesty, as has already been stated. Thus, the individual soul (jīva), drawn by the application of the "net" (jāla), enters a body made of darbha grass, a nutmeg, or the like.
He becomes possessed and yet does not move, due to the absence of the capacity of the mind, vital breath, and so forth;

however, by the power of meditation upon that [deity], he may indeed move even while in such a state. Even in that condition, the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), ending with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the union (*yojanikā*), are performed as before. Herein lies the supreme distinction.
The meaning is: "to this extent here. By means of the *pūrṇāhuti*, the dissolution of that form made of darbha grass and so forth into the supreme light must be performed.

Thus, having been extracted, he is liberated by the *pūrṇāhuti* itself—[the meaning is that he becomes released]. This applies even if he is situated among the gods, in hell, as a ghost, or as an animal; but as for a human being...

At that very moment, one obtains knowledge, yoga, initiation, or discernment because of possessing a body fit for such authority; this is "rescue from death. Even for one who is living but out of sight, when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred, this same sequence applies, with the exception of the fashioning of a figure from darbha grass, the conceptualization of its form, and the summoning of the soul (*jīva*). For such a person, it is sufficient that they are present through mere meditation.

Ritual action (*saṃskāra*) and initiation (*dīkṣā*) both bestow both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). However, because one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are so powerful, the severance of the latent impressions for enjoyment is impossible [in that case];

thus, regarding this procedure for indirect initiation (*parokṣadīkṣā*), it is said: "One should perform sacrifice for the sake of enjoyment for one who has transcended *māyā*. Furthermore, because [the severance of enjoyment-impulses] is not possible through many initiations...

The impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the higher teaching is powerful, whereas any other [impression] would serve to produce that very impression. Thus, even for one who has been initiated while absent, there is likewise the manifestation of knowledge and so forth.
Through the firmness of the immersion into the state of the Supreme Lord, the Guru partakes in absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
What wonder is there in [calling] one who has been initiated "dīkṣita" with reference to something out of sight?
O supreme Śivatanu,
you who have entered the ultimate reality through the power of your own sovereign will!
This host of Pisacas has been tormented as if it were something beyond perception.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Impersonal Initiation," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now follows the extraction of the *liṅga*.
It is said in the *Tantrāloka* regarding those who abide in the lower systems, beginning with the Vaiṣṇava and ending with the Dakṣiṇa Tantras: "Now,
when the lotus of the heart of those following the Tantras of the Vaiṣṇavas, Buddhists, and others— down to the lowest— is blossomed by the rays of the sun that is Śiva..."
First there is the extraction of the *liṅga*, and after that, the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Even one who previously resided within another *liṅga* shall attain the state of Śiva through initiation.
Having made him observe the fast there, on the following day, he should worship the Lord upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with the sādhāraṇa-mantra and cause him to hear his own religious duties.
This man was previously a bearer of the sectarian mark (liṅgin), but now he has been urged by you who are gracious;
therefore, bestow upon him your perfect favor.
O sir, having cast aside the penance arising from the fear of abandoning one's own characteristic mark, may he,
becoming one with that [reality] without delay, attain both enjoyment and liberation.
Having received his command with the words "So be it," one should cast that vow of his into the water,
discard it, and bathe him in the appropriate manner.
"Immediately thereafter, one should sprinkle the bathed person with the waters from the *argha* vessel;

then, one should offer him the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the tooth-stick. [Thus it is said. This applies to those who abide in the teachings, or those who have taken their vows, as well as even those established in the supreme teaching.

When those who have not been authorized by the lower scriptures and have served their gurus are turned upward [unmukhīkriyante] by the descent of power (śaktipāta) from the Supreme Lord, then for them this is the procedure: on another day, in the presence of the Blessed One— who has been worshipped with common mantras and whose activity has been made known to him— he [the disciple] should observe a fast.

Having caused him to enter there and having made him take the vow, one should cast [the flower] into the water; then he should bathe. Then, having sprinkled him and purified him with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), and having led him in with his eyes bound, one should cause the worship of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) to be performed with the common mantra. Then, with the common mantra...

Once the fire has been made auspicious (*śivīkṛta*), one should perform the purification of the vow (*vrataśuddhi*). Having performed what is called "enclosing with its mantra" (*tanmantrasampuṭa*), one should offer a hundred oblations ending in *svāhā*, saying: "I purify the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Then follows the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Thereafter, having summoned and worshipped Vrateśvara, [one acts] by his command from Śiva.

Having made the proclamation, "Be of no effect for him," and having gratified and dismissed him, one should dismiss the fire; this is the extraction of the *liṅga*. Then, for him, the preliminary rites (*adhivāsa*) and so forth are as before. The initiation (*dīkṣā*) is according to one’s wish.

Even one situated at a lower level, whose mind has been impelled by the intense power (śakti) of the Lord, and who is to be initiated after being purified—provided he was previously devoted to a false teacher; [note: the reading "nirataḥ sadgurāvabhūt" is found in manuscript kh].
Having obtained the supreme grace of the Lord of Wealth through the excellent teaching that follows the path of liberation, he now seeks the accomplishment of the understanding of the true Guru.
He undergoes the initiation that removes the sectarian marks.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Linga," in the *Śrītantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. ||17||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Now follows the consecration (abhiṣeka).
One should consecrate a person who has well-practiced knowledge for the role of a practitioner (sādhaka) or for the role of a teacher (guru), because:

Even one who is devoid of all auspicious marks (lakṣaṇa) is indeed authorized for the role of an achiever (sādhaka) and for bestowing grace, provided he possesses knowledge; no other is so authorized, even if he has been consecrated (abhiṣikta). A Guru, when entrusting his own authority, does not incur sin even if he does not perform initiation (dīkṣā) and the like, whereas previously [if he had failed to do so], he would have incurred sin.

By means of the binding of authority (*adhikārabandha*), which bestows the station of a Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*), his very bondage constitutes the non-performance of initiation and other rites; once consecrated, he should observe the *vidyāvrata* for six months, performing daily recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and specific worship in order to achieve identity with the deity of the mantra.

Immediately thereafter, having attained identification with that [state], one becomes qualified for initiation and other rites; therein, one should not initiate the unqualified, nor should one reject the qualified. Even one who has been initiated should be tested regarding the bestowal of knowledge, and even if he has acquired knowledge through deception, one should recognize this and disregard him. And in this regard, by means of the splendor of the consecration (*abhiṣeka-vibhava*), [the teacher acts].
[He performs] the worship of the deities and so forth;
because his knowledge is well-practiced,
he bears the responsibility for both his own welfare and the welfare of others.
In that context, the yoga of the practitioner’s status as a guru must be performed, as well as his consecration.
Whatever excellence of the scriptures there may be,
let my activity be for the benefit of that;
furthermore, whatever I have said is for the sake of those who desire it.
And indeed, they have mounted upon our thought.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter. Now,
even for those who abide in lower teachings— including their gurus— immediately upon death,
solely through the application of the descent of power (śaktipāta) described as "the extraction of the dead" (mṛtoddhāra), there occurs that which is called the final consecration (antyasaṃskāra).

The reading is *anyasaṃskāra*. One should perform initiation even for those established in the Higher Teaching (*ūrdhvaśāsana*) who have violated their observances—meaning those whose conduct has perished—and who have not performed penance; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. In that regard, there is the procedure for the "extraction of the deceased" (*mṛtoddhāra*).

All of that which was mentioned must be performed upon the body; the cremation of the corpse is to be done with the *pūrṇāhuti*. However, for the sake of establishing conviction among the ignorant, the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) is performed with a visible sign (*sapratyayām*). As it has been said: "With a visible sign...
[it is so stated].
"Liberation without [this] means is not to be trusted by those who are deluded;

this has been stated for that purpose, and not because it is useful for liberation," and so forth. [In the reading "by the power of knowledge" (*jñānabalāt*), the text says: one should perform the funeral rites upon that corpse by the power of ritual action, knowledge, and yoga.

Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras according to the sequence of withdrawal— from the feet up to the crown of the head— one draws [the deity] in through the lattice-pattern (*jālakrama*),
performing the acts of blocking, piercing, shaking, and so forth; therein, "blocking" is done with the *bindu*, and "piercing" with the seed-syllable of *śakti*.

One should perform the striking with the trident—the first [tool]—and the beating with the Visarga; doing so according to the sequence of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) in the heart, throat, and forehead, the corpse's body thus trembles. Thereafter, having performed the union (yojanikā) with Paramaśiva, one should burn it with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi).
For others who are pure— or for others who are impure—
the initiation of faith (*śrāddhadīkṣā*) should be performed for three days, on the fourth day, every month, or every year.

Having performed the ritual procedure up to the end of the *homa* there, and having placed the food offering (*naivedya*) in one hand, [one should contemplate] its essence as the form of virility (*vīrya*).

Having meditated upon the power (*śakti*) in the form of the object of enjoyment—perceived as having attained identity with the power of enjoyment residing in the bound soul (*paśu*)—one should offer it to the Supreme Lord, the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). In this way, when the state of being an object of enjoyment has ceased, one becomes the Lord himself;
for even by any one of the following—funeral rites, the extraction of the deceased, the *śrāddha* ceremony, or initiation—one achieves the fulfillment of purpose.
Nevertheless, for one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), the abundance of ritual action leads to the abundance of fruit; thus, he should perform everything.

Even for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), this [performance] serves to achieve identification with That (*tanmayībhāva*), just like the daily practice of performance for one who lives. But for the knower of reality (*tattvajñānin*), none of this—from the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) to the ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*)—applies.
The ritual procedure is applicable; his death is a festival day for those belonging to the lineage of that knowledge,

because it completes a portion of the realization, since such a lineage has as its ultimate reality nothing other than a single consciousness— just like a day in the lineage of one who has attained knowledge while still living.

And in all these rituals, such as those for the ancestors (*śrāddha*), the sacrifice to the image (*mūrtiyāga*) is the primary element; this is the teaching of the *Śrīsiddhāmata*, and its procedure will be explained in the *Naimittikaprakāśana*.
Śiva, intent on bestowing grace, favors whoever he chooses by his sovereign power.

He indeed becomes the Supreme Goddess— what wonder is there in this? For the wise man, knowing that the mere application of means is nothing more than her own sovereignty, does not hesitate even when the means are limited.
This entire body, or rather this ocean of worldly existence,
possesses such variety through the power of desire; yet that very [desire],
when [transformed], bestows supreme bliss.
Those who do not know the wide-ranging path of conduct.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Śrāddha Initiation," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.

Next follows another section for the purpose of describing the remaining procedures. In that regard, there is the initiation (*dīkṣā*) intended for the perfection of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for those who are fit for knowledge, and that which is intended for those who are incapable of it.
The initiation for liberation with seed (*savījā mokṣadīkṣā*); when that has been performed, there is the conduct for the remainder of one's life (*ājīvaṃ śeṣavartanam*). As it is said:
"Now the conduct for the remainder is declared, which is useful for those who are living."
This initiation (dīkṣā), which is proclaimed to have many forms ending with the ancestral rite (śrāddha), is of various kinds.
That initiation is for the sake of purification, liberation, enjoyment, or both;
among these, that which is for the accomplishment of purification does not liberate directly.
And for those who have been initiated by both— that which, by virtue of its continuity, directly liberates and possesses seeds— their mode of conduct throughout life is as follows.

"It must be explained to the spiritual sons (*putraka*) and others for the sake of establishing their identity with that. Thus the Guru should instruct. In this regard, the "subsistence on remnants" (*śeṣavartana*) is threefold—daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*)—and it should not be determined here that the last [type] belongs exclusively to the seeker (*sādhaka*). Among these, that which occurs regularly is the daily; the very state of becoming one with that [deity] is the occasional.

The practices conducive to that [liberation] include the performance of the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) every day, observances on festival days (*parvadin*), the sacred thread (*pavitraka*), and so forth. Some maintain that these are also obligatory (*nitya*) because they must be performed at their fixed times; however, others consider them occasional (*naimittika*), even for those who abide by the [Vedic] injunctions.

Some say that the "unfixed" (aniyata) consists of such things as the arrival of the Guru or his circle of disciples, festival days (parva-dina), and the day of attaining knowledge, and so forth. Among these, the fixed worship (niyata-pūjā)—consisting of the twilight rites (sandhyopāsā), worship of the Guru, worship on festival days, and the sacred thread rite (pavitraka)—is necessarily obligatory. The occasional (naimittika) includes the attainment of knowledge and the attainment of the scriptures.
The arrival at the house of the guru or his family; the days of his birth, consecration, and departure (or death, according to another reading); worldly festivals; the exposition of the scriptures;
the beginning, middle, and end; and the vision of the deity.

The gathering (*melaka*), the command in a dream (*svapnājñā*), and the attainment of the fulfillment of the observance (*samayaniṣkṛtilābha*)—these are the specific causes for special worship (*naimittika-viśeṣārcana*). In that regard, one should impart the principal mantra, which possesses vitality (*savīryaka*) and has the essence of the vibration of consciousness (*saṃvittisphuraṇasāra*), to the disciple who has received initiation; this should be done through oral tradition alone (*vaktrāgamena*) and not by means of writing. Thereafter...
For the sake of achieving identification (*tanmayībhāva*) with that [deity], the disciple should practice such identification during the junctions of the day (*sandhyā*).

Through that means, for the sake of attaining the corresponding latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) at all times, he should worship the Supreme Lord every day either on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or in a linga. Therein, on a pleasing sacrificial mound...
Having meditated upon [the deity] as being like a stainless mirror, seeing one's own form reflected therein as if it were an image, inseparable from the circle of the deities to be worshipped,
and having offered flowers, perfumes, incense, water for sipping, food offerings, smoke, lamps, and gifts, along with hymns, songs, and instrumental music within the heart—
Once the assembly of mantras has been invoked, an offering of satisfaction (tarpaṇa) should be performed with flowers,
drinks, food offerings, and incense, according to the strength of one's faith and devotion.
First, there is the satiation with blood and the juices and meat of the blazing mantras, such as Śakti and Nāda; afterwards follows the extensive offering of flowers, incense, and so forth.

"If one does not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for a mantra that has been received, it shall take away half of one's body; so indeed was it said by Śambhu. Thus, one should worship, recite, and offer praise in order to attain, without doubt, the state of being absorbed in that [mantra]. For, as in a mirror, one's own face is seen incessantly.
For one who observes, the ascertainment of its true nature occurs in no time at all; nor is there any sequence here other than the primary absorption into that [nature],
for one who is possessed by absorption into the supreme mantra and whose stain of animal-like tendencies has ceased.

Our teachers maintain that for one whose entire web of bonds has been dissolved by the penetration of the aesthetic savor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*), that alone which dwells within the heart is the supreme object to be attained.
Thus, resting upon the ultimate reality—
That which shines forth as the manifestation of existence—
those who know the secret worship it as the state of the vision of supreme nectar.
Having made the foundational earth purified by the sprinkling of the nectar of wonder, and having taken up from the mind its own natural flowers which abound with their own fragrance,
one proceeds through the sequence of the priceless vessel of worship— the heart of one's own being, overflowing with the nectar of bliss.
I worship you day and night along with the Goddess in the temple of the body.

Incorporating the meaning expressed in these two verses, one should meditate upon the mandala of deities (*devatācakra*). Then follows the display of mudrās; this display of mudrās should be understood as occurring through the mind by way of yoga, through speech by way of mantra-yoga, and through the body by way of its physical configuration. This is followed by recitation (*japa*) and the offering thereof.
The dismissal is performed through identity with awakening (*bodhi*). One should eat the primary food offering (*naivedya*) oneself, or else throw everything into water.

"Living beings were initiated long ago by Śambhu, who descended as the Lord of Fishes (*mīnanātha*)," so say those who know the scriptures. Indeed, all creatures have been previously initiated by means of the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Those who know the scriptures maintain that if one consumes [the meat of] cats, mice, dogs, and the like, suspicion arises which leads to hell;

therefore, even a knower (*jñānin*), out of a desire to favor the world, should not act in such a way, nor should he remain having abandoned the world—this is the *sthaṇḍilayāga* (sacrifice on the bare ground). Now, regarding the *liṅga*, there is no [word "not" (*na*)] there.
Regarding "with secret mantras" (*rahasyamantraiḥ*): as it has been stated, these mantras taught in the *Ūrdhva-śāstra* are not established [in common practice].
For one should exclude them, since they bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*) precisely by virtue of their secrecy.

"For those who bestow accomplishment characterized by mastery over the entry into the majesty of the bliss of one's own vigor, their externality consists in the loss of form. Thus, one should especially install a manifest *liṅga* among those previously installed.
One should perform the worship according to the sequence of invocation and dismissal as the foundational basis. In that regard, [one should worship] the body of the Guru,
one’s own body, the body of Śakti, the book of the secret scriptures,
the vessel of the heroes (vīrapātra), the rosary, and the weapon.
[The reading: One should worship the Liṅga made of clay, pearl, gold, or a mirror fashioned from pleasing materials such as flowers and fragrant substances.
[Regarding the word "should worship" (arcayet), there is this specific distinction here:]
One should not fashion a linga made of stone produced by an artisan;
however, among those made of metal, one should avoid any other except that which is made of gold.
"And in this matter, no inference or other means of knowledge is of any use;

for that which is illumined by mantras of noble potency is indeed fruit-bearing. And in that regard, through the power of the support alone, there occurs the increasingly superior accomplishment of mantras; thus, each preceding [support]...

The teachers of the scriptures maintain that because mantras conform to the qualities of their substratum, whatever is the primary object in each respective case, that is the principal element therein; in all instances, the supreme consecration is precisely the conceit of non-difference from the Supreme Lord.

Now, the procedure for the festivals (*parva*). In this regard, the festival is sixfold—due to its completion (*pūraṇa*) and its ritual injunction (*vidhi*)—namely: the general (*sāmānya*), the general-general (*sāmānyasāmānya*), the general-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), the particular-general (*viśeṣasāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and the particular-particular (*viśeṣaviśeṣa*). Among these, [the first occurs] month after month.
The first and fifth days are common; the fourth, eighth, ninth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both fortnights are common-to-the-common for both of these lunar mansions.
Regarding the conjunction of the specific lunar days (*tithi*) and asterisms (*nakṣatra*) to be described below, there is both a general and a specific rule:

the first part of the night of Mārgaśīrṣa occurs on the ninth day of the dark fortnight; the middle of the night of Pauṣa occurs on the ninth day of the dark fortnight; the middle of the night of Māgha occurs on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight; [and so on] for Phālguna.
The middle of the day on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra; the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha;

the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Jyaiṣṭha; the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha; the first day of Śrāvaṇa; the forenoon of Bhādrapada; and the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada.

The midday of the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, and the first part of the night on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika are special festivals (*viśeṣaparva*). [The conjunctions are: Citrā with the Moon, Maghā with Jupiter, Tiṣya with the Moon, Pūrvaphālgunī with Mercury, Śravaṇa with Venus, and Śatabhiṣaj with the Moon.
"Malādityau, Rohiṇīśukrau, Viśākhābṛhaspatī, and Śravaṇacandrau"—
if these occur in the sequence beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, corresponding respectively to their order, excluding Āśvayuja, then [the conjunction is auspicious].
This is a specific distinction. If it is a different specific [time] occurring on another lunar day (*parvan*), then they call that "subsequent" (*anuparva*).

Furthermore, in the conjunction of a lunar mansion (*bha*) and a planet (*graha*), the specific time (*velā*) is not the primary factor, because the distinction is obtained from the lunar day (*tithi*) itself. However, the persistence of the time for the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) on the day of the *parvan* is primary, due to the predominance of the subsequent sacrifice.
The *anuyāga* (subsequent sacrifice) of all sacrifices (*parvayāgānām*) is the *mūrtiyāga* (sacrifice to the embodied forms).
Indeed, the *mūrtiyāga* is traditionally taught to be fivefold, as stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
"It is solitary (*kevala*), paired (*yāmala*), mixed (*miśra*), joined with the wheel (*cakrayuk*), and the assembly of heroes (*vīrasaṃkara*)."
It is pure when mixed with pure gurus alone; however, it is further [mixed] by gurus.
That [union] is again twofold: as a couple with the practitioner and so forth, or with his wife; or else through union with a courtesan acquired by purchase.
The Cakriṇī and other goddesses shall now be described according to their appropriate association with Śaktis;
through union with them, the sacrifice performed in the circle (cakra) bestows all fruits.

"A sacrifice performed with all [of these] together is called the *vīrasaṃkara*. Thus, "wheel-sacrifice" (*cakrayāga*) is a synonym. In that regard, the primary objects of worship in the wheel-sacrifice—specifically—are the Guru, his fellow-initiates, those with their lineages, the knowers of reality (*tattvavid*), virgins, low-caste women (*antyā*), courtesans, or young women who are knowers of reality.

In its entirety: there, in the center, the Guru; then, according to the sequence of that enclosure, from the Guru down to the *samayin*, in the order of Vīra and Śakti, or by way of the arrangement of the *cakra* or the arrangement in rows, he should sit; thereafter, with perfumes, incense, flowers, and so forth.

Then, one should worship in sequence; having meditated upon the vessel as the form of Sadāśiva and having filled it with liquor (āsava) visualized as the nectar of Śakti, one should worship the consuming Śakti therein as Śiva. Having performed the satiation of the circle of deities (*devatācakra*) by means of that very [liquor], one should meditate upon the union of the triad consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva.

Following the sequence of entering the coverings (*āvaraṇa*), one should perform the primary satisfaction for liberation and enjoyment both externally and internally; then again, by the sequence of re-absorption—as it has been said:
"By the yoga of re-absorption, there is a further entry within."

"Up to the presence of the Guru, that twofold complete circumambulation is so called. Thus, the complete circumambulation nourishes the wheel (*cakra*). Therein, in the foundation (*ādhāra*)—as it has been stated, "the libation (*tarpaṇa*) must be joined with the foundation, not devoid of the foundation."

"Without a vessel there is no [proper] offering, and the rays of light are not satisfied. Thus, having placed the vessel consisting of the universe and having gratified the circle of deities, one should satisfy oneself with that which has been offered.
In the absence of a vessel, a "bhadra" (auspicious) shell turned upward, or the hand in the form of a vessel held auspiciously by the right hand, [should be used].

With two [hands] raised above and joined at the right, forming a *vellita-śukti* (twisted shell) mudrā, the *vetālas* and *guhyakas* are satisfied by the falling drops, while Bhairava is satisfied by the continuous stream.
No one should be allowed entry here; if anyone enters through negligence, one must not show them any consideration once they have entered.

One should again perform the wheel-sacrifice (*cakrayāga*) with double the [previous] scale; then, one should scatter snacks, food, and so forth as desired in front, or in a secret house. One should unite everyone with the name of the deity, omitting specific personal names. This is the *vīrasaṃkarayāga*. Then, at the conclusion, [one should honor them] with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), betel, clothing, and other such items.

"One should satisfy [the deities]"—this Mūrtiyāga (Image Sacrifice) is the most essential. Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, by worshipping during festival days through the Mūrtiyāga, attains within a year the fruit described for a *putraka* (spiritual son), even without performing the *saṃdhyā* rites and so forth. This is the rule for the elderly, the wealthy, and women.
When the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred, the disciple should be instructed by the Guru.

Now follows the ritual for the sacred thread (*pavitraka*). This is performed according to the prescribed rules in the *Śrīratnamālā*, the *Triśiromata*, the *Śrīsiddhāmata*, and other such texts, and it fulfills the command of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarājñāpūraka*). Regarding the phrase "fulfilling the command," as it has been said:
In the *Tantrāloka*,
it is said that the King of Serpents, rendered unconscious by the sleep induced by the poison arising from the churning of the ocean of milk,
did not remain in his own abode during the rainy season.
But for a hundred years, subsisting only on air and using only a sacred thread,
he worshipped the divine lord Bhairava with tenfold intensity.
And he informed that gratified Lord: "O Master, I am not able to dwell in my own abode in Pātāla"; and the Supreme Lord [replied] to him:
He arranged the Naga to rest upon the seat of his own matted locks;
thereafter, he was borne upon his head by the entire host of gods.
Therefore, preceded by the sacrifice, one should perform that purification upon the head of Maheśvara, upon all the deities, and upon oneself.
Ten billion acts of worship are not equal to the performance of the Pavitrārohaṇa;
initiation is in vain, knowledge is in vain, and even the propitiation of the Guru is in vain [without it].
"Without this [rite of] the purifier (*pavitra*) and so forth, the Lord does not accept [the offering], by the command of Śiva. And this has been stated in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"Without the purifier, everything is fruitless."
Thus it is said. In that regard, the *pavitraka* rite should be performed from the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha until the full moon day of the *kula*.

Regarding this, the experts of the *Śrīnityātantra* maintain that the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika fulfills the *kulacakra* and the *nityācakra*. The experts of the *Śrībhairavakulormi* maintain that it is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha.

"The fifteenth day at the end of the sun's southern course," so say the knowers of the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*. There, having worshipped the deity with all his might and having gratified him with oblations, one should offer the *pavitraka* (sacred thread), which may be fashioned from gold, pearls, and gems, down to even those made of cloth, thread, cotton, or *kuśa* grass. And that... [k: and then...]

[The reading: For the deity, there are four purificatory threads (*pavitraka*): one with knots numbering the [sixteen] principles (*tattva*), one with knots numbering the words (*pada*), the worlds (*bhuvana*), the phonemes (*varṇa*), and the mantras; one reaching to the knees, another reaching to the navel, another reaching to the throat, and another on the head.
And one should offer [the thread] to the Guru by meditating upon his form as being complete with all the paths; to the remaining [deities], one [thread] each.

Then a great festival should be performed for four months, seven days, or three days—these are the primary, secondary, and alternative rites. If there is the means, the *pavitraka* rite should be performed every month, or else once every four months.

Alternatively, one should recite the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) even once for its non-performance; for even a knower (*jñānin*), even if he possesses wealth, incurs sin through non-performance, because by failing to act out of knowledge tainted by greed, he falls into the censure of knowledge.
This occurs when, despite having attained higher realization, one defiles the teaching of the Supreme Lord.
"In that case, there is expiation," according to this statement.
Such is the procedure for the *pavitraka* rite.

Since the proximity of the circle of deities (*devatācakra*) occurs everywhere— whether at the attainment of knowledge and so forth, or even at the conclusion of a worldly festival— there is an intensification of the expansion of consciousness; therefore, by reflecting upon such an intensification,
one should perform a corresponding special rite during the secondary sacrifice (*anuyāga*) and other such occasions.
Now, the method of exposition:

One should request a teacher who is fully accomplished in all the scriptures for the purpose of exposition; that teacher, in turn, should expound the scripture—suitable for the specific refinement required—to either his own disciple or even to the disciple of another.

Even while remaining within a lower teaching, one whose heart is imbued with the possibility of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) manifested through the diversity of the Lord’s will may, out of compassion, provide instruction— excluding the disclosure of the vital secrets— to those who are seated on a lower seat and are intent upon that [teaching]. In that regard, for those situated on a lower seat who are devoted to it...
An exposition being delivered by those who have restrained their speech, mind, and body becomes fruitful. First,
having drawn or mentally conceived a square base for a lotus on ground smeared with fragrant substances and the like,
one should worship Vāgīśī in the center of the lotus, and Gaṇapati and the Guru on the left and right sides.
One should visualize the deity of the kalpa to be explained within the foundational lotus (or, according to the reading *adharapadme*, the lower lotus).

Then, by means of the application of the general water-offering vessel (*sāmānyārghapātra*), one should satisfy the maṇḍala. Thereafter, one should expound the text of the chapters and sentences of the sūtra, ensuring that it is not contradicted by what precedes or follows.
In accordance with the logical principles of the treatises concerning *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, *prasaṅga*, *samuccaya*, *vikalpa*, and so forth:

*tantra* is that which provides assistance simultaneously, according to the "lamp on the threshold" analogy; *āvṛtti* is that which provides assistance separately, according to the "plate for eating" analogy; and *prasaṅga* is the drawing out of an undesirable consequence.
"Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the connection of multiple actions, agents, and relations; conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows from verbal cognition but is devoid of a real object.
Having properly formulated the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and having properly refuted it, he establishes the thesis (*sādhya*).
Explaining the *Tātparyavṛtti*,

one should expound the end of the chapter without adding anything further; therein, at the conclusion of each subject, having performed the libation and worship, one should dismiss the seat of the Vidyā (*vidyāpīṭha*), smear the ground, and cast it into deep water.
Thus is the procedure for exposition. Now follows the expiation for transgressions of the observance (*samaya*).
Although there is no need for penance or the like for one who is established in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), nevertheless, it [is required] merely on account of the conduct (*caryā*).

To show favor to those who are destined for liberation, he should demonstrate the path of conduct (*ācāravartanī*). However, one who does not know reality, whose enjoyment and liberation depend solely upon his practice,
becomes a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*) for a hundred years if he transgresses the rules (*samaya*) and fails to perform the requisite expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Thus the rule for expiation is to be stated: in that regard, there is no expiation for the killing of a woman; however, in other cases, having understood the relative strength [of the offense], one should repeat the unbroken *Bhagavatī Mālinī* from one recitation up to three hundred thousand.
Until doubt and wavering have ceased, at their conclusion there is a special worship; therein also is the wheel-sacrifice (*cakrayāga*), for that indeed subsists everywhere.
This is the rule for the expiation of transgressions of the observance (*samaya*).
Now follows the procedure for the worship of the Guru.

At the conclusion of all sacrifices, once the sacrifice has been withdrawn, one should perform the worship of the Guru on the following day; for previously he was gratified as a subordinate part of the ritual, and not as the primary object—therefore, one performs that worship now with primacy.
Thinking, "He becomes bound by the bond of authority," one should perform that [rite] in every way.
There, having drawn a svastika mandala and placed a golden seat upon it, having worshipped the entire path there,
having empowered that seat with him, and having performed worship for him, [one should perform] the libation (tarpaṇa).

Having offered the food, the sacrificial fee, and himself, and having requested the remains of the offering (naivedya-ucchiṣṭa), bowed down, and consumed it himself, he should perform the worship of the maṇḍala (cakrapūjā).
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the Guru.
By performing the daily and occasional rites while remaining free from the constraints of the scriptures,
one is liberated through mere conduct alone, even without the practice of knowledge and yoga.
Śiva has declared that the self is independent, possessing the power of reality and free from desire;
it is the friend of conduct, O Jinajanman.
Whatever desire one has for becoming.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Remaining Conduct," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.

Thus, the entire range of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites has been described. Now, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of this very scripture (*āgama*) is being stated. In that regard, [it concerns] the universe, which consists of nothing but consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), and consciousness itself.
When it is established that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is essentially verbalization (*śabdanātmaka*),

then the very act of reflecting upon every object residing within the entire universe, as well as the diversity of the relationship between actions and their fruits inherent therein, is itself the scripture; thus, everything is non-different from the nature of the Supreme Lord.
In reality, the composition of a scripture leads to a single result and is intended for a single qualified recipient;

however, it is solely through the power of the Supreme Lord’s will and destiny that people become established in various parts of it. Some are established in scriptures such as the Vedas and Āgamas, which consist of reflections on duality appropriate to *māyā*, while others are likewise [established in other parts].

Thus, by means of the conceit of liberation, some [adhere] to the Sāṃkhya, Vaiṣṇava, and other scriptures; others, however, to the Śaiva Siddhānta and so forth, which consist essentially in the reflective awareness of the nature of Śiva as distinct [from all else];
and still others to the Mataṅga-tantra and other scriptures, which consist essentially in the reflective awareness of the Supreme Lord as comprising all things.

The reading is "in the Mata and other scriptures. However, there are some— though very few— who, within the sequence of the venerable Trika scripture, which consists of the self-reflection of the essential nature of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), who is composed of the supreme consciousness that is absolute freedom devoid of all limitations, [proceed as follows].

[The meaning is that for the sake of the growth of the entire triad of scriptures existing above, there is a reliance on each preceding one, just as the construction of a staircase is for the purpose of ascending; "abandonment" means leaping over after having first ascended it, or rather, not ascending it at all. However, some [proceed] by way of abandoning each preceding one in succession.

Or by transgression— thus, the accomplishment of a single result follows from a single scripture alone. Even in the doctrine of difference (the Nyāya view), although all scriptures are the products of a single Lord,
their validity remains established, because the basis for validity— namely, correspondence with a portion of reality— is present.
Since the lack of contradiction and the absence of non-occurrence are equal, their mutual sublation is ineffective due to the difference in their respective objects;
it is like the distinction between the killing of a Brahmin and its prohibition, which constitutes a specific refinement and a superior refinement.
Regarding what was stated as "the excellence of the latent impressions" (*saṃskārātiśaya*):
"Among the various fruits— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— which differ according to whether they are complete or incomplete, the Śāmbhava Āgama is the singular means."

"In that case, because it bestows various fruits due to the distinctness of the objects [of practice], even the instruction of diverse means would not entail contradiction. In the absence of that [qualification], there is non-eligibility in certain cases; this is the same as in the case of the different stages of life (*āśrama*), as stated in the *Tantrāloka*: [text follows].

Just as even within a single tradition such as the Veda, there are various further purificatory rites for those entering different stages of life (āśrama), so too here [in this system], there are rites such as the extraction of the sectarian mark (liṅga-uddhṛti) and others.

"And just as in that case one does not obtain the fruit of the subsequent stage of life from the preceding stage of life, so too in the Pañcarātra and other systems, one does not attain the nature of Śiva. Thus, superiority [is established] there precisely because of the excellence of the fruit.
Although the Upaniṣads have different authors, they are nonetheless composed by an omniscient being;
as it is stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
"Therefore, its status as preceded by an omniscient being is established through this [scripture]."
Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the existence of many omniscient beings in the past.
Adorned by hundreds of established instances of worldly enjoyment, liberation, and their causes,
this Bhairava, the Supreme Lord, has that very reflective awareness as His essential nature.
Then, through the connection of parts and sub-parts, that mutual renown—
whether relying upon scripture or otherwise— being expanded, causes the worlds to engage in worldly transaction.

"In the same way, from childhood onwards, all virtuous people who abide by the laws of worldly conduct rely exclusively upon the primordial Śaiva scripture. Thus, because it contains well-reasoned meanings both stated therein and beyond those [explicit statements], the authority of the scriptures is established even if they are eternal.
[From each of those, the agent is the remainder. To that extent,
positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), perception (*adhyakṣa*), and so forth [the meaning of "perception and so forth" being direct perception and the like],
must necessarily be accepted, because the validity of those [cognitions] is rooted in them.

The meaning is: "because it is rooted in common consensus. For the statement "I see real silver" has its validity precisely through the consensus of others, such as goldsmiths and the like (the word *prāmāṇyam* is to be supplied).
Consensus itself is the tradition (*āgama*); it is of a certain kind, for the activity regarding the fruits of the scriptures is fourfold.
Regarding those which are the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), he states the classification of their objects with the words beginning "some" (*kācit*) and so forth.

[The aim] having visible results is for one who desires to eat; because this is well-known even to a child, activity occurs in various instances [without formal inquiry], since at that time there is an absence of the methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as is the case during the stage of youth.

Even its existence [the meaning of "its existence" is the state of positive and negative concomitance] is ineffective; however, let that [existence] be established by taking common consensus as its foundation [it is stated with the concession "let it be," because without establishing it through common consensus, no effect whatsoever can be proven]. For some specific effect, some...

Regarding the unseen nature of the Veda: it was stated that the first section (Pūrvakāṇḍa) is twofold, distinguished by the seen and the unseen; therein, the results of *anvīkṣikī* and so forth are seen, while those beginning with *Karmamīmāṃsā* and extending to the portion of the Upaniṣads are unseen, and so on.

The passage ending with "bestowing the fruit of isolation" (*kaivalyaphaladā*) shows that even within the *Uttarakāṇḍa*, there is a twofold division based on initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the knowledge of self-luminous, independent awakening (*svaprakāśasvatantraprabodhajñāna*).

[This is indicated by the words] beginning with "certain" (*kācit*): "A certain [initiation] bestows the fruit of the dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) or the isolation of the person (*puruṣakaivalya*)."

That [practice], which bestows the fruit of equality with Śiva and culminates in oneness—[meaning that it is both seen and unseen]—is of many kinds for each [individual]. Thus, in this world filled with manifold renown, whoever is destined to be [meaning: whoever is to be united with the fruit], he [attains it].
One merely conceives such a well-known reputation as being forcibly established within the heart; thus, for an empty person— born ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done—
who has these attachments to philosophical tenets been bestowed by whom?

Thus ends the position of the theory of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For one who accepts some established usage regarding the linguistic expressions of a living being as authoritative, the authority of scripture (*āgama*) must necessarily be admitted;
therefore, that scripture should be relied upon wherein the most excellent fruit is found—enough said of further elaboration.
Discerning that just as [reality] shines by virtue of being the ultimate truth of the light of consciousness, so too does one perceive it,
the wise ones [attain] the reflective awareness of the manifestation of the all-encompassing consciousness.
Take refuge in the essence of the scripture, whose nature is unsurpassed.
I am that very person who is free from doubt regarding the legal proceedings established by his firm reputation; therefore, act according to my word.
Paramaśiva is established by way of conventional usage.
When people are free from doubt regarding worldly transactions established by their own firm consensus,
then they have transcended the world.
Paramaśiva is established through conventional usage.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Authority of the Āgamas," in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.

Now, this entire system of worship is described according to the venerable Kaulika method for those qualified aspirants in whom such firm latent impressions have begun to manifest; regarding this, it has been said:
In the *Yogasaṃcāra* and other texts, it is stated:
"Brahman is bliss; it resides in that body in three ways, established at the end of the three [channels]. [Alternatively:
"established at the beginning, middle, and end of the three."]
Thus is the reading elsewhere. There is also an explanation based on the following meaning: "Of these three, two are auxiliaries; therein, the fruit is the other, which consists of those [two]."
Because of his abandonment of the practice of celibacy, they were deprived of bliss.
The officiating priests of the wheel, with the exception of artificial food that causes bliss, [fall] into both types of terrible hells; therefore, one should adhere to this rule.

In this state, the *kulayāga* is sixfold: external, in the *śakti*, in one's own body, in the couple (*yāmala*), in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and in consciousness (*saṃvit*). Among these, each subsequent one is superior and each preceding one is inferior; this is for the sake of [the practitioner’s] preference. For one who desires supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the second, fourth, and fifth must be performed in every way, while the sixth—

For one seeking liberation, the primary [observance] is that; yet the second and subsequent ones must also be performed as occasion demands, according to what is possible, for the sake of fulfilling the injunctions. In this regard, the external sacrificial ground, the vessel full of bliss, the hero’s cup, and the saffron-colored cloth—though previously mentioned—are also required here.

Or [the ritual may be performed] with the *liṅga* and so forth. In that case, having attained purity simply by resting in full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*) without regard for the performance of bathing and other such rites, one should first contemplate the unification of the body of vital breath (*prāṇa*) with consciousness (*saṃvit*).
And because consciousness is of the nature of Paramaśiva, one should recite the mantra twenty-seven times while facing upward.

In the forms of the Heart, the Secret, and the Embodiment, through both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order, there is the complete fulfillment of the entire path within the Supreme Lord— whether in His state of non-supremacy (aparatva), in His intermediate state (parāparatva), or even in His state of supremacy (paratva). For instance, the twenty-seven principles beginning with Māyā, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, the Guṇas, the Intellect (dhī), and so forth, down to the Earth, are included therein, because the Kalās and the other categories are subsumed within them.

Even regarding the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*), its state as both supreme and non-supreme (*parāpara*) consists precisely of twenty-seven forms of the five Brahmans— namely, the qualities of *sadyas*, *ajāta*, *bhava*, *udbhava*, and so forth—
as stated by the venerable Lakuleśa and other masters. For even in its supreme state (*paratve*), the Supreme Lord indeed possesses five powers.
Each power likewise possesses five forms; thus there are twenty-five powers. These are mutually inseparable from one another, and that [unity] is itself inseparable from its divisions.
In this way, through this pervasion consisting of twenty-seven forms, one should [perceive] the flame of the fire of consciousness, which takes the form of intellect and vital breath.
By the mere act of uttering [the mantra] once, one should bind [the object] such that it becomes bound to Paramaśiva himself; nothing other than that [Śiva] then moves toward it.
Through the piercing of the wheel of the senses presided over by such an intellect, [one binds] that which stands before one.

One should cause even the sacrificial materials, the house, the directions, the supports, and so forth, to become identical with that [consciousness]. Then, one should fill the *argha* vessel by means of the very pervasion of the binding of the crest-lock (*śikhābandha*) and worship it; likewise, one should worship the sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) with its droplets and with its essence through the union of the left ring finger and the thumb. One should worship and satisfy the wheel of mantras within the wheels of the body.
And from that [comes] *prāṇānta*. Then, upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), one should fashion a seat consisting of a trident and ending with the three powers (*śaktitraya*).

Indeed, in the case of the *sārṇa* [mantra], one should fashion the seat ending with *māyā* and the letter *au*; and in the case of the letter *au*, one should fashion the seat ending with the three powers. Above that is the object of worship (*yājyā*), whose nature is *vimarśa*.

By uttering the word "Śakti" just once, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the container and the contained; then, within that very consciousness which serves as the container, one should perceive the universe, and [realize] that too is composed of consciousness.

In this way, there occurs a mutual encapsulation (saṃpuṭībhāva) of the universe by consciousness and of that consciousness by the universe, for everything arisen from consciousness is situated right there.

Since the universe culminates therein, and consciousness arises from the object of knowledge and rests in that very same place, the reality of consciousness is obtained through these two forms of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭībhāva*). [The reading "this much is the reality of consciousness" (*etāvat tattvaṃ saṃvittattvam*) appears to be the correct one. Thus it has been said:
"Having encapsulated the emanation...

and so forth. Then, having offered the perfumes, incense, wine, flowers, and so on, ending with one's own prostration, and having performed the recitation while resting in one's own [divine] state, one should withdraw [the visualization] and cast it into the water.
Thus concludes the external sacrifice.
